title: Module 16: Emerging Directions
text:
Health Informatics in R · Part IV: Advanced Topics · Module 16 of 16
The final module looks at where health informatics is heading: large language models for documentation and coding, FHIR + generative AI patterns, agentic AI (plan-over-tools over a claims book), federated approaches that analyze data without moving it, and the ethics, regulation, and equity questions that decide whether any of it should ship.

title: Module 16: Emerging Directions
text:
Learning objectives
By the end of this module you will be able to:

Describe how LLMs are applied to clinical documentation and autocoding.
Implement the extract → structure → validate pattern for LLM-assisted coding (with a deterministic mock so it runs offline).
Explain the FHIR + generative AI integration pattern.
Build a small agentic controller: named tools, a fixed plan, intent routing, and an audit trail — with the LLM allowed only to rephrase numbers.
Demonstrate a federated computation that shares statistics, not records.
Run a basic equity/bias check on subgroup performance.

title: Module 16: Emerging Directions
text:
Dataset
The synthetic EHR plus the clinical-note style text from Module 10. The “LLM” here is a deterministic mock so the notebook runs without external API calls; the pattern is identical to a real LLM integration.
The agentic section uses a compact synthetic claims book (the shape of Module 13’s member-year table) so the controller has tools to call — still offline, still no PHI.

library(dplyr)
library(tibble)
library(jsonlite)
library(lubridate)

# --- Self-contained synthetic EHR generator (identical to earlier parts) ---

# This function generates a synthetic electronic health record (EHR) dataset with several tables.
make_synthetic_ehr <- function(n_patients = 200, seed = 42) {
  set.seed(seed)  # Random seed for reproducibility

  # Define some sample names
  first <- c("Ava","Liam","Noah","Mia","Zoe","Omar","Ivan","Sara","Leo","Nina",
             "Ruth","Kai","Yara","Theo","Ida","Sam","Ana","Eli","Rex","Uma")
  last  <- c("Khan","Ortiz","Chen","Diaz","Patel","Ali","Brown","Nash","Reed","Vega",
             "Cole","Frost","Grant","Hale","Iqbal","Jain","Kerr","Lund","Mora","Park")

  # Generate patient demographics
  ages <- sample(18:89, n_patients, replace = TRUE)
  patients <- tibble(
    patient_id = sprintf("P%d", 1000 + 0:(n_patients - 1)),
    given_name = sample(first, n_patients, replace = TRUE),
    family_name = sample(last, n_patients, replace = TRUE),
    sex = sample(c("male", "female"), n_patients, replace = TRUE, prob = c(0.49, 0.51)),
    age = ages,
    birth_year = 2026 - ages
  )

  # Generate random healthcare encounters for each patient
  enc_types <- c("ambulatory", "emergency", "inpatient", "wellness")
  enc_rows <- vector("list", n_patients)
  eid <- 0
  for (i in seq_len(n_patients)) {
    pid <- patients$patient_id[i]
    n_enc <- sample(1:4, 1)  # Each patient gets 1-4 encounters
    day <- sample(0:(365 * 3 - 1), n_enc, replace = TRUE)  # Random day in a 3-year window
    ids <- sprintf("E%05d", eid + seq_len(n_enc))
    eid <- eid + n_enc
    enc_rows[[i]] <- tibble(
      encounter_id = ids,
      patient_id = pid,
      encounter_type = sample(enc_types, n_enc, replace = TRUE, prob = c(0.55, 0.15, 0.10, 0.20)),
      date = as.Date("2023-01-01") + day
    )
  }
  encounters <- bind_rows(enc_rows)

  # Generate observations for each encounter
  obs_defs <- tribble(
    ~observation,               ~unit,   ~lo,  ~hi,
    "Body height",               "cm",    150,  195,
    "Body weight",                "kg",    50,   110,
    "Systolic blood pressure",   "mmHg",  100,  165,
    "Heart rate",                 "/min",  55,   100,
    "Hemoglobin A1c",             "%",     4.8,  9.5
  )
  obs_rows <- vector("list", nrow(encounters))
  for (i in seq_len(nrow(encounters))) {
    e <- encounters[i, ]
    keep <- runif(nrow(obs_defs)) < 0.7  # 70% chance that the observation appears for the encounter
    if (any(keep)) {
      d <- obs_defs[keep, ]
      obs_rows[[i]] <- tibble(
        encounter_id = e$encounter_id, patient_id = e$patient_id,
        observation = d$observation, value = round(runif(nrow(d), d$lo, d$hi), 1),
        unit = d$unit, date = e$date
      )
    }
  }
  observations <- bind_rows(obs_rows) %>%
    mutate(observation_id = sprintf("O%06d", row_number())) %>%
    relocate(observation_id)

  # Generate conditions (diagnoses) for each patient
  cond_pool <- c("Essential hypertension", "Type 2 diabetes mellitus", "Asthma",
                 "Acute bronchitis", "Major depressive disorder", "Osteoarthritis",
                 "Chronic kidney disease", "Anemia")
  cond_rows <- vector("list", n_patients)
  for (i in seq_len(n_patients)) {
    pid <- patients$patient_id[i]
    # Each patient has 0-3 random conditions
    n_c <- sample(0:3, 1)
    if (n_c > 0) cond_rows[[i]] <- tibble(patient_id = pid, condition = sample(cond_pool, n_c, replace = FALSE))
  }
  conditions <- bind_rows(cond_rows) %>%
    mutate(condition_id = sprintf("C%05d", row_number())) %>%
    relocate(condition_id)

  # Generate medications for each patient
  med_pool <- c("Lisinopril", "Metformin", "Albuterol", "Atorvastatin", "Sertraline",
                "Amoxicillin", "Ibuprofen", "Hydrochlorothiazide")
  med_rows <- vector("list", n_patients)
  for (i in seq_len(n_patients)) {
    pid <- patients$patient_id[i]
    # Each patient takes 0-3 random medications
    n_m <- sample(0:3, 1)
    if (n_m > 0) med_rows[[i]] <- tibble(patient_id = pid, medication = sample(med_pool, n_m, replace = FALSE))
  }
  medications <- bind_rows(med_rows) %>%
    mutate(medication_id = sprintf("M%05d", row_number())) %>%
    relocate(medication_id)

  # Return all generated tables in a list
  list(patients = patients, encounters = encounters, observations = observations,
       conditions = conditions, medications = medications)
}

# Generate the synthetic dataset and print the number of rows in each table.
ehr <- make_synthetic_ehr()
cat("Tables:", paste(sprintf("%s (%d)", names(ehr), sapply(ehr, nrow)), collapse = ", "), "\n")

Tables: patients (200), encounters (507), observations (1746), conditions (302), medications (313)

title: Module 16: Emerging Directions
section: 16.1 LLMs for clinical documentation and coding
text:
16.1 LLMs for clinical documentation and coding
Large Language Models (LLMs) are increasingly utilized in clinical documentation workflows for a range of applications:

Ambient scribing: Transforming real-time physician-patient conversations into structured clinical notes.
Summarization: Creating concise summaries from lengthy, complex patient charts to assist clinician review.
Autocoding: Automatically suggesting diagnostic (ICD) or clinical finding (SNOMED) codes from unstructured text, e.g., physician notes.

A robust and safe engineering approach for integrating LLM outputs in healthcare follows this pipeline:

Extract — The LLM identifies relevant information or codes from the source text.
Structure — The extracted outputs are converted into a predefined, structured format (such as JSON with explicit fields).
Validate — Deterministic rules or lookups check whether the suggested outputs (e.g., codes) are syntactically valid, allowed, and sufficiently confident.
Human review — Qualified clinicians review, accept, or edit the LLM’s proposals before they’re entered into the record.

This ensures that the LLM only proposes outputs; automated checks and expert review prevent propagation of errors. Raw, unchecked model suggestions should never be finalized without such validation and human oversight.

# Define a codebook that maps clinical terms to ICD-10 and SNOMED codes.
CODE_BOOK <- list(
  "hypertension" = list(icd10 = "I10", snomed = "38341003"),
  "type 2 diabetes" = list(icd10 = "E11.9", snomed = "44054006"),
  "asthma" = list(icd10 = "J45.909", snomed = "195967001"),
  "depression" = list(icd10 = "F32.9", snomed = "370143000")
)

# Simulates an LLM that proposes medical codes based on input note text.
#
# Args:
#   note_text (character): Clinical note text.
#
# Returns:
#   list: A list containing code suggestions the LLM might return.
#         Each suggestion includes the mention, ICD-10 code, SNOMED code,
#         and a model confidence score.
mock_llm_autocode <- function(note_text) {
  text <- tolower(note_text)
  suggestions <- list()
  # For each term in the code book, check if it appears in the note.
  for (term in names(CODE_BOOK)) {
    if (grepl(term, text, fixed = TRUE)) {
      # If found, add a suggestion with a high (simulated) confidence.
      codes <- CODE_BOOK[[term]]
      suggestions[[length(suggestions) + 1]] <- list(
        mention = term, icd10 = codes$icd10, snomed = codes$snomed, model_confidence = 0.9
      )
    }
  }
  list(suggested_codes = suggestions)
}

# Example patient note for demonstration.
note <- paste(
  "58 y/o with history of hypertension and type 2 diabetes presents for",
  "follow-up. Screen for depression."
)

# Get mock model output for the note.
raw <- mock_llm_autocode(note)

cat("Raw model output (as an LLM would return):\n")

Raw model output (as an LLM would return):

cat(toJSON(raw, auto_unbox = TRUE, pretty = TRUE))

{
  "suggested_codes": [
    {
      "mention": "hypertension",
      "icd10": "I10",
      "snomed": "38341003",
      "model_confidence": 0.9
    },
    {
      "mention": "type 2 diabetes",
      "icd10": "E11.9",
      "snomed": "44054006",
      "model_confidence": 0.9
    },
    {
      "mention": "depression",
      "icd10": "F32.9",
      "snomed": "370143000",
      "model_confidence": 0.9
    }
  ]
}



Milestone 1 — validate model output before trusting it
Before using the LLM’s output, we must rigorously validate the suggested codes. This includes checking each suggestion for acceptable ICD-10 codes and ensuring that the model’s confidence is above a minimum threshold. Only suggestions that meet these criteria should be considered for clinician review; others should be flagged for further inspection and never automatically entered into the clinical record.

# Define a set of ICD-10 codes that are considered valid for further review.
VALID_ICD <- c("I10", "E11.9", "J45.909", "F32.9", "J20.9")

# Validates model-suggested codes before they are sent for clinician review.
#
# Args:
#   model_output (list): Model output containing 'suggested_codes', where each suggestion is a
#                         list with fields including 'icd10' and 'model_confidence'.
#   min_conf (double): Minimum model confidence required to accept a suggestion.
#
# Returns:
#   list(accepted, flagged): tibble of accepted suggestions (valid code + confident)
#                             and tibble of flagged suggestions (invalid code or low confidence)
validate_autocode <- function(model_output, min_conf = 0.5) {
  accepted <- list()
  flagged <- list()
  for (s in model_output$suggested_codes) {
    # Accept the suggestion if the code is in the allowed set and confidence is high enough.
    ok <- (s$icd10 %in% VALID_ICD) && (s$model_confidence >= min_conf)
    if (ok) accepted[[length(accepted) + 1]] <- s else flagged[[length(flagged) + 1]] <- s
  }
  list(
    accepted = if (length(accepted)) bind_rows(lapply(accepted, as_tibble)) else tibble(),
    flagged = if (length(flagged)) bind_rows(lapply(flagged, as_tibble)) else tibble()
  )
}

# Run validation on the mock model's output.
result <- validate_autocode(raw)
accepted <- result$accepted
flagged <- result$flagged

cat("ACCEPTED (valid code + confident) -> queued for clinician review:\n")

ACCEPTED (valid code + confident) -> queued for clinician review:

# Show core columns of accepted (validated) suggestions.
print(as.data.frame(accepted[, c("mention", "icd10", "snomed", "model_confidence")]), row.names = FALSE)

         mention icd10    snomed model_confidence
    hypertension   I10  38341003              0.9
 type 2 diabetes E11.9  44054006              0.9
      depression F32.9 370143000              0.9

cat(sprintf("\nFlagged/rejected: %d  (would never post automatically)\n", nrow(flagged)))


Flagged/rejected: 0  (would never post automatically)

Module 16: Emerging Directions
text:
16.3 Agentic AI — plan over tools (claims)
A chatbot answers in prose. An agent is a controller that calls named tools with contracts, in a plan, and leaves an audit trail. Module 13 built the claims analytics pipeline by hand. Wrapping that pipeline as an agent is how health systems are starting to expose informatics work to analysts in plain English — without letting a language model invent an HCC score.
  raw claims + eligibility
           │
           ▼
     [clean] → [features: PMPM · HCC] → [risk tiers] → [brief / worklist]
           │                                      ▲
           └──────── ask("who is high risk?") ────┘   (router, not a guessing LLM)
Decision support, not autonomous payment or care. The agent recommends (risk tiers, outreach lists). A human (care manager, actuary, medical director) decides. This is not a certified CMS-HCC grouper, a HEDIS engine, or medical advice.







Pattern
What the model is allowed to do




Single LLM call (16.1)
Propose codes from a note — then validate


FHIR + gen AI (16.2)
Read FHIR, write FHIR after review


Agent (this section)
Choose a tool; the tool computes; the model may rephrase KPIs



The engine below is deterministic and offline. An optional live model would only rewrite the briefing — the metrics stay with kpis().

# Mini claims *book* — the member-year table Module 13 would have produced.
# Kept small so the agent (not the simulator) is the teaching point.
set.seed(7)
n <- 80
ages <- sample(55:89, n, replace = TRUE)
hcc <- pmin(pmax(round(0.6 + (ages - 55) * 0.015 + rnorm(n, 0, 0.15), 3), 0.4), 2.4)
pmpm <- pmin(pmax(round(400 + hcc * 420 + rnorm(n, 0, 180), 2), 80), 8000)
er <- pmin(rpois(n, 0.35), 5)
ip <- pmin(rpois(n, 0.20), 3)
diabetes <- rbinom(n, 1, 0.28)

tier_fn <- function(h, e, i) {
  if (h >= 1.45 || i >= 2 || e >= 3) return("4 - Critical")
  if (h >= 1.15 || i >= 1 || e >= 2) return("3 - High")
  if (h >= 0.9) return("2 - Rising")
  "1 - Low"
}

book <- tibble(
  member_id = sprintf("M%d", 2000 + 0:(n - 1)),
  age = ages,
  hcc = hcc,
  pmpm = pmpm,
  er_visits = er,
  ip_visits = ip,
  has_diabetes = diabetes,
  glucose_tested = rbinom(n, 1, 0.72) * diabetes  # only diabetics can "count"
)
book$risk_tier <- mapply(tier_fn, book$hcc, book$er_visits, book$ip_visits)
# Diabetics without a glucose test are the care-gap list (HEDIS-like, educational)
book$care_gap <- (book$has_diabetes == 1) & (book$glucose_tested == 0)

cat(sprintf("Agent book: %d members · mean PMPM $%s · mean HCC %.3f\n",
            nrow(book), formatC(mean(book$pmpm), format = "f", digits = 0, big.mark = ","), mean(book$hcc)))

Agent book: 80 members · mean PMPM $777 · mean HCC 0.880

print(table(book$risk_tier))


     1 - Low   2 - Rising     3 - High 4 - Critical 
          25           28           23            4 



# ClaimsInformaticsAgent: a thin controller, implemented as a mutable environment.
#   run()       = compute KPIs from the book (the "plan")
#   ask()       = keyword router onto tools  (not an LLM inventing numbers)
#   log_event() = audit trail so you can reconstruct what ran

make_claims_agent <- function(book_df) {
  self <- new.env()
  self$book <- book_df
  self$focus <- NULL       # last member_id named (conversation memory)
  self$audit <- list()
  self$kpis_cache <- NULL

  self$log_event <- function(tool, detail = "") {
    self$audit[[length(self$audit) + 1]] <- list(
      ts = format(now(), "%Y-%m-%dT%H:%M:%S"),
      tool = tool,
      detail = substr(as.character(detail), 1, 180)
    )
  }

  self$kpis <- function() {
    df <- self$book
    high <- df$risk_tier %in% c("3 - High", "4 - Critical")
    top_n <- max(1, as.integer(nrow(df) * 0.05))
    top5 <- head(df[order(-df$pmpm), ], top_n)
    list(
      n_members = nrow(df),
      avg_age = mean(df$age),
      avg_pmpm = mean(df$pmpm),
      avg_hcc = mean(df$hcc),
      high_critical = sum(high),
      high_critical_pct = mean(high) * 100,
      top5_cost_share = sum(top5$pmpm) / sum(df$pmpm) * 100,
      care_gap_n = sum(df$care_gap),
      n_diabetes = sum(df$has_diabetes)
    )
  }

  # Fixed plan: feature table is already here; freeze KPIs for the briefing.
  self$run <- function() {
    self$log_event("run", "freeze KPIs from member-year book")
    self$kpis_cache <- self$kpis()
    invisible(self)
  }

  self$briefing <- function() {
    k <- if (!is.null(self$kpis_cache)) self$kpis_cache else self$kpis()
    action_lines <- c(
      strwrap("1. Assign High/Critical members to intensive case management.", width = 70, indent = 2, exdent = 5),
      strwrap("2. Work the glucose-test gap list, highest PMPM first.", width = 70, indent = 2, exdent = 5),
      strwrap("3. Do not treat these figures as a CMS settlement or HEDIS submission.", width = 70, indent = 2, exdent = 5)
    )
    lines <- c(
      "CLAIMS INFORMATICS — LEADERSHIP BRIEFING (synthetic)",
      strrep("-", 54),
      sprintf("Population   %d members · mean age %.1f", k$n_members, k$avg_age),
      sprintf("Spend        $%s mean PMPM", formatC(k$avg_pmpm, format = "f", digits = 2, big.mark = ",")),
      sprintf("Risk         mean HCC %.3f (1.0 would be a real book's average)", k$avg_hcc),
      sprintf("             High/Critical %d (%.1f%%)", k$high_critical, k$high_critical_pct),
      sprintf("Concentration top 5%% of members = %.1f%% of PMPM mass", k$top5_cost_share),
      sprintf("Quality      %d of %d diabetics missing a glucose test", k$care_gap_n, k$n_diabetes),
      "",
      "Recommended actions (human review required)",
      action_lines
    )
    paste(lines, collapse = "\n")
  }

  self$worklist <- function(n = 8) {
    df <- self$book[startsWith(self$book$risk_tier, "3") | startsWith(self$book$risk_tier, "4"), ]
    cols <- c("member_id", "age", "risk_tier", "pmpm", "hcc", "er_visits", "ip_visits")
    df <- df[order(-df$pmpm), ]
    head(df[, cols], n)
  }

  self$ask <- function(question) {
    q <- trimws(question)
    ql <- tolower(q)
    self$log_event("ask", q)

    member_key <- NULL
    m <- regmatches(q, regexpr("\\bM\\d{4}\\b", q, ignore.case = TRUE))
    if (length(m) > 0 && nzchar(m)) {
      member_key <- toupper(m)
      self$focus <- member_key
    } else if (!is.null(self$focus) && grepl("\\b(it|its|this member|that member)\\b", ql)) {
      member_key <- self$focus
    }

    if (!is.null(member_key)) {
      row <- self$book[self$book$member_id == member_key, ]
      if (nrow(row) == 0) return(sprintf("%s is not in this book.", member_key))
      r <- row[1, ]
      return(sprintf(
        "%s · age %d · %s\nHCC %.2f · PMPM $%s · ER %d · IP %d\n(Recommendation only — a clinician confirms any outreach.)",
        r$member_id, as.integer(r$age), r$risk_tier, r$hcc,
        formatC(r$pmpm, format = "f", digits = 2, big.mark = ","), as.integer(r$er_visits), as.integer(r$ip_visits)
      ))
    }

    if (grepl("care management|high risk|critical|worklist|who needs|outreach", ql)) {
      wl <- self$worklist()
      lines <- c("Care-management worklist (High/Critical, highest PMPM first)",
                 "Human review required before outreach.\n")
      for (i in seq_len(nrow(wl))) {
        r <- wl[i, ]
        lines <- c(lines, sprintf("  %s  %s  PMPM $%s  HCC %.2f", r$member_id, r$risk_tier,
                                   formatC(r$pmpm, format = "f", digits = 0, big.mark = ","), r$hcc))
      }
      return(paste(lines, collapse = "\n"))
    }

    if (grepl("care gap|glucose|quality|diabetes", ql)) {
      g <- self$book[self$book$care_gap, ]
      g <- head(g[order(-g$pmpm), ], 6)
      lines <- sprintf("Glucose-test gap: %d diabetic members\n", sum(self$book$care_gap))
      for (i in seq_len(nrow(g))) {
        r <- g[i, ]
        lines <- c(lines, sprintf("  %s  %s  $%s PMPM", r$member_id, r$risk_tier,
                                   formatC(r$pmpm, format = "f", digits = 0, big.mark = ",")))
      }
      return(paste(lines, collapse = "\n"))
    }

    if (grepl("brief|summary|kpi|leadership", ql)) return(self$briefing())

    if (grepl("\\bhelp\\b", ql)) {
      return("Ask: 'who needs care management?', 'care gaps', 'brief leadership', or 'profile M2000'.")
    }

    "I could not route that. Try 'help'."
  }

  class(self) <- "ClaimsInformaticsAgent"
  self
}

agent <- make_claims_agent(book)
agent$run()
cat("Pipeline complete. KPIs frozen:\n")

Pipeline complete. KPIs frozen:

cat(toJSON(agent$kpis_cache, auto_unbox = TRUE, pretty = TRUE))

{
  "n_members": 80,
  "avg_age": 72.8,
  "avg_pmpm": 776.5409,
  "avg_hcc": 0.8805,
  "high_critical": 27,
  "high_critical_pct": 33.75,
  "top5_cost_share": 7.2978,
  "care_gap_n": 5,
  "n_diabetes": 24
}

cat("\n")
cat("Audit:", paste(sapply(agent$audit, function(a) a$tool), collapse = ", "), "\n")

Audit: run 



Milestone 2 — ask the agent in plain English
ask() is a router: keywords → tool → formatted string. “What’s its HCC?” uses conversation memory (the last member you named). A production system could swap in Claude to phrase the same payload — not to compute it.

# Scripted transcript — the questions a plan analyst actually types
top_member <- agent$book$member_id[which.max(agent$book$pmpm)]
questions <- c(
  "Who needs care management?",
  "Where are our quality / care gaps?",
  sprintf("Profile %s", top_member),
  "What's its HCC?",
  "Brief leadership."
)
for (q in questions) {
  cat(strrep("=", 68), "\n")
  cat("Q:", q, "\n")
  cat(strrep("-", 68), "\n")
  cat(agent$ask(q), "\n\n")
}

Grounded narrative. If a language model writes the memo, it receives the KPI JSON. It must not invent a PMPM, member, or savings figure. Offline we use a deterministic “rewrite” that only templates those JSON fields — the same contract as a live call.

# Stand-in for a live LLM. May only interpolate values from kpis().
mock_llm_memo <- function(kpis) {
  para <- sprintf(
    paste(

title: Module 16: Emerging Directions
section: 16.4 Federated analytics – move the computation, not the data
text:
16.4 Federated analytics – move the computation, not the data
In healthcare, data privacy laws and regulatory requirements frequently prevent the movement or pooling of actual patient records across different institutions or clinical sites. As a result, organizations often cannot simply combine all their raw data into a single, centralized database for analysis.
Federated analytics is a privacy-preserving solution to this challenge. In a federated approach, each participating site (for example, hospitals or clinics) keeps its patient records locally. Instead of sharing sensitive, row-level data, each site computes local summary statistics (such as totals, means, or other aggregates) on its own data, and then only these statistics are communicated to a central coordinator or aggregated further. No individual patient-level data ever leaves the institution where it originated, greatly reducing privacy risks.
For example, to calculate the average Hemoglobin A1c (HbA1c, a marker of blood sugar control) across three simulated sites, each site would: - Compute the sum and count of their patients’ A1c values locally, - Share only (sum, count) pairs, not any raw measurements or records, - The central coordinator then combines these numbers to compute the overall mean, without ever seeing any patient’s full data.
This paradigm supports privacy, regulatory compliance, and cross-institutional collaboration. The code below demonstrates a federated mean A1c computation using simulated site splits.

# Extract the Hemoglobin A1c (HbA1c) observation values from the EHR data.
obs <- ehr$observations
a1c <- obs$value[obs$observation == "Hemoglobin A1c"]

# Fix a seed for reproducibility.
set.seed(1)

# Randomly permute and split the A1c values into 3 "sites" (contiguous, near-equal chunks).
# Each site gets a portion of the data and never shares raw patient-level rows with others.
split_into_n <- function(x, n) {
  len <- length(x)
  base <- len %/% n
  rem <- len %% n
  sizes <- rep(base, n)
  if (rem > 0) sizes[seq_len(rem)] <- sizes[seq_len(rem)] + 1
  ends <- cumsum(sizes)
  starts <- ends - sizes + 1
  lapply(seq_len(n), function(i) x[starts[i]:ends[i]])
}
sites <- split_into_n(sample(a1c), 3)

# For federated analytics, each site locally computes aggregate statistics:
# Only the 'sum' of values and the 'count' of patients are shared externally; no raw values leave the site.
local_stats <- lapply(seq_along(sites), function(i) {
  s <- sites[[i]]
  list(site = i, n = length(s), sum = sum(s))  # Sum of A1c values at this site
})

cat("Per-site shared statistics (no raw values leave the site):\n")

Per-site shared statistics (no raw values leave the site):

for (st in local_stats) {
  cat(" ", sprintf("{site: %d, n: %d, sum: %.4f}", st$site, st$n, st$sum), "\n")
}

  {site: 1, n: 115, sum: 812.9000} 
  {site: 2, n: 115, sum: 814.4000} 
  {site: 3, n: 115, sum: 813.6000} 

# The central coordinator receives only the aggregates, not any individual records,
# and computes the overall (global) mean A1c by combining per-site sums and counts.
global_n <- sum(sapply(local_stats, function(s) s$n))
global_mean <- sum(sapply(local_stats, function(s) s$sum)) / global_n

cat(sprintf("\nFederated global mean A1c: %.3f %% (n=%d)\n", global_mean, global_n))


Federated global mean A1c: 7.075 % (n=345)

# For validation, calculate the mean as if centralizing all data (i.e., if pooling were allowed).
# This should match the federated result if all math is correct.
cat(sprintf("Centralized check (if pooling were allowed): %.3f %%  -> identical\n", mean(a1c)))

Centralized check (if pooling were allowed): 7.075 %  -> identical



Milestone 3 - an equity / bias check
This step involves performing an equity or bias check to assess whether our screening flag is applied fairly across different demographic groups (e.g., by sex). We compare the flagging rate in each group to look for large disparities, which could indicate bias in the data or model. If a significant gap is found, it may require further investigation and mitigation to ensure fair and equitable model performance.

# The following code assesses whether the A1c screening flag (which indicates possible diabetes) is being applied equitably across different sex groups.

# 1. Retrieve patient table and A1c observation data.
patients <- ehr$patients
# 2. For each patient, find their highest Hemoglobin A1c (HbA1c) value.
a1c_max <- obs %>%
  filter(observation == "Hemoglobin A1c") %>%
  group_by(patient_id) %>%
  summarize(value = max(value), .groups = "drop")
# 3. Merge this maximum A1c value with the patient demographic table using patient_id.
df <- patients %>% left_join(a1c_max %>% rename(a1c = value), by = "patient_id")
# 4. Create a 'flagged' column: patients are flagged if their A1c is 6.5 or above (possible diabetes threshold).
df$flagged <- df$a1c >= 6.5

# 5. For each sex group, calculate the screening flag rate (percentage of patients flagged) and the subgroup count.
equity <- df %>%
  filter(!is.na(a1c)) %>%                        # Exclude patients with missing A1c
  group_by(sex) %>%                               # Group by sex, look at "flagged" column
  summarize(flag_rate = mean(flagged), count = n(), .groups = "drop")
# 6. Convert flag rates to percentages (rounded to 1 decimal).
equity$flag_rate <- round(equity$flag_rate * 100, 1)

cat("Screening-flag rate by sex (watch for large gaps):\n")

Screening-flag rate by sex (watch for large gaps):

print(as.data.frame(equity), row.names = FALSE)

    sex flag_rate count
 female      77.2    92
   male      78.6    84

# 7. Calculate the absolute difference in flag rates between the two sex groups.
gap <- abs(equity$flag_rate[1] - equity$flag_rate[2])

# 8. Print a message interpreting the gap.
cat(sprintf(
  "\nAbsolute gap: %.1f percentage points -> %s\n",
  gap, ifelse(gap > 10, "review for bias", "within a reasonable band (synthetic data)")
))


Absolute gap: 1.4 percentage points -> within a reasonable band (synthetic data)

title: Module 16: Emerging Directions
text:
16.5 Ethics, regulation, and equity
The technical work is necessary but not sufficient. Responsible health AI/informatics weighs:

Regulation - FDA oversight of AI/ML as software-as-a-medical-device (SaMD); HIPAA; emerging AI-specific rules.
Transparency - model cards, documented training data, explainability where decisions affect care.
Equity - auditing for disparate performance across race, sex, age, language, and socioeconomic status; representative training data.
Human oversight - AI (including agents that call tools) augments clinicians and analysts; it does not replace accountable human judgment. Worklists and risk scores are recommendations, not orders.

These are entry points, not the last word — each is an active area your work will keep engaging with.

title: Module 16: Emerging Directions
text:
16.6 Data Governance
Data governance is the framework of processes, policies, and standards that ensure health data is accurate, secure, and used appropriately throughout its lifecycle.
Key elements of data governance in health informatics include:

Data Quality: Ensuring that data is complete, accurate, timely, and consistent.
Privacy and Security: Protecting patient information to comply with laws like HIPAA; applying access controls, audits, and de-identification where needed.
Data Stewardship and Ownership: Defining responsibilities for data management, from custodianship to authorized access and consent management.
Lineage and Provenance: Tracking where data comes from, how it is transformed, and recording any changes for full auditability.
Compliance: Meeting regulatory obligations and best practices for data handling, retention, sharing, and disposal.
Interoperability Standards: Using shared vocabularies (like FHIR, SNOMED, LOINC) and data structures for safe and seamless data exchange between systems.

Good data governance builds trust, ensures ethical use, and is essential for responsible health AI development and collaboration across institutions.

Extend the equity check to age bands as well as sex, and report the largest subgroup gap.

title: Module 16: Emerging Directions
text:
Key takeaways

LLMs assist documentation and autocoding, but the pattern is always extract → structure → validate → human review.
Keep FHIR as source of truth: LLMs read from and write back to it, tagged for provenance.
Agentic AI is a plan over tools (clean → features → risk → brief), not a chatbot inventing PMPM. Numbers stay with code; the model may only rephrase.
Federated analytics shares statistics, not records — and can match pooled results exactly.
Ethics, regulation, and equity decide what should ship, not just what can.

title: Module 14: Clinical Data Warehousing and Analytics-Ready Data
text:
Health Informatics in R · Part IV: Advanced Topics · Module 14 of 16
Transactional EHR data is optimized for recording care, not analyzing it. A clinical data warehouse reshapes it into an analytics-friendly structure. This module covers dimensional modeling (star schemas), computational phenotyping, and building an ML-ready feature matrix.

title: Module 14: Clinical Data Warehousing and Analytics-Ready Data
text:
Learning objectives
By the end of this module you will be able to:

Contrast transactional (OLTP) and analytical (OLAP) data shapes.
Design a star schema (fact + dimension tables) for clinical encounters.
Build a computational phenotype combining diagnoses, labs, and medications.
Assemble an analytics-ready feature matrix for machine learning.
Explain why cohort + phenotype + features is the standard analytics pipeline.

title: Module 14: Clinical Data Warehousing and Analytics-Ready Data
text:
Dataset
The synthetic EHR, reshaped from its transactional tables into a star schema and then into a patient-level feature matrix.

library(dplyr)
library(tidyr)
library(tibble)

# --- Self-contained synthetic EHR generator (identical to earlier parts) ---

# This function creates a synthetic electronic health record (EHR) dataset for demonstration purposes.
make_synthetic_ehr <- function(n_patients = 200, seed = 42) {
  set.seed(seed)

  # Generate random demographic details for n_patients
  first <- c("Ava","Liam","Noah","Mia","Zoe","Omar","Ivan","Sara","Leo","Nina",
             "Ruth","Kai","Yara","Theo","Ida","Sam","Ana","Eli","Rex","Uma")
  last  <- c("Khan","Ortiz","Chen","Diaz","Patel","Ali","Brown","Nash","Reed","Vega",
             "Cole","Frost","Grant","Hale","Iqbal","Jain","Kerr","Lund","Mora","Park")
  ages <- sample(18:89, n_patients, replace = TRUE)
  patients <- tibble(
    patient_id = sprintf("P%d", 1000 + 0:(n_patients - 1)),
    given_name = sample(first, n_patients, replace = TRUE),
    family_name = sample(last, n_patients, replace = TRUE),
    sex = sample(c("male", "female"), n_patients, replace = TRUE, prob = c(0.49, 0.51)),
    age = ages,
    birth_year = 2026 - ages  # Synthetic current year assumed to be 2026
  )

  # Generate encounters (visits) for each patient
  enc_types <- c("ambulatory", "emergency", "inpatient", "wellness")
  enc_rows <- vector("list", n_patients)
  eid <- 0
  for (i in seq_len(n_patients)) {
    pid <- patients$patient_id[i]
    n_enc <- sample(1:4, 1)  # Each patient gets 1-4 encounters
    day <- sample(0:(365 * 3 - 1), n_enc, replace = TRUE)  # Any day in 3 years from 2023-01-01
    ids <- sprintf("E%05d", eid + seq_len(n_enc))
    eid <- eid + n_enc
    enc_rows[[i]] <- tibble(
      encounter_id = ids,
      patient_id = pid,
      encounter_type = sample(enc_types, n_enc, replace = TRUE, prob = c(0.55, 0.15, 0.10, 0.20)),
      date = as.Date("2023-01-01") + day
    )
  }
  encounters <- bind_rows(enc_rows)

  # Generate clinical observations (labs, vitals) for encounters
  obs_defs <- tribble(
    ~observation,               ~unit,   ~lo,  ~hi,
    "Body height",               "cm",    150,  195,
    "Body weight",                "kg",    50,   110,
    "Systolic blood pressure",   "mmHg",  100,  165,
    "Heart rate",                 "/min",  55,   100,
    "Hemoglobin A1c",             "%",     4.8,  9.5
  )
  obs_rows <- vector("list", nrow(encounters))
  for (i in seq_len(nrow(encounters))) {
    e <- encounters[i, ]
    keep <- runif(nrow(obs_defs)) < 0.7  # 70% chance of that observation being present
    if (any(keep)) {
      d <- obs_defs[keep, ]
      obs_rows[[i]] <- tibble(
        encounter_id = e$encounter_id,
        patient_id = e$patient_id,
        observation = d$observation,
        value = round(runif(nrow(d), d$lo, d$hi), 1),
        unit = d$unit,
        date = e$date
      )
    }
  }
  observations <- bind_rows(obs_rows) %>%
    mutate(observation_id = sprintf("O%06d", row_number())) %>%
    relocate(observation_id)

  # Generate medical conditions ("problems") per patient
  cond_pool <- c("Essential hypertension", "Type 2 diabetes mellitus", "Asthma",
                 "Acute bronchitis", "Major depressive disorder", "Osteoarthritis",
                 "Chronic kidney disease", "Anemia")
  cond_rows <- vector("list", n_patients)
  for (i in seq_len(n_patients)) {
    pid <- patients$patient_id[i]
    # Each patient gets 0-3 unique random diagnoses
    n_c <- sample(0:3, 1)
    if (n_c > 0) {
      cond_rows[[i]] <- tibble(patient_id = pid, condition = sample(cond_pool, n_c, replace = FALSE))
    }
  }
  conditions <- bind_rows(cond_rows) %>%
    mutate(condition_id = sprintf("C%05d", row_number())) %>%
    relocate(condition_id)

  # Generate medications per patient
  med_pool <- c("Lisinopril", "Metformin", "Albuterol", "Atorvastatin", "Sertraline",
                "Amoxicillin", "Ibuprofen", "Hydrochlorothiazide")
  med_rows <- vector("list", n_patients)
  for (i in seq_len(n_patients)) {
    pid <- patients$patient_id[i]
    # Each patient gets 0-3 unique random medications
    n_m <- sample(0:3, 1)
    if (n_m > 0) {
      med_rows[[i]] <- tibble(patient_id = pid, medication = sample(med_pool, n_m, replace = FALSE))
    }
  }
  medications <- bind_rows(med_rows) %>%
    mutate(medication_id = sprintf("M%05d", row_number())) %>%
    relocate(medication_id)

  # Return all tables as a list
  list(
    patients = patients,
    encounters = encounters,
    observations = observations,
    conditions = conditions,
    medications = medications
  )
}

# Create the synthetic EHR data
ehr <- make_synthetic_ehr()

# Print the number of rows for each generated table
cat("Tables:", paste(sprintf("%s (%d)", names(ehr), sapply(ehr, nrow)), collapse = ", "), "\n")

Tables: patients (200), encounters (507), observations (1746), conditions (302), medications (313)

text:
13.1 Transactional vs. analytical
The operational EHR is normalized for fast, consistent writes — great for care, awkward for analysis (every question needs many joins). A warehouse denormalizes into a shape optimized for reads and aggregation: the star schema.




Transactional (OLTP)
Warehouse (OLAP)




Optimized for
writes, consistency
reads, aggregation


Shape
normalized, many tables
star: fact + dimensions


Query
“record this visit”
“visits per condition per quarter”

title: Module 14: Clinical Data Warehousing and Analytics-Ready Data
text:
14.2 Designing a star schema
A star schema is a data warehousing modeling approach characterized by a single, central fact table, which stores quantitative, measurable data about business events, surrounded by multiple dimension tables, which provide descriptive, contextual attributes for these facts.
In this context, the fact table records information about clinical encounters—each row relates to a unique healthcare encounter (such as a doctor visit, emergency visit, or inpatient admission). This is called the “grain” of the fact table: here, it is set as one row per encounter, meaning each record reflects a single, specific patient encounter.
The surrounding dimension tables (such as patient, date, or encounter type) store additional data that describes, categorizes, or provides context for each encounter (like patient demographics, calendar dates, or encounter settings), enabling flexible and efficient analytical queries.
This structure allows for efficient aggregation, summarization, and slicing/dicing of the data by various dimensions, making it especially suitable for analytical workloads and reporting.

patients <- ehr$patients
enc <- ehr$encounters
enc$date <- as.Date(enc$date)

# ---- dimension: patient ----
dim_patient <- patients %>%
  mutate(age_band = cut(age, breaks = c(17, 29, 39, 49, 59, 69, 120),
                         labels = c("18-29", "30-39", "40-49", "50-59", "60-69", "70+"))) %>%
  select(patient_id, sex, age, age_band)

# ---- dimension: date ----
dim_date <- tibble(date = seq(min(enc$date), max(enc$date), by = "day"))
dim_date$year <- as.integer(format(dim_date$date, "%Y"))
dim_date$quarter <- paste0(format(dim_date$date, "%Y"), "Q", ceiling(as.integer(format(dim_date$date, "%m")) / 3))
dim_date$month <- as.integer(format(dim_date$date, "%m"))

# ---- dimension: encounter type ----
dim_enc_type <- tibble(encounter_type = unique(enc$encounter_type))
dim_enc_type$is_acute <- dim_enc_type$encounter_type %in% c("emergency", "inpatient")

cat("Dimensions built:\n")

Dimensions built:

cat("  dim_patient:", nrow(dim_patient), "x", ncol(dim_patient),
    "| dim_date:", nrow(dim_date), "x", ncol(dim_date),
    "| dim_enc_type:", nrow(dim_enc_type), "x", ncol(dim_enc_type), "\n")

  dim_patient: 200 x 4 | dim_date: 1093 x 4 | dim_enc_type: 4 x 2 



Milestone 1 - the fact table
The fact table is the central, quantitative table in a star schema, where each row represents a specific business event or transaction—in this case, a single clinical encounter. It contains keys linking to related dimension tables (such as patient, date, and encounter type) and stores measurable data (known as measures), such as the number of observations recorded during each encounter.

# Build the central fact table for the star schema: one row per encounter, with foreign keys and measures

# 1. Copy the observations table for later use
obs <- ehr$observations

# 2. Calculate the number of observations recorded in each encounter;
#    this will serve as a "measure" in the fact table and is grouped by encounter_id
obs_per_enc <- obs %>% count(encounter_id, name = "n_observations")

# 3. Merge the encounters table with the number of observations
#    - Left join ensures every encounter is kept, even if it had no observations
#    - Fill missing (NA) counts with 0 and cast to integer
fact_encounter <- enc %>%
  left_join(obs_per_enc, by = "encounter_id") %>%
  mutate(n_observations = as.integer(ifelse(is.na(n_observations), 0, n_observations)))

# 4. Select fact table columns:
#    - encounter_id (primary key for the fact table)
#    - patient_id, encounter_type, date (dimension keys)
#    - n_observations (measure)
fact_encounter <- fact_encounter %>%
  select(encounter_id, patient_id, encounter_type, date, n_observations)

# Display a preview of the fact table
cat("FACT_ENCOUNTER (grain = one encounter):\n")

FACT_ENCOUNTER (grain = one encounter):

print(as.data.frame(head(fact_encounter)), row.names = FALSE)

       E00001      P1000      inpatient 2023-03-19              3
       E00002      P1000       wellness 2023-08-18              2
       E00003      P1000     ambulatory 2023-03-15              3
       E00004      P1001     ambulatory 2023-09-22              4
       E00005      P1001     ambulatory 2024-09-02              4
       E00006      P1002     ambulatory 2024-12-29              3

# Example analytical "star" query:
#    - Join the fact table to dimension tables (date, encounter type)
#    - Group by calendar quarter and acute/non-acute status
#    - Count encounters in each category
cat("\nStar query example — encounters per quarter by acuity:\n")

star <- fact_encounter %>%
  left_join(dim_date %>% select(date, quarter), by = "date") %>%
  left_join(dim_enc_type, by = "encounter_type") %>%
  group_by(quarter, is_acute) %>%
  summarize(n = n(), .groups = "drop")

title: Module 14: Clinical Data Warehousing and Analytics-Ready Data
text:
14.3 Computational phenotyping
A phenotype is a formal, algorithmic definition of “who has condition X” in a dataset, designed to be both reproducible and executable. Phenotypes combine data from multiple sources, including diagnoses, laboratory results, and medication prescriptions, applying logic to systematically identify patients that meet specific clinical criteria. For instance, real-world phenotype definitions (such as those on PheKB) may require certain diagnoses to be present, specific lab values to exceed thresholds, and the use of corresponding medications. Below is an implementation of a computational phenotype for type 2 diabetes, demonstrating how multiple domains of EHR data (diagnoses, labs, medications) are used in combinatorial logic.

# 1. Extract the relevant condition and medication tables from the EHR
cond <- ehr$conditions
meds <- ehr$medications

# 2. Identify patients with a diabetes diagnosis:
#    - For each patient, check if they have *any* diagnosis of "Type 2 diabetes mellitus"
dx_patients <- unique(cond$patient_id[cond$condition == "Type 2 diabetes mellitus"])

# 3. Identify patients with high A1c lab values:
#    - Filter hemoglobin A1c results, group by patient, take *maximum* value
#    - A1c >= 6.5 is considered diagnostic for diabetes
a1c_max <- obs %>%
  filter(observation == "Hemoglobin A1c") %>%
  group_by(patient_id) %>%
  summarize(value = max(value), .groups = "drop")
lab_patients <- a1c_max$patient_id[a1c_max$value >= 6.5]

# 4. Identify patients with a prescription for Metformin:
#    - For each patient, check if they have *any* record of Metformin medication
med_patients <- unique(meds$patient_id[meds$medication == "Metformin"])

# 5. Create a phenotype table indexed by all patients
pheno <- tibble(patient_id = patients$patient_id)
#    - For each patient, assign whether they meet the diagnosis, lab, or medication criteria
#      (FALSE if there is no record)
pheno$dx  <- pheno$patient_id %in% dx_patients
pheno$lab <- pheno$patient_id %in% lab_patients
pheno$med <- pheno$patient_id %in% med_patients

# 6. Define the phenotype logic:
#    - A patient is considered to have the diabetes phenotype if they have
#      (a) a diagnosis *OR* (b) BOTH a high A1c lab *AND* Metformin prescription
#    - This represents a classic "2 out of 3" logic used in computational phenotyping
pheno$diabetes_phenotype <- pheno$dx | (pheno$lab & pheno$med)

# 7. Output: show counts of diabetes phenotype cases, and contribution of each criterion
cat("Diabetes phenotype (multi-criteria):\n")

Diabetes phenotype (multi-criteria):

print(table(pheno$diabetes_phenotype))


FALSE  TRUE 
  124    76 

cat("\nContribution of each criterion:\n")


Contribution of each criterion:

print(c(dx = sum(pheno$dx), lab = sum(pheno$lab), med = sum(pheno$med)))

 dx lab med 
 51 137  46 



Milestone 2 - an analytics-ready feature matrix
At this stage, we’ve constructed an analytics-ready feature matrix: a single table where each row represents a patient and each column is a feature summarizing clinically relevant traits (e.g., demographics, lab values, clinical phenotypes). This matrix is formatted so it can be directly used as input for machine learning models or statistical analyses. Continuous variables (like lab means), binary indicators (such as the diabetes phenotype), and encoded demographic variables are all included, with one row per unique patient.

# Build a machine learning-ready feature matrix with one row per patient:
#
# 1. wide_obs: Pivot the observations table so that each patient's row contains the mean value
#    for each lab/measurement type as a separate column, rounded to one decimal.
wide_obs <- obs %>%
  group_by(patient_id, observation) %>%
  summarize(value = mean(value), .groups = "drop") %>%
  pivot_wider(names_from = observation, values_from = value) %>%
  mutate(across(-patient_id, ~ round(.x, 1)))

# 2. n_enc: Count the number of encounters (visits) for each patient.
n_enc <- fact_encounter %>% count(patient_id, name = "n_encounters")

# 3. n_cond: Count the number of conditions recorded for each patient.
n_cond <- cond %>% count(patient_id, name = "n_conditions")

# 4. Start with demographic data ('sex', 'age') for each patient from the dimension table.
#    Encode sex as a binary variable indicating female.
features <- dim_patient %>%
  select(patient_id, sex, age) %>%
  mutate(sex = as.integer(sex == "female")) %>%  # 1 for female, 0 for other
  # 5. Join with the wide-format observations, encounter counts, and condition counts.
  left_join(wide_obs, by = "patient_id") %>%
  left_join(n_enc, by = "patient_id") %>%
  left_join(n_cond, by = "patient_id") %>%
  # 6. Add a binary indicator for diabetes phenotype (from previous steps).
  left_join(pheno %>% select(patient_id, diabetes_phenotype), by = "patient_id") %>%
  mutate(diabetes_phenotype = as.integer(diabetes_phenotype))

# 7. Replace missing encounter or condition counts with 0 and ensure integer type.
features$n_encounters <- as.integer(ifelse(is.na(features$n_encounters), 0, features$n_encounters))
features$n_conditions <- as.integer(ifelse(is.na(features$n_conditions), 0, features$n_conditions))

# 8. Display shape and column names of the resulting feature matrix.
cat("Feature matrix shape:", nrow(features), "x", ncol(features), "\n")

title: Module 14: Clinical Data Warehousing and Analytics-Ready Data
text:
14.4 The standard analytics pipeline
The overarching structure presented in this module reflects the standard workflow found in many clinical analytics and data science projects. This process consists of the following key stages:
warehouse (star schema)  →  cohort  →  phenotype  →  feature matrix  →  model

Warehouse (star schema): Clinical data from multiple sources is transformed and organized into a unified, denormalized schema, often a star schema, to enable efficient and flexible querying.
Cohort: From the warehouse, a specific group of patients relevant to the downstream analysis is selected, often based on inclusion/exclusion criteria. This step narrows the population to those for whom the study question is pertinent.
Phenotype: For each patient in the cohort, executable logic is used to define clinical phenotypes—typically the outcome, condition, or label of interest (e.g., identifying patients with diabetes), based on combinations of diagnoses, labs, or medication records.
Feature matrix: For machine learning or statistical modeling, relevant variables (such as demographics, lab results, and encoded phenotypes) are assembled into a structured, analytic-ready table where rows correspond to patients and columns to features. This tabular format can then be directly input to models.
Model: Finally, predictive or explanatory models are trained on the feature matrix to answer clinical questions, support decision-making, or discover new insights.

This pipeline provides a systematic approach to leverage raw clinical data for actionable analytics and AI applications: starting from making data accessible, then narrowing it and labeling it for analysis, extracting relevant features, and finally applying computational models.

title: Module 12: Public Health and Population Informatics
text:
Health Informatics in R · Part IV: Advanced Topics · Module 12 of 16
Clinical informatics focuses on the individual patient; public health informatics shifts the unit of analysis to the population. This module covers disease surveillance, reportable conditions, syndromic monitoring, registries, and the standards that move data from clinics to health departments.

title: Module 12: Public Health and Population Informatics
text:
Learning objectives
By the end of this module you will be able to:

Explain disease surveillance and the difference between case-based and syndromic surveillance.
Implement a reportable-condition trigger from clinical data.
Build a syndromic time series and detect an aberration (outbreak signal).
Construct a simple disease registry and compute population indicators.
Name the public-health reporting standards: eCR and ELR.

title: Module 12: Public Health and Population Informatics
text:
Dataset
The synthetic EHR aggregated to the population level, plus a daily syndromic time series we derive from encounters and into which we inject a synthetic outbreak so the aberration detector has something to find.

library(dplyr)
library(tibble)
library(ggplot2)

# --- Self-contained synthetic EHR generator (identical to earlier parts) ---

# This function creates a synthetic Electronic Health Record (EHR) dataset with multiple tables.
make_synthetic_ehr <- function(n_patients = 200, seed = 42) {
  set.seed(seed)

  # 1. Generate basic patient demographics
  first <- c("Ava","Liam","Noah","Mia","Zoe","Omar","Ivan","Sara","Leo","Nina",
             "Ruth","Kai","Yara","Theo","Ida","Sam","Ana","Eli","Rex","Uma")
  last  <- c("Khan","Ortiz","Chen","Diaz","Patel","Ali","Brown","Nash","Reed","Vega",
             "Cole","Frost","Grant","Hale","Iqbal","Jain","Kerr","Lund","Mora","Park")
  ages <- sample(18:89, n_patients, replace = TRUE)
  patients <- tibble(
    patient_id = sprintf("P%d", 1000 + 0:(n_patients - 1)),
    given_name = sample(first, n_patients, replace = TRUE),
    family_name = sample(last, n_patients, replace = TRUE),
    sex = sample(c("male", "female"), n_patients, replace = TRUE, prob = c(0.49, 0.51)),
    age = ages,
    birth_year = 2026 - ages
  )

  # 2. Simulate encounters for each patient (each patient has 1-4 encounters)
  enc_types <- c("ambulatory", "emergency", "inpatient", "wellness")
  enc_rows <- vector("list", n_patients)
  eid <- 0
  for (i in seq_len(n_patients)) {
    pid <- patients$patient_id[i]
    n_enc <- sample(1:4, 1)
    day <- sample(0:(365 * 3 - 1), n_enc, replace = TRUE)  # encounter at random day over 3 years
    ids <- sprintf("E%05d", eid + seq_len(n_enc))
    eid <- eid + n_enc
    enc_rows[[i]] <- tibble(
      encounter_id = ids,
      patient_id = pid,
      encounter_type = sample(enc_types, n_enc, replace = TRUE, prob = c(0.55, 0.15, 0.10, 0.20)),
      date = as.Date("2023-01-01") + day
    )
  }
  encounters <- bind_rows(enc_rows)

  # 3. Generate observations for each encounter (70% chance per observation type per encounter)
  obs_defs <- tribble(
    ~observation,               ~unit,   ~lo,  ~hi,
    "Body height",               "cm",    150,  195,
    "Body weight",                "kg",    50,   110,
    "Systolic blood pressure",   "mmHg",  100,  165,
    "Heart rate",                 "/min",  55,   100,
    "Hemoglobin A1c",             "%",     4.8,  9.5
  )
  obs_rows <- vector("list", nrow(encounters))
  for (i in seq_len(nrow(encounters))) {
    e <- encounters[i, ]
    keep <- runif(nrow(obs_defs)) < 0.7  # 70% probability to record the observation
    if (any(keep)) {
      d <- obs_defs[keep, ]
      obs_rows[[i]] <- tibble(
        encounter_id = e$encounter_id,
        patient_id = e$patient_id,
        observation = d$observation,
        value = round(runif(nrow(d), d$lo, d$hi), 1),
        unit = d$unit,
        date = e$date
      )
    }
  }
  observations <- bind_rows(obs_rows) %>%
    mutate(observation_id = sprintf("O%06d", row_number())) %>%
    relocate(observation_id)

  # 4. Assign 0-3 random conditions per patient from a predefined pool
  cond_pool <- c("Essential hypertension", "Type 2 diabetes mellitus", "Asthma",
                 "Acute bronchitis", "Major depressive disorder", "Osteoarthritis",
                 "Chronic kidney disease", "Anemia")
  cond_rows <- vector("list", n_patients)
  for (i in seq_len(n_patients)) {
    pid <- patients$patient_id[i]
    n_c <- sample(0:3, 1)
    if (n_c > 0) {
      cond_rows[[i]] <- tibble(patient_id = pid, condition = sample(cond_pool, n_c, replace = FALSE))
    }
  }
  conditions <- bind_rows(cond_rows) %>%
    mutate(condition_id = sprintf("C%05d", row_number())) %>%
    relocate(condition_id)

  # 5. Assign 0-3 random medications per patient from a medication pool
  med_pool <- c("Lisinopril", "Metformin", "Albuterol", "Atorvastatin", "Sertraline",
                "Amoxicillin", "Ibuprofen", "Hydrochlorothiazide")
  med_rows <- vector("list", n_patients)
  for (i in seq_len(n_patients)) {
    pid <- patients$patient_id[i]
    n_m <- sample(0:3, 1)
    if (n_m > 0) {
      med_rows[[i]] <- tibble(patient_id = pid, medication = sample(med_pool, n_m, replace = FALSE))
    }
  }
  medications <- bind_rows(med_rows) %>%
    mutate(medication_id = sprintf("M%05d", row_number())) %>%
    relocate(medication_id)

  # Return the complete synthetic EHR as a list of tables
  list(
    patients = patients,
    encounters = encounters,
    observations = observations,
    conditions = conditions,
    medications = medications
  )
}

# Actually generate the data and display a summary of each table's size
ehr <- make_synthetic_ehr()
cat("Tables:", paste(sprintf("%s (%d)", names(ehr), sapply(ehr, nrow)), collapse = ", "), "\n")

Tables: patients (200), encounters (507), observations (1746), conditions (302), medications (313)

title: Module 12: Public Health and Population Informatics
text:
12.1 Two modes of surveillance
Case-based (notifiable disease) surveillance involves the mandatory reporting of specific, confirmed diagnoses, such as measles or tuberculosis, to public health authorities. Each case is investigated and reported individually, which ensures very high specificity and data accuracy. However, because reporting relies on confirmation (often lab-based) and follow-up, this approach is slower and less useful for providing early warning of emerging health threats.
Syndromic surveillance monitors patterns of health-related data before a definitive diagnosis is made. It tracks symptoms, chief complaints, or visit counts in sources like emergency departments to rapidly detect unusual trends (such as an uptick in respiratory symptoms). This method is much faster, enabling early detection and potentially timely interventions, but it is less specific: many different diseases or non-infectious conditions can cause similar symptom patterns, making the data “noisy” and prone to false alarms.
In practice, public health systems use both approaches: syndromic surveillance provides rapid alerts for unexpected activity, allowing early situational awareness, while case-based reporting follows as a more definitive, confirmatory process that guides official response and containment.

title: Module 12: Public Health and Population Informatics
text:
12.2 Reportable-condition triggers
Certain diagnoses, such as specific infectious diseases or conditions with significant public health impact, are legally reportable to government authorities. This means that, when a healthcare provider or EHR system records the diagnosis of such a condition, an automated process (called a “trigger”) identifies the case and prepares the relevant clinical information for prompt, secure transmission. This process is known as electronic case reporting (eCR). eCR enables rapid, standardized, and reliable notification to public health agencies—ensuring they are alerted about new cases quickly enough to investigate, monitor trends, and initiate appropriate disease control or preventive actions.

# Define two lists mimicking reportable conditions and those that are actually notifiable (require action).
# In reality, these lists are determined by state or national public health laws and may be much longer.
REPORTABLE <- list(
  "Acute bronchitis" = "respiratory-syndrome-monitored",  # Imagine this code means the condition is tracked for public health
  "Asthma" = "chronic-not-reportable"                     # While asthma is relevant, it's not mandated for reporting here
)
NOTIFIABLE <- c("Acute bronchitis")  # Of the reportable list, this condition is to be automatically flagged for action

# Extract the 'conditions' table from our synthetic electronic health record (EHR)
cond <- ehr$conditions

# Find all rows where the patient's condition matches a 'notifiable' condition, i.e., should be reported
triggered <- cond %>% filter(condition %in% NOTIFIABLE)

# Annotate these flagged rows with a new column: the type of report they trigger (here, an "electronic case report" or eCR)
triggered <- triggered %>% mutate(report_type = "eCR (electronic case report)")

# Print how many cases were triggered for reporting
cat(sprintf("Reportable cases triggered: %d\n", nrow(triggered)))

Reportable cases triggered: 41

# Display a few columns (patient id, condition, report type) of the first triggered cases, without row index numbers
print(as.data.frame(head(triggered %>% select(patient_id, condition, report_type))), row.names = FALSE)

title: Module 12: Public Health and Population Informatics
text:
12.3 Building a syndromic time series
Syndromic surveillance is concerned with monitoring trends by tracking how counts of specific health events change over time. In this example, we construct a time series by tallying the number of respiratory-related emergency encounters for each day. To demonstrate how syndromic surveillance detects unusual activity, we artificially add (or “inject”) a surge of cases—a synthetic outbreak—in the middle of the series. This creates an abnormal spike in counts, mimicking the kind of sudden event that surveillance systems are designed to identify as a potential public health concern.

# Make a copy of the encounters table and ensure the 'date' column is in Date format
enc <- ehr$encounters
enc$date <- as.Date(enc$date)

# Calculate the number of emergency encounters per day:
# 1. Filter to only emergency encounters
# 2. Group by date, count occurrences, and name the result 'count'
daily_counts <- enc %>%
  filter(encounter_type == "emergency") %>%
  count(date, name = "count")

# Create a complete date range from the earliest to latest encounter date, one entry per day
idx <- seq(min(enc$date), max(enc$date), by = "day")
# Reindex the series to this full date range, filling days with no events with zero
daily <- tibble(date = idx) %>%
  left_join(daily_counts, by = "date") %>%
  mutate(count = ifelse(is.na(count), 0, count))

# Simulate a 10-day outbreak in the middle of the time series by adding elevated counts for those days
set.seed(7)  # Fixed seed for reproducibility
outbreak_start <- daily$date[floor(nrow(daily) / 2) + 1]  # Middle date of the series
outbreak_days <- seq(outbreak_start, by = "day", length.out = 10)
bump <- sample(4:8, 10, replace = TRUE)  # Add 4-8 events per outbreak day
daily$count[daily$date %in% outbreak_days] <- daily$count[daily$date %in% outbreak_days] + bump

# Output summary stats
cat("Daily syndromic series built:", nrow(daily), "days\n")

Daily syndromic series built: 1093 days

# Baseline mean is calculated as the average count in the first quarter of the series
cat("Baseline mean:", round(mean(daily$count[1:floor(nrow(daily) / 4)]), 2), "\n")

Baseline mean: 0.06 



Milestone 1 - aberration detection (a simple EARS-style C1)
Aberration detection involves identifying days where the number of observed events is unexpectedly high compared to recent history.
In this example, we use a simple version of the CDC EARS (Early Aberration Reporting System) method, specifically the C1 algorithm: - For each day, we calculate the mean and standard deviation of event counts over a trailing baseline window (e.g., the previous 14 days, not including the current day). - We set a threshold as: mean + k × standard deviation (where k is typically 3). - Any day where the observed count exceeds this threshold is flagged as a possible aberration (“alarm”).
This technique allows us to automatically detect sudden, unusual increases in health events, such as might occur in a disease outbreak.

# Function to detect statistical aberrations in a time series using a simplified CDC EARS C1 algorithm.
# This identifies days where the number of observed events ("count") is unexpectedly high
# compared to the preceding days, indicating a possible outbreak.

detect_aberrations <- function(dates, counts, window = 14, k = 3) {
  n <- length(counts)
  roll_mean <- rep(NA_real_, n)
  roll_sd <- rep(NA_real_, n)

  # Rolling mean/sd over a trailing window (excluding the current day, i.e. shift(1))
  for (i in seq_len(n)) {
    lo <- max(1, i - window)
    hi <- i - 1
    if (hi >= lo && (hi - lo + 1) >= 7) {  # min_periods = 7
      w <- counts[lo:hi]
      roll_mean[i] <- mean(w)
      roll_sd[i] <- sd(w)
    }
  }
  roll_sd[is.na(roll_sd)] <- 1  # Use 1 as default std if insufficient prior data

  # The threshold for flagging a potential aberration: mean + k*std
  threshold <- roll_mean + k * roll_sd

  # Alarm (TRUE/FALSE): did today's count exceed the calculated threshold?
  flags <- counts > threshold
  flags[is.na(flags)] <- FALSE

  # Return a tibble showing the day's count, calculated threshold, and alarm status
  tibble(date = dates, count = counts, threshold = round(threshold, 1), alarm = flags)
}

# Apply aberration detection to the daily time series
signal <- detect_aberrations(daily$date, daily$count)

# Extract the days that triggered alarms (potential outbreaks)
alarms <- signal %>% filter(alarm)

cat(sprintf("Aberration days flagged: %d\n", nrow(alarms)))

Aberration days flagged: 63

# Display first 8 alarms with their observed count and calculated threshold
print(as.data.frame(head(alarms[, c("date", "count", "threshold")], 8)), row.names = FALSE)

# Plot the time series with detected aberrations and thresholds for visual inspection.

# Plot daily emergency department (ED) counts, alarm threshold, and flagged aberrations.
ggplot(signal, aes(x = date)) +
  geom_line(aes(y = count, color = "daily ED count"), linewidth = 0.7) +
  geom_line(aes(y = threshold, color = "alarm threshold"), linetype = "dashed", linewidth = 0.7) +
  geom_point(data = alarms, aes(y = count, color = "aberration"), size = 2, zorder = 5) +
  scale_color_manual(
    name = NULL,
    values = c("daily ED count" = "#4C72B0", "alarm threshold" = "#DD8452", "aberration" = "#C44E52")

  theme_minimal(base_size = 11) +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom")

title: Module 12: Public Health and Population Informatics
text:
12.4 Disease registries
A registry is an organized database that contains a systematically assembled group of individuals who share a specific condition or set of characteristics. These registries are actively maintained and track individuals over time for purposes such as public health surveillance, monitoring care quality, research, and improving clinical outcomes.
Examples include cancer registries, which record cancer diagnoses and follow up with patients over years, or diabetes registries, where people diagnosed with diabetes are monitored for changes in health status, treatment outcomes, and population-level trends.
Disease registries collect key data points including diagnoses, laboratory results, demographics, treatments, and outcomes, making it possible to calculate statistics (indicators) such as incidence and prevalence rates, mortality, and measures of disease control.
In the code below, we create a diabetes registry by identifying patients with Type 2 diabetes mellitus (T2DM) either by having a coded diagnosis or an elevated Hemoglobin A1c (A1c ≥ 6.5), and then compute population health indicators based on this curated group.

# --- Create a diabetes registry: patients with either a T2DM diagnosis OR elevated A1c (>= 6.5) ---

# 1. Gather all lab observations.
obs <- ehr$observations

# 2. Identify patients with a diagnosis code for Type 2 diabetes mellitus (T2DM).
dx_dm <- unique(cond$patient_id[cond$condition == "Type 2 diabetes mellitus"])

# 3. For each patient, get their highest Hemoglobin A1c lab value.
a1c <- obs %>%
  filter(observation == "Hemoglobin A1c") %>%
  group_by(patient_id) %>%
  summarize(value = max(value), .groups = "drop")

# 4. Identify patients who have ever had an A1c indicating diabetes (A1c >= 6.5).
lab_dm <- a1c$patient_id[a1c$value >= 6.5]

# 5. Combine patients identified by diagnosis or by lab result to form the registry.
registry_ids <- union(dx_dm, lab_dm)

# 6. Extract patient records for those in the registry.
registry <- ehr$patients %>% filter(patient_id %in% registry_ids)

# 7. Merge each registry patient with their highest recorded A1c value (if any).
registry <- registry %>% left_join(a1c %>% rename(max_a1c = value), by = "patient_id")

# 8. Compute population metrics and output summary:
n_total <- nrow(ehr$patients)
cat(sprintf("Diabetes registry: %d patients (%.1f%% of population)\n",
            nrow(registry), 100 * nrow(registry) / n_total))

Diabetes registry: 153 patients (76.5% of population)

cat(sprintf("  identified by diagnosis: %d | by A1c lab: %d\n", length(dx_dm), length(lab_dm)))

  identified by diagnosis: 51 | by A1c lab: 137

cat(sprintf("  mean age: %.1f\n", mean(registry$age)))

  mean age: 51.8

poor_control <- !is.na(registry$max_a1c) & registry$max_a1c >= 8
cat(sprintf("  %% with poor control (A1c>=8): %.1f%%\n", 100 * mean(poor_control)))

  % with poor control (A1c>=8): 52.9%

title: Module 12: Public Health and Population Informatics
text:
12.5 Public-health reporting standards
In public health, two main automated standards ensure that important clinical and laboratory data from clinics and hospitals are sent quickly and reliably to health departments:

eCR (electronic Case Reporting) — This system automatically sends reports about specific health conditions (called “reportable conditions,” like tuberculosis or HIV) from the electronic health record (EHR) system to public health departments. The trigger can be a diagnosis, lab result, or other EHR event. Information is sent using standardized clinical document formats such as FHIR (Fast Healthcare Interoperability Resources) or CDA (Clinical Document Architecture). eCR allows public health agencies to receive timely details about new cases, demographics, provider information, and other relevant clinical data automatically, without manual paperwork.
ELR (electronic Laboratory Reporting) — This standard is used specifically for laboratory test results. When a laboratory identifies a positive result for a reportable infectious disease (for example, a positive blood culture for Salmonella), the information is sent directly to the relevant public health authorities, usually using the HL7 Version 2 messaging standard. ELR provides structured data about laboratory findings, specimen types, collection dates, and results, speeding up case detection and outbreak investigations.

Both eCR and ELR have replaced older, manual methods like phone calls or faxing of results, dramatically reducing reporting delays and enabling near-real-time disease surveillance and rapid public health response to new cases.

title: Module 10: Clinical Natural Language Processing
text:
Dataset
The two fabricated clinical notes from Module 9. No real patients; the point is the shape of clinical language (abbreviations like “h/o”, negations like “denies”, family-history mentions).

library(dplyr)
library(tibble)
library(stringr)

# Synthetic clinical notes containing FABRICATED identifiers (no real people)
notes <- list(
  list(note_id = "N001", patient_id = "P1000", text =
    paste0("Ava Khan (MRN 4471982) seen on 03/12/2024. Contact 607-555-0148. ",
           "58 yo F with h/o hypertension and type 2 diabetes presents for follow-up. ",

           "recheck A1c in 3 months. Lives at 12 Elm St, Ithaca NY.")),
  list(note_id = "N002", patient_id = "P1001", text =
    paste0("Liam Ortiz, DOB 07/22/1969, MRN 5580321. Presents with acute bronchitis. ",
           "Reports cough x5 days. Negative for fever. Family history of asthma. ",
           "Started amoxicillin. Follow up if not improving. Email liam.o@example.com."))
)

title: Module 10: Clinical Natural Language Processing
text:
10.1 Why clinical NLP is hard
General-purpose NLP stumbles on clinical text because of:

Abbreviations & jargon —-“h/o”, “SOB”, “BP”, “x5 days”.
Negation - “denies chest pain” asserts the absence of a finding; naive keyword search would wrongly flag chest pain.
Context - “family history of asthma” is about a relative, not the patient.
Structure - notes have sections (HPI, PMH, Meds, Assessment) that change meaning.

A pipeline that ignores negation and context produces dangerously wrong structured data.

title: Module 10: Clinical Natural Language Processing
text:
10.2 Tokenization and sentence segmentation
Tokenization and sentence segmentation are foundational pre-processing steps in NLP. - Tokenization splits text into smaller units called tokens (typically words, numbers, punctuation). In clinical text, this must robustly handle abbreviations, medical terms, and identifiers (e.g., “h/o”, “03/12/2024”, “A1c”). - Sentence segmentation (sentence boundary detection) divides text into sentences. This can be tricky in clinical notes due to telegraphic style (missing periods), bulleted lists, or fragmentary findings.
A production R pipeline would reach for spacyr (a reticulate bridge to spaCy), udpipe, or quanteda for this step. Here we implement a simple regex-based sentence splitter directly in R: it needs no external model and demonstrates the same idea — split on sentence-ending punctuation, being careful not to split on the decimal-like patterns inside clinical abbreviations (dates, “A1c”, numeric ranges).

# A lightweight sentence segmenter: split on ". " / "! " / "? " while keeping
# the terminal punctuation attached to each sentence.
sentencize <- function(text) {
  # Split after a sentence-ending punctuation mark followed by whitespace
  # (mirrors a default spaCy sentencizer's punctuation-based rule).
  pieces <- str_split(text, "(?<=[.!?])\\s+")[[1]]
  str_trim(pieces)
}

# Process the first clinical note into sentences.
sents_note0 <- sentencize(notes[[1]]$text)

cat("Sentences detected:\n")

Sentences detected:

for (i in seq_along(sents_note0)) {
  cat(sprintf("  %d. %s\n", i, sents_note0[i]))
}

  1. Ava Khan (MRN 4471982) seen on 03/12/2024.
  2. Contact 607-555-0148.
  3. 58 yo F with h/o hypertension and type 2 diabetes presents for follow-up.
  4. BP 148/88.
  5. Denies chest pain.
  6. No shortness of breath.
  7. Continue lisinopril; recheck A1c in 3 months.
  8. Lives at 12 Elm St, Ithaca NY.

section: 10.3 Concept extraction with a clinical gazetteer
text:
10.3 Concept extraction with a clinical gazetteer
A cornerstone technique in rule-based clinical NLP is the dictionary lookup approach. Here, a pre-defined, curated list of relevant clinical terms, known as a gazetteer, is matched directly to text using exact or near-exact string matches. This enables quick identification of medical problems, medications, symptoms, and other entities of interest. In R we implement this as a small set of stringr regex patterns built from the gazetteer terms — the same idea as spaCy’s PhraseMatcher in the Python version: - It matches entire multi-word phrases (not just single tokens). - Matching is performed case-insensitively. - It is a simple vectorized scan, so it stays fast even over many notes. With this dictionary-matching approach, the pipeline can rapidly flag the presence of terms from the clinical gazetteer, providing a foundation for further semantic analysis.

# Define a small clinical gazetteer (dictionary):
# It maps semantic type labels (like "problem" and "medication") to lists of term strings representing clinical entities.
GAZETTEER <- list(
  problem = c("hypertension", "type 2 diabetes", "acute bronchitis", "asthma",
              "chest pain", "shortness of breath", "fever", "cough"),
  medication = c("lisinopril", "amoxicillin", "metformin", "atorvastatin")
)

# Find sentence boundaries as character offsets so each match can be tied back
# to the sentence that contains it (mirrors spaCy's `span.sent`).
sentence_spans <- function(text) {
  sents <- sentencize(text)
  spans <- tibble(sent = sents, start = NA_integer_, end = NA_integer_)
  pos <- 1L
  for (i in seq_along(sents)) {
    idx <- str_locate(str_sub(text, pos), fixed(sents[i]))
    s <- pos + idx[1, "start"] - 1L
    e <- pos + idx[1, "end"] - 1L
    spans$start[i] <- s
    spans$end[i] <- e
    pos <- e + 1L
  }
  spans
}

# Define a function to extract concepts from input text using the gazetteer:
extract_concepts <- function(text) {
  spans <- sentence_spans(text)
  out <- list()
  # For every semantic type and term, scan the text (case-insensitive, "LOWER" style match).
  for (semtype in names(GAZETTEER)) {
    for (term in GAZETTEER[[semtype]]) {
      m <- str_locate_all(text, regex(term, ignore_case = TRUE))[[1]]
      if (nrow(m) > 0) {
        for (i in seq_len(nrow(m))) {
          start <- m[i, "start"]; end <- m[i, "end"]
          sent_idx <- which(spans$start <= start & start <= spans$end)[1]
          out[[length(out) + 1]] <- tibble(
            text = str_sub(text, start, end),   # matched phrase as-is in text
            type = semtype,                     # "problem" or "medication"
            start = start,                       # character offset where phrase starts
            end = end,                           # character offset where phrase ends
            sent = if (!is.na(sent_idx)) spans$sent[sent_idx] else NA_character_
          )
        }
      }
    }
  }
  bind_rows(out) %>% arrange(start)
}

# Extract concepts from the first note in our clinical notes collection.
concepts <- extract_concepts(notes[[1]]$text)

cat("Concepts extracted from note N001:\n")

Concepts extracted from note N001:

print(as.data.frame(concepts[, c("text", "type")]), row.names = FALSE)

                text       type
        hypertension    problem
     type 2 diabetes    problem
          chest pain    problem
 shortness of breath    problem
          lisinopril medication
