title: Module 10: Clinical Natural Language Processing
text:
10.4 Negation and context detection
Extracting clinical concepts is only the first step: we also need to determine the context in which a concept appears. For example, in sentences like “Denies chest pain” or “no shortness of breath”, the clinical problem is actually negated—the patient does not have the problem. To address this, we implement a simple ConText-style rule engine. This approach involves scanning the words before (and sometimes after) each concept in its sentence, searching for specific cue words or phrases—known as triggers—that change the assertion status of the concept. Common triggers can indicate that a finding is negated (e.g., “no”, “denies”), historical, or related to family history. By detecting these triggers, we can assign each identified concept an assertion status, such as “present”, “negated”, “historical”, or “family”, thereby capturing more accurate clinical meaning from the text.

# Negation and context triggers for clinical concept assertion detection.
NEG_TRIGGERS    <- c("denies", "no", "not", "negative for", "without", "rules out", "never")  # Indicative of negation (the patient does NOT have the problem)
FAMILY_TRIGGERS <- c("family history", "mother", "father", "sibling", "parent")                # Indicates the problem relates to family, not the patient
HIST_TRIGGERS   <- c("h/o", "history of", "previous", "prior", "past")                         # Indicates a historical problem, not currently present

#' Determines the assertion status (e.g., present, negated, family, historical) of a
#' clinical concept within a document using simple keyword-based (ConText-style) rules.
#'
#' - Looks to the left of a concept mention in its sentence for cue words.
#' - Returns a string indicating context status (family, negated, historical, or present).
assert_status <- function(concept, text, spans) {
  # Find the sentence that contains the concept's mention based on character offsets.
  sent_idx <- which(spans$start <= concept$start & concept$start <= spans$end)[1]
  # Examine the sentence fragment to the left of the mention, lowercased for easier matching.
  window <- if (!is.na(sent_idx)) {
    str_to_lower(str_sub(text, spans$start[sent_idx], concept$start - 1))
  } else ""
  # Assign assertion status based on which trigger words are found in the window.
  if (any(str_detect(window, fixed(FAMILY_TRIGGERS)))) return("family")
  if (any(str_detect(window, fixed(NEG_TRIGGERS)))) return("negated")
  if (any(str_detect(window, fixed(HIST_TRIGGERS)))) return("historical")
  "present"  # Default: the problem is actively present
}

# Apply assertion classification to each detected concept in the note.
spans0 <- sentence_spans(notes[[1]]$text)
concepts$assertion <- vapply(seq_len(nrow(concepts)), function(i) {
  assert_status(concepts[i, ], notes[[1]]$text, spans0)
}, character(1))


Milestone 1 - asserted vs negated problems
In clinical NLP, it’s important to distinguish between problems that are actively present (asserted) and those that are specifically stated to be absent (negated) in the documentation.
Asserted problems are conditions explicitly documented as affecting the patient (e.g., “Patient has hypertension”).
Negated problems are conditions the patient specifically denies or is documented as not having (e.g., “Denies chest pain”; “No shortness of breath”).
This distinction is made possible by using contextual rules that look for negation cues (like “no”, “denies”) near mentions of clinical problems, ensuring more accurate extraction and interpretation of the patient’s medical status.

# The following code block organizes all detected clinical concepts,
# displays each concept with its type and assertion status, and then summarizes which problems
# are currently active versus those explicitly marked as absent (negated).

# 1. concepts is already a tibble/data frame of concept rows for easier inspection/manipulation.
df <- concepts

# 2. Print all concepts, showing their textual mention, their type (e.g., problem, medication), and their assertion status
#    (such as "present", "negated", etc.).
cat("Concepts with assertion status (note N001):\n")

Concepts with assertion status (note N001):

print(as.data.frame(df[, c("text", "type", "assertion")]), row.names = FALSE)

                text       type  assertion
        hypertension    problem historical
     type 2 diabetes    problem historical
          chest pain    problem    negated
 shortness of breath    problem    negated
          lisinopril medication    present

# 3. Extract and print the list of problems that are actively present (not negated, not family, not historical).
cat("\nActive problems (present only):",
    paste(df %>% filter(type == "problem", assertion == "present") %>% pull(text), collapse = ", "), "\n")


Active problems (present only):  

# 4. Extract and print the list of concept mentions that have been classified as explicitly negated.
cat("Explicitly negated       :",
    paste(df %>% filter(assertion == "negated") %>% pull(text), collapse = ", "), "\n")

Explicitly negated       : chest pain, shortness of breath 



# This code demonstrates how the assertion classification identifies family-history and historical mentions in a clinical note (Note N002).
# 1. Extract clinical concepts and their sentence spans from the note text.
concepts2 <- extract_concepts(notes[[2]]$text)
spans2 <- sentence_spans(notes[[2]]$text)

# 2. For each detected concept, determine the assertion status (such as present, negated, family, or historical).
concepts2$assertion <- vapply(seq_len(nrow(concepts2)), function(i) {
  assert_status(concepts2[i, ], notes[[2]]$text, spans2)
}, character(1))

# 3. Organize and display all concepts along with their type and assertion results.
df2 <- concepts2
cat("Note N002 concepts:\n")

Note N002 concepts:

print(as.data.frame(df2[, c("text", "type", "assertion")]), row.names = FALSE)

             text       type assertion
 acute bronchitis    problem   present
            cough    problem   present
            fever    problem   negated
           asthma    problem    family
      amoxicillin medication   present

# 4. Highlight the tagging of 'asthma' as a 'family' problem, indicating it belongs to a relative, not the patient themself.
cat("\nNote 'asthma' is tagged 'family' — it belongs to a relative, not the patient.\n")


Note 'asthma' is tagged 'family' — it belongs to a relative, not the patient.

text:
10.5 Mapping mentions to terminology codes
In the last step, we connect each clinical concept that is currently present in the note to a standardized terminology code (using mapping dictionaries introduced earlier in Module 3). This transforms free-text extractions into structured, coded data that can be consistently interpreted and analyzed across systems.

TERM_TO_CODE <- list(
  "hypertension"     = c(system = "SNOMED", code = "38341003"),
  "type 2 diabetes"  = c(system = "SNOMED", code = "44054006"),
  "acute bronchitis" = c(system = "SNOMED", code = "10509002"),
  "asthma"           = c(system = "SNOMED", code = "195967001"),
  "lisinopril"       = c(system = "RxNorm", code = "29046"),
  "amoxicillin"      = c(system = "RxNorm", code = "723"),
  "metformin"        = c(system = "RxNorm", code = "6809")
)
code_concept <- function(text) {
  hit <- TERM_TO_CODE[[str_to_lower(text)]]
  if (is.null(hit)) c(system = NA_character_, code = NA_character_) else hit
}

present <- df %>% filter(assertion == "present")
coded <- t(vapply(present$text, code_concept, character(2)))
present$system <- coded[, "system"]
present$code <- coded[, "code"]

cat("Coded structured output from note N001 (present concepts):\n")

Coded structured output from note N001 (present concepts):

print(as.data.frame(present[, c("text", "type", "assertion", "system", "code")]), row.names = FALSE)

       text       type assertion system  code
 lisinopril medication   present RxNorm 29046

href: Notebooks/Part III - Privacy, Text, and Applied Informatics (Intermediate–Advanced)/10_clinical_nlp.html#section-detection
title: Module 10: Clinical Natural Language Processing
text:
10.6 Section detection
Clinical notes are divided into sections, each identified by a header such as “HPI”, “Assessment”, or “Medications”. The meaning of information found in a note often depends on which section it appears in—e.g., “Family History” indicates a condition applies to a relative, while “History of Present Illness” applies to the patient now. To analyze notes accurately, it’s important to detect and segment these sections. A straightforward approach uses pattern matching to locate standard headers and split the note accordingly, so each segment can be interpreted with the proper clinical context.

SECTION_HEADERS <- c("HPI", "History of Present Illness", "PMH", "Past Medical History",
                     "Medications", "Assessment", "Plan", "Family History")
sample_note <- paste0("HPI: 58 yo F with hypertension. ",
                       "Medications: lisinopril 10mg daily. ",
                       "Assessment: BP suboptimal, uptitrate.")

parts <- str_split(sample_note, paste0("(", paste(SECTION_HEADERS, collapse = "|"), ")\\s*:"),
                    simplify = FALSE)[[1]]
headers <- str_extract_all(sample_note, paste0("(", paste(SECTION_HEADERS, collapse = "|"), ")\\s*:"))[[1]]
headers <- str_trim(str_remove(headers, ":$"))
# parts[1] is text before the first header (empty here); parts[2..] align with headers[1..]
sections <- setNames(str_trim(parts[-1][seq_along(headers)]), headers)
for (name in names(sections)) {
  cat(sprintf("[%s] %s\n", name, sections[[name]]))
}

[HPI] 58 yo F with hypertension.
[Medications] lisinopril 10mg daily.
[Assessment] BP suboptimal, uptitrate.

Key takeaways

Clinical NLP must handle abbreviations, negation, context, and sections — naive keyword search is unsafe.
A practical pipeline is segment → extract → assert → code → sectionize.
Negation/context detection is what separates “patient has X” from “patient denies X” — clinically decisive.

Health-Informatics: An R Tutorial
Health Informatics in R · Part II: Interoperability & Data Engineering · Module 8 of 16
Analytics is only as trustworthy as the data underneath it. Health data is notoriously messy — missing labs, impossible values, broken links between tables. This module builds a systematic data-quality (DQ) assessment using the widely adopted Kahn framework: conformance, completeness, plausibility.

objectID: Notebooks/Part II -  Interoperability and Data Engineering (Intermediate)/08_data_quality_and_validation.html#dataset
href: Notebooks/Part II -  Interoperability and Data Engineering (Intermediate)/08_data_quality_and_validation.html#dataset
title: Module 8: Data Quality and Validation
text:
Dataset
The synthetic EHR - but we deliberately inject a few defects (an impossible age, a broken foreign key, an out-of-range lab, a missing value) so the checks have something to catch. This mirrors what real DQ tooling faces.

# --- Self-contained synthetic EHR generator (identical to Part I) ---
# This is the SAME generator from Module 1. We rebuild the fake hospital database
# here so this notebook can run on its own. Nothing here is a real patient.
library(dplyr)
library(tibble)

# This function generates a synthetic electronic health record (EHR) dataset.
# It creates mock tables for patients, encounters, observations, conditions, and medications,
# all with plausible structure, but not referencing any real patients or requiring external data.
make_synthetic_ehr <- function(n_patients = 200, seed = 42) {
  # Generate a small, internally-consistent synthetic EHR dataset.
  # Returns a list of linked tibbles: patients, encounters, observations,
  # conditions, and medications. This is for illustrative, educational use.
  set.seed(seed)  # same seed => same fake people every run

  # --- patients table ---
  # Create a tibble with n_patients patients, each with a name, sex, age, and birth year.
  first <- c("Ava","Liam","Noah","Mia","Zoe","Omar","Ivan","Sara","Leo","Nina",
             "Ruth","Kai","Yara","Theo","Ida","Sam","Ana","Eli","Rex","Uma")
  last  <- c("Khan","Ortiz","Chen","Diaz","Patel","Ali","Brown","Nash","Reed","Vega",
             "Cole","Frost","Grant","Hale","Iqbal","Jain","Kerr","Lund","Mora","Park")
  sexes <- sample(c("male", "female"), size = n_patients, replace = TRUE, prob = c(0.49, 0.51))
  ages  <- sample(18:89, size = n_patients, replace = TRUE)
  # Columns:
  #   patient_id  — unique ID, e.g. "P1000", "P1001"
  #   given_name / family_name — randomly chosen from the name lists
  #   sex, age — pre-generated vectors
  #   birth_year — derived from age, assuming the reference year 2026
  patients <- tibble(
    patient_id  = sprintf("P%d", 1000 + (0:(n_patients - 1))),
    given_name  = sample(first, size = n_patients, replace = TRUE),
    family_name = sample(last,  size = n_patients, replace = TRUE),
    sex         = sexes,
    age         = ages,
    birth_year  = 2026 - ages
  )

  # --- encounters table ---
  # Each patient gets 1–4 visits. Types and dates are random but internally consistent.
  #   encounter_id    — unique, zero-padded (E00001, E00002, ...)
  #   encounter_type  — ambulatory 55%, emergency 15%, inpatient 10%, wellness 20%
  #   date            — a random day in a 3-year window starting 2023-01-01
  enc_types <- c("ambulatory", "emergency", "inpatient", "wellness")
  enc_list <- vector("list", 0)
  n <- 0
  for (pid in patients$patient_id) {
    n_visits <- sample.int(4, 1)  # 1 to 4 encounters per patient
    for (j in seq_len(n_visits)) {
      n <- n + 1
      day <- sample(0:(365 * 3 - 1), 1)  # offset within 3 years
      enc_list[[n]] <- tibble(
        encounter_id = sprintf("E%05d", n),
        patient_id = pid,
        encounter_type = sample(enc_types, 1, prob = c(0.55, 0.15, 0.10, 0.20)),
        date = as.Date("2023-01-01") + day
      )
    }
  }
  encounters <- bind_rows(enc_list)

  # --- observations table ---
  # Labs and vitals attached to encounters. Each row is (name, unit, lo, hi).
  # A value is drawn uniformly in [lo, hi]; 70% of (encounter, measure) pairs exist
  # so the table looks sparse the way a real EHR does.
  obs_defs <- tribble(
    ~name, ~unit, ~lo, ~hi,
    "Body height", "cm", 150, 195,
    "Body weight", "kg", 50, 110,
    "Systolic blood pressure", "mmHg", 100, 165,
    "Heart rate", "/min", 55, 100,
    "Hemoglobin A1c", "%", 4.8, 9.5
  )
  obs_list <- vector("list", 0)
  m <- 0
  for (i in seq_len(nrow(encounters))) {
    e <- encounters[i, ]
    for (k in seq_len(nrow(obs_defs))) {
      if (runif(1) < 0.7) {
        m <- m + 1
        obs_list[[m]] <- tibble(
          observation_id = sprintf("O%06d", m),
          encounter_id = e$encounter_id,
          patient_id = e$patient_id,
          observation = obs_defs$name[k],
          value = round(runif(1, obs_defs$lo[k], obs_defs$hi[k]), 1),
          unit = obs_defs$unit[k],
          date = e$date
        )
      }
    }
  }
  observations <- bind_rows(obs_list)

  # --- conditions table ---
  # Each patient is assigned 0–3 unique diagnoses from a small pool.
  cond_pool <- c("Essential hypertension", "Type 2 diabetes mellitus", "Asthma",
                 "Acute bronchitis", "Major depressive disorder", "Osteoarthritis",
                 "Chronic kidney disease", "Anemia")
  cond_list <- vector("list", 0)
  cn <- 0
  for (pid in patients$patient_id) {
    n_cond <- sample(0:3, 1)
    if (n_cond > 0) {
      chosen <- sample(cond_pool, size = n_cond, replace = FALSE)
      for (cc in chosen) {
        cn <- cn + 1
        cond_list[[cn]] <- tibble(condition_id = sprintf("C%05d", cn), patient_id = pid, condition = cc)
      }
    }
  }
  conditions <- bind_rows(cond_list)

  # --- medications table ---
  # Same pattern as conditions: 0–3 unique drugs per patient.
  med_pool <- c("Lisinopril", "Metformin", "Albuterol", "Atorvastatin",
                "Sertraline", "Amoxicillin", "Ibuprofen", "Hydrochlorothiazide")
  med_list <- vector("list", 0)
  mn <- 0
  for (pid in patients$patient_id) {
    n_med <- sample(0:3, 1)
    if (n_med > 0) {
      chosen <- sample(med_pool, size = n_med, replace = FALSE)
      for (mm in chosen) {
        mn <- mn + 1
        med_list[[mn]] <- tibble(medication_id = sprintf("M%05d", mn), patient_id = pid, medication = mm)
      }
    }
  }
  medications <- bind_rows(med_list)

  list(
    patients = patients,
    encounters = encounters,
    observations = observations,
    conditions = conditions,
    medications = medications
  )
}

# Generate the five linked tables. Each notebook in this series starts from here.
ehr <- make_synthetic_ehr()
cat("Tables:", paste(sprintf("%s (%d rows)", names(ehr), sapply(ehr, nrow)), collapse = ", "), "\n")

Tables: patients (200 rows), encounters (505 rows), observations (1753 rows), conditions (299 rows), medications (312 rows) 



# Inject controlled defects into COPIES of the tables so the original `ehr`
# list stays clean. Real DQ tooling is tested the same way: you need known
# bad rows to confirm the checks actually fire.
#
# The five defects cover the three Kahn dimensions we will check:
#   age = 210          -> plausibility (impossible age)
#   sex = "unknown"    -> conformance / value-domain (not in {male, female})
#   value = 480        -> plausibility (impossible systolic BP)
#   value = NA         -> completeness (missing lab)
#   patient_id = P9999 -> conformance / relational (broken foreign key)
patients <- ehr$patients
observations <- ehr$observations

patients$age[1] <- 210        # implausible age
patients$sex[2] <- "unknown"  # nonconformant category

# We target a Systolic blood pressure row specifically (rather than a fixed
# row number, as the Python notebook does) so the anomaly-detection example
# in 8.3 has a guaranteed outlier to find — R's random stream doesn't line up
# with the same row positions as numpy's.
sbp_idx <- which(observations$observation == "Systolic blood pressure")[1]
observations$value[sbp_idx] <- 480  # impossible systolic BP

miss_idx <- which(observations$observation != "Systolic blood pressure")[3]
observations$value[miss_idx] <- NA  # missing value

fk_idx <- which(observations$observation != "Systolic blood pressure")[1]
observations$patient_id[fk_idx] <- "P9999"  # broken referential link

cat("Injected 5 defects across patients & observations for the checks to find.\n")

Injected 5 defects across patients & observations for the checks to find.

title: Module 8: Data Quality and Validation
section: 8.1 Conformance - does the data match its expected structure?
text:
8.1 Conformance - does the data match its expected structure?
This section introduces the concept of “conformance” in data quality checks. Conformance checks ensure that: - Values are of the correct data type (e.g., strings, numbers). - Values fall within a specified, allowed set (the value domain; e.g., sex must be either “male” or “female”). - Relationships between tables are valid and intact (relational integrity; e.g., every patient_id referenced in an observation should exist in the patients table). These checks are generally broken down into three subcategories: 1. Value type - do data values have the expected type? 2. Value domain - are data values from the allowed set? 3. Relational - do references across tables (like foreign keys) point to real rows?

# Conformance asks: are values the RIGHT TYPE, in the ALLOWED DOMAIN, and are
# RELATIONSHIPS intact? We implement two of those sub-checks here.
#
# Each issue is a length-5 list:
#   (dimension, table, column, row-id, bad-value)
# so a scorecard later can group them without parsing free text.
check_conformance <- function(patients, observations) {
  issues <- list()

  # Value-domain: sex must be in the allowed set {male, female}.
  # ! flips the boolean mask, so we keep rows whose sex is NOT in that set.
  bad_sex <- patients[!(patients$sex %in% c("male", "female")), ]
  for (i in seq_len(nrow(bad_sex))) {
    r <- bad_sex[i, ]
    issues[[length(issues) + 1]] <- list("conformance/value-domain", "patients", "sex",
                                          r$patient_id, r$sex)
  }

  # Relational (referential integrity): every observations.patient_id must
  # exist in patients. An orphan row is a broken link — the lab has no owner.
  valid_ids <- unique(patients$patient_id)
  orphans <- observations[!(observations$patient_id %in% valid_ids), ]
  for (i in seq_len(nrow(orphans))) {
    r <- orphans[i, ]
    issues[[length(issues) + 1]] <- list("conformance/relational", "observations", "patient_id",
                                          r$observation_id, r$patient_id)
  }
  issues
}

conf_issues <- check_conformance(patients, observations)
for (i in conf_issues) {
  cat(sprintf("('%s', '%s', '%s', '%s', '%s')\n", i[[1]], i[[2]], i[[3]], i[[4]], i[[5]]))
}

('conformance/value-domain', 'patients', 'sex', 'P1001', 'unknown')
('conformance/relational', 'observations', 'patient_id', 'O000001', 'P9999')


Explain code

title: Module 8: Data Quality and Validation
text:
8.2 Completeness - is expected data present?
Completeness refers to whether all the expected or required data is present in the dataset. For example, if we collect lab results, are there any missing values for those lab tests? Checking completeness helps identify missing or incomplete records that could impact analysis or decisions.

# Completeness asks: is expected data PRESENT?
# We count missing observation values overall, then break the rate down by
# observation type (A1c vs heart rate vs ...) so you can see which measure
# is holey — a missing A1c is a different operational problem than a missing height.
check_completeness <- function(observations) {
  miss <- sum(is.na(observations$value))  # how many NA values
  pct <- 100 * miss / nrow(observations)  # as a percent of all rows

  # Group by observation name and take the mean of a TRUE/FALSE missing flag.
  # mean() of a logical vector is the proportion missing; * 100 turns it into %.
  profile <- observations %>%
    mutate(missing = is.na(value)) %>%
    group_by(observation) %>%
    summarise(pct_missing = round(100 * mean(missing), 1), .groups = "drop")

  list(miss = miss, pct = pct, profile = profile)
}

comp <- check_completeness(observations)
cat(sprintf("Missing observation values: %d (%.1f%%)\n", comp$miss, comp$pct))

Missing observation values: 1 (0.1%)

cat("\nMissingness by observation type:\n")


Missingness by observation type:

print(as.data.frame(comp$profile), row.names = FALSE)

             Body height         0.0
             Body weight         0.0
              Heart rate         0.3
          Hemoglobin A1c         0.0

title: Module 8: Data Quality and Validation
text:
8.3 Plausibility - are the values believable?
Plausibility means: are the data values actually believable, not just present? This breaks down into two types: - Atemporal plausibility: Checks if a single value seems reasonable and possible (e.g., a person’s age is between 0 and 120, or a blood pressure is within human limits). - Temporal plausibility: Checks if events happen in a logically correct order (e.g., a birth date must be before any medical encounter for that person, or hospital admission comes before discharge).

# Plausibility asks: are the values BELIEVABLE even if they have the right type?
# Atemporal = a single value in a sane range (age, lab). Temporal (exercise 1)
# would check order: birth before any encounter, admission before discharge.
#
# These bounds are coarse "could a living human have this?" ranges, not
# clinical reference ranges. Age 210 and SBP 480 should never survive.
RANGES <- list(
  "Systolic blood pressure" = c(60, 250),
  "Heart rate" = c(30, 220),
  "Hemoglobin A1c" = c(3, 20),
  "Body weight" = c(2, 350),
  "Body height" = c(30, 250)
)

check_plausibility <- function(patients, observations) {
  issues <- list()

  # Atemporal: age must be in [0, 120]
  bad_age <- patients[patients$age < 0 | patients$age > 120, ]
  for (i in seq_len(nrow(bad_age))) {
    r <- bad_age[i, ]
    issues[[length(issues) + 1]] <- list("plausibility/atemporal", "patients", "age",
                                          r$patient_id, r$age)
  }

  # Atemporal: each observation value must fall in its RANGES entry.
  # Rows with a missing value are skipped -- we already counted those under
  # completeness. A measure with no RANGES entry never gets flagged (-Inf, Inf).
  obs_nonmiss <- observations[!is.na(observations$value), ]
  for (i in seq_len(nrow(obs_nonmiss))) {
    r <- obs_nonmiss[i, ]
    rng <- RANGES[[r$observation]]
    if (is.null(rng)) rng <- c(-Inf, Inf)
    if (!(r$value >= rng[1] && r$value <= rng[2])) {
      issues[[length(issues) + 1]] <- list("plausibility/atemporal", "observations", r$observation,
                                            r$observation_id, r$value)
    }
  }
  issues
}

plaus_issues <- check_plausibility(patients, observations)
for (i in plaus_issues) {
  cat(sprintf("('%s', '%s', '%s', '%s', %s)\n", i[[1]], i[[2]], i[[3]], i[[4]], i[[5]]))
}

('plausibility/atemporal', 'patients', 'age', 'P1000', 210)
('plausibility/atemporal', 'observations', 'Systolic blood pressure', 'O000003', 480)



Milestone 1 - anomaly detection on a measurement distribution
In this section, we perform anomaly detection on a measurement distribution to identify data points that are statistically extreme (outliers) within the dataset, even if they are physically possible values.

# Range checks catch values that are physically impossible. Anomaly detection
# catches values that are *possible* but statistically extreme in THIS dataset.
# A z-score of 3 means "3 standard deviations from the mean" — a common cutoff.
#
# z = (value - mean) / sd
# |z| > 3 -> flag as an outlier (the injected SBP of 480 will light up)
library(ggplot2)

sbp <- observations %>%
  filter(observation == "Systolic blood pressure") %>%
  filter(!is.na(value))

mean_sbp <- mean(sbp$value)
std_sbp <- sd(sbp$value)
sbp <- sbp %>% mutate(z = (value - mean_sbp) / std_sbp)
outliers <- sbp %>% filter(abs(z) > 3)

cat(sprintf("Systolic BP: mean=%.1f, std=%.1f\n", mean_sbp, std_sbp))

Systolic BP: mean=133.8, std=26.7

cat(sprintf("Outliers (|z|>3): %d\n", nrow(outliers)))

Outliers (|z|>3): 1

print(as.data.frame(outliers[, c("observation_id", "value", "z")]), row.names = FALSE)

 observation_id value        z
        O000003   480 12.98644

ggplot(sbp, aes(x = value)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 30, fill = "#4C72B0", color = "white") +
  geom_vline(aes(xintercept = mean_sbp + 3 * std_sbp, linetype = "+3σ"), color = "#C44E52") +
  scale_linetype_manual(name = "", values = "dashed") +
  labs(title = "Systolic BP distribution with anomaly threshold",
       x = "Systolic blood pressure (mmHg)", y = "Count") +
  theme_minimal()










Milestone 2 - assemble a DQ scorecard
In this step, we’ll assemble a Data Quality (DQ) scorecard. The scorecard summarizes the main dimensions of data quality—conformance, completeness, and plausibility—by reporting the number of issues detected for each. This provides a quick overview so a data steward can easily scan and assess the overall quality of the dataset.

# A scorecard rolls the three Kahn dimensions into one table a steward can scan.
# n_issues = 0 -> PASS, anything else -> FLAG. This is the same idea as Module 6's
# validation gate, just reported instead of aborting the load.
dq_scorecard <- function(patients, observations) {
  conf <- check_conformance(patients, observations)
  plaus <- check_plausibility(patients, observations)
  comp <- check_completeness(observations)

  card <- tibble(
    dimension = c("Conformance", "Completeness", "Plausibility"),
    check = c("value-domain + referential", "missing observation values", "range/age violations"),
    n_issues = c(length(conf), as.integer(comp$miss), length(plaus))
  )
  # ifelse() is vectorized if-then: 0 issues -> PASS, otherwise FLAG
  card$status <- ifelse(card$n_issues == 0, "PASS", "FLAG")
  card
}

scorecard <- dq_scorecard(patients, observations)
cat("DATA QUALITY SCORECARD\n")

DATA QUALITY SCORECARD

print(as.data.frame(scorecard), row.names = FALSE)

    dimension                      check n_issues status
  Conformance value-domain + referential        2   FLAG
 Completeness missing observation values        1   FLAG
 Plausibility       range/age violations        2   FLAG

title: Module 8: Data Quality and Validation
text:
8.4 Provenance and lineage
Data quality (DQ) findings are only useful if you can trace the origin and transformations of each data value—that is, track its provenance. Provenance ensures that, for any piece of data, you know where it came from and what processing steps it went through. At a minimum, provenance records for any processed dataset should capture: - The original data source and how the dataset was generated (including code, parameters, and seeds, if any). - When the data was processed. - The size or row counts of tables after processing. - Which data quality checks were applied. - Any known issues or caveats (e.g., intentionally injected errors for testing). This information makes DQ assessments trustworthy, reproducible, and auditable.

# A DQ result is only actionable if you can trace WHERE each value came from
# and WHAT happened to it. This list is the minimum provenance to store with
# any processed dataset: who generated it, when, how big it was, which checks
# ran, and any known caveats (here: we injected 5 defects on purpose).
library(lubridate)
library(jsonlite)

provenance <- list(
  dataset = "synthetic_ehr_v1",
  generated_by = "make_synthetic_ehr(seed=42)",  # seed makes it re-runnable
  processed_at = format(with_tz(now(), "UTC"), "%Y-%m-%dT%H:%M:%S+00:00"),
  row_counts = setNames(as.list(sapply(ehr, nrow)), names(ehr)),
  dq_checks_run = list("conformance", "completeness", "plausibility"),
  known_defects_injected = 5
)

# toJSON() pretty-prints the list so it can be saved beside the dataset
cat(toJSON(provenance, auto_unbox = TRUE, pretty = TRUE))

{
  "dataset": "synthetic_ehr_v1",
  "generated_by": "make_synthetic_ehr(seed=42)",
  "processed_at": "2026-08-28T01:18:38+00:00",
  "row_counts": {
    "patients": 200,
    "encounters": 505,
    "observations": 1753,
    "conditions": 299,
    "medications": 312
  },
  "dq_checks_run": [
    "conformance",
    "completeness",
    "plausibility"
  ],
  "known_defects_injected": 5
}

title: Module 6: Data Ingestion and ETL Pipelines
text:
Dataset
Two deliberately messy sources describing the same kind of data: a CSV export with mixed units and missing values, and a small FHIR-style JSON feed. The goal is to reconcile them into one clean table.

# --- Self-contained synthetic EHR generator (identical to Part I) ---
# This is the SAME generator from Module 1. We rebuild the fake hospital database
# here so this notebook can run on its own. Nothing here is a real patient.
library(dplyr)
library(tibble)

# This function generates a synthetic electronic health record (EHR) dataset.
# It creates mock tables for patients, encounters, observations, conditions, and medications,
# all with plausible structure, but not referencing any real patients or requiring external data.
make_synthetic_ehr <- function(n_patients = 200, seed = 42) {
  # Generate a small, internally-consistent synthetic EHR dataset.
  # Returns a list of linked tibbles: patients, encounters, observations,
  # conditions, and medications. This is for illustrative, educational use.
  set.seed(seed)  # same seed => same fake people every run

  # --- patients table ---
  # Create a tibble with n_patients patients, each with a name, sex, age, and birth year.
  first <- c("Ava","Liam","Noah","Mia","Zoe","Omar","Ivan","Sara","Leo","Nina",
             "Ruth","Kai","Yara","Theo","Ida","Sam","Ana","Eli","Rex","Uma")
  last  <- c("Khan","Ortiz","Chen","Diaz","Patel","Ali","Brown","Nash","Reed","Vega",
             "Cole","Frost","Grant","Hale","Iqbal","Jain","Kerr","Lund","Mora","Park")
  sexes <- sample(c("male", "female"), size = n_patients, replace = TRUE, prob = c(0.49, 0.51))
  ages  <- sample(18:89, size = n_patients, replace = TRUE)
  # Columns:
  #   patient_id  — unique ID, e.g. "P1000", "P1001"
  #   given_name / family_name — randomly chosen from the name lists
  #   sex, age — pre-generated vectors
  #   birth_year — derived from age, assuming the reference year 2026
  patients <- tibble(
    patient_id  = sprintf("P%d", 1000 + (0:(n_patients - 1))),
    given_name  = sample(first, size = n_patients, replace = TRUE),
    family_name = sample(last,  size = n_patients, replace = TRUE),
    sex         = sexes,
    age         = ages,
    birth_year  = 2026 - ages
  )

  # --- encounters table ---
  # Each patient gets 1–4 visits. Types and dates are random but internally consistent.
  #   encounter_id    — unique, zero-padded (E00001, E00002, ...)
  #   encounter_type  — ambulatory 55%, emergency 15%, inpatient 10%, wellness 20%
  #   date            — a random day in a 3-year window starting 2023-01-01
  enc_types <- c("ambulatory", "emergency", "inpatient", "wellness")
  enc_list <- vector("list", 0)
  n <- 0
  for (pid in patients$patient_id) {
    n_visits <- sample.int(4, 1)  # 1 to 4 encounters per patient
    for (j in seq_len(n_visits)) {
      n <- n + 1
      day <- sample(0:(365 * 3 - 1), 1)  # offset within 3 years
      enc_list[[n]] <- tibble(
        encounter_id = sprintf("E%05d", n),
        patient_id = pid,
        encounter_type = sample(enc_types, 1, prob = c(0.55, 0.15, 0.10, 0.20)),
        date = as.Date("2023-01-01") + day
      )
    }
  }
  encounters <- bind_rows(enc_list)

  # --- observations table ---
  # Labs and vitals attached to encounters. Each row is (name, unit, lo, hi).
  # A value is drawn uniformly in [lo, hi]; 70% of (encounter, measure) pairs exist
  # so the table looks sparse the way a real EHR does.
  obs_defs <- tribble(
    ~name, ~unit, ~lo, ~hi,
    "Body height", "cm", 150, 195,
    "Body weight", "kg", 50, 110,
    "Systolic blood pressure", "mmHg", 100, 165,
    "Heart rate", "/min", 55, 100,
    "Hemoglobin A1c", "%", 4.8, 9.5
  )
  obs_list <- vector("list", 0)
  m <- 0
  for (i in seq_len(nrow(encounters))) {
    e <- encounters[i, ]
    for (k in seq_len(nrow(obs_defs))) {
      if (runif(1) < 0.7) {
        m <- m + 1
        obs_list[[m]] <- tibble(
          observation_id = sprintf("O%06d", m),
          encounter_id = e$encounter_id,
          patient_id = e$patient_id,
          observation = obs_defs$name[k],
          value = round(runif(1, obs_defs$lo[k], obs_defs$hi[k]), 1),
          unit = obs_defs$unit[k],
          date = e$date
        )
      }
    }
  }
  observations <- bind_rows(obs_list)

  # --- conditions table ---
  # Each patient is assigned 0–3 unique diagnoses from a small pool.
  cond_pool <- c("Essential hypertension", "Type 2 diabetes mellitus", "Asthma",
                 "Acute bronchitis", "Major depressive disorder", "Osteoarthritis",
                 "Chronic kidney disease", "Anemia")
  cond_list <- vector("list", 0)
  cn <- 0
  for (pid in patients$patient_id) {
    n_cond <- sample(0:3, 1)
    if (n_cond > 0) {
      chosen <- sample(cond_pool, size = n_cond, replace = FALSE)
      for (cc in chosen) {
        cn <- cn + 1
        cond_list[[cn]] <- tibble(condition_id = sprintf("C%05d", cn), patient_id = pid, condition = cc)
      }
    }
  }
  conditions <- bind_rows(cond_list)

  # --- medications table ---
  # Same pattern as conditions: 0–3 unique drugs per patient.
  med_pool <- c("Lisinopril", "Metformin", "Albuterol", "Atorvastatin",
                "Sertraline", "Amoxicillin", "Ibuprofen", "Hydrochlorothiazide")
  med_list <- vector("list", 0)
  mn <- 0
  for (pid in patients$patient_id) {
    n_med <- sample(0:3, 1)
    if (n_med > 0) {
      chosen <- sample(med_pool, size = n_med, replace = FALSE)
      for (mm in chosen) {
        mn <- mn + 1
        med_list[[mn]] <- tibble(medication_id = sprintf("M%05d", mn), patient_id = pid, medication = mm)
      }
    }
  }
  medications <- bind_rows(med_list)

  list(
    patients = patients,
    encounters = encounters,
    observations = observations,
    conditions = conditions,
    medications = medications
  )
}

# Generate the five linked tables. Each notebook in this series starts from here.
ehr <- make_synthetic_ehr()
cat("Tables:", paste(sprintf("%s (%d rows)", names(ehr), sapply(ehr, nrow)), collapse = ", "), "\n")

Tables: patients (200 rows), encounters (505 rows), observations (1753 rows), conditions (299 rows), medications (312 rows) 



# SOURCE A is a messy CSV export — the kind a warehouse dump or vendor feed
# actually looks like. Three problems we will have to fix later:
#   1. Mixed units: weight in lb AND kg, height in in AND cm
#   2. Inconsistent labels: "a1c" instead of "Hemoglobin A1c"
#   3. Missing values and mixed date formats (2023-05-02 vs 2023/06/11)
#
# readr::read_csv() can read an inline multi-line string directly, so we don't
# need to write anything to disk. We read every column as character so the
# messy mixed date formats and the blank A1c cell survive intact -- the
# Extract step below is what fixes types deliberately, not the CSV reader.
library(readr)

messy_csv <- "patient_id,measure,reading,units,recorded
P1000,weight,187,lb,2023-05-02
P1000,height,70,in,2023-05-02
P1000,a1c,7.1,%,2023-05-02
P1001,weight,82,kg,2023/06/11
P1001,a1c,,%,2023-06-11
P1002,weight,205,lb,2023-07-19
P1002,height,168,cm,2023-07-19"

source_a <- read_csv(messy_csv, col_types = cols(.default = col_character()))
cat("SOURCE A (messy CSV):\n")

SOURCE A (messy CSV):

print(as.data.frame(source_a), row.names = FALSE)

section: 6.1 Extract - normalize each source to a common schema
text:
6.1 Extract - normalize each source to a common schema
In the Extract step, we take columns with different names and formats from each source and map them into a common structure. This means renaming columns and reformatting where necessary, so that whether the data comes from a messy CSV file or a FHIR-style JSON feed, each row will have the same set of columns: (patient_id, measure, value, unit, date). This standardization is essential so further processing steps can treat all data uniformly.

# The first transform is STRUCTURAL: map each source's idiosyncratic columns
# onto a shared target schema. After this, every row looks the same:
#   patient_id, measure, value, unit, date
# regardless of whether it came from a CSV dump or a FHIR feed.
library(purrr)

TARGET_COLS <- c("patient_id", "measure", "value", "unit", "date")

extract_source_a <- function(df) {
  # CSV used "reading"/"units"/"recorded"; rename them to the target names.
  out <- df %>% rename(value = reading, unit = units, date = recorded)
  # as.numeric() turns the empty A1c cell into NA instead of a blank string.
  # suppressWarnings() silences the "NAs introduced by coercion" note — that
  # coercion is exactly what we want.
  out$value <- suppressWarnings(as.numeric(out$value))
  out[, TARGET_COLS]
}

extract_source_b <- function(records) {
  # Walk the list of named lists and pick the fields we care about.
  # tolower() + removing "body " turns "Body weight" into "weight" so it
  # matches Source A's "weight" / "height" labels.
  rows <- map_dfr(records, function(r) {
    tibble(
      patient_id = r$subject,
      measure = gsub("body ", "", tolower(r$display), fixed = TRUE),
      value = r$value,
      unit = r$unit,
      date = r$date
    )
  })
  rows[, TARGET_COLS]
}

a <- extract_source_a(source_a)
b <- extract_source_b(source_b)

# Harmonize leftover label differences: Source A said "a1c", we want one name.
a$measure <- ifelse(a$measure == "a1c", "hemoglobin a1c", a$measure)
b$measure <- ifelse(b$measure == "a1c", "hemoglobin a1c", b$measure)

# Stack the two sources into one table. bind_rows() rebuilds row numbers.
raw <- bind_rows(a, b)
cat("Extracted + unified schema:\n")

text:
6.2 Transform - unit normalization
Health data often comes in a mix of units (like pounds vs. kilograms, inches vs. centimeters), which can lead to serious mistakes if not handled—imagine treating a weight in pounds as if it were kilograms. To avoid such errors, we standardize (normalize) all measurements to SI units (kg, cm, %).

# Mixed units are a classic source of silent, dangerous errors in health data.
# A weight of 187 lb read as kg is a 2.2x error — enough to change a drug dose.
# We convert everything that isn't already SI into SI (kg, cm, %).
normalize_units <- function(df) {
  # case_when() is the vectorized version of the Python (measure, unit) -> conversion
  # lookup: for each row, check whether it needs a conversion; otherwise leave
  # the value and unit unchanged (already SI: kg, cm, %).
  df %>%
    mutate(
      new_unit = case_when(
        measure == "weight" & unit == "lb" ~ "kg",   # pounds -> kilograms
        measure == "height" & unit == "in" ~ "cm",   # inches -> centimetres
        TRUE ~ unit
      ),
      new_value = case_when(
        measure == "weight" & unit == "lb" ~ round(value * 0.453592, 1),
        measure == "height" & unit == "in" ~ round(value * 2.54, 1),
        TRUE ~ value
      ),
      unit = new_unit,
      value = new_value
    ) %>%
    select(-new_unit, -new_value)
}

normalized <- normalize_units(raw)
cat("After unit normalization (all SI):\n")

After unit normalization (all SI):

print(as.data.frame(normalized), row.names = FALSE)

      P1000         weight  84.8   kg 2023-05-02
      P1000         height 177.8   cm 2023-05-02
      P1000 hemoglobin a1c   7.1    % 2023-05-02
      P1001         weight  82.0   kg 2023/06/11
      P1001 hemoglobin a1c    NA    % 2023-06-11
      P1002         weight  93.0   kg 2023-07-19
      P1002         height 168.0   cm 2023-07-19
      P1003         weight  74.0   kg 2023-08-01
      P1003 hemoglobin a1c   6.4    % 2023-08-01
      P1004         height 181.0   cm 2023-08-03



Milestone 1 - align timestamps and handle missingness
In this step, we standardize the date formats (align timestamps) so all dates are uniform and machine-readable, and we handle missing data by removing any rows that do not have a measured value, ensuring only complete, properly-timestamped records are used downstream.

# Two remaining messes: dates in mixed formats, and a row with no measured value.
library(lubridate)

clean_temporal_and_missing <- function(df) {
  # Source A mixed "2023-05-02" and "2023/06/11". lubridate::ymd() accepts
  # either separator and parses both into Date objects; anything unparseable
  # becomes NA instead of crashing.
  df <- df %>% mutate(date = suppressWarnings(ymd(date)))

  before <- nrow(df)
  # Drop rows with no measured value. We do NOT impute a lab that was never
  # taken — inventing an A1c is worse than leaving the row out.
  df <- df %>% filter(!is.na(value))
  dropped <- before - nrow(df)
  cat(sprintf("Dropped %d row(s) with missing value; %d remain.\n", dropped, nrow(df)))
  df
}

clean <- clean_temporal_and_missing(normalized)

section: 6.3 Load — a validation gate before anything ships
text:
6.3 Load — a validation gate before anything ships
Before loading data into downstream systems, the pipeline must enforce basic data quality checks—rejecting any records that fail plausibility rules. Here, we introduce a validation “gate” that catches obviously erroneous values (such as impossible heights or weights), inspired by practices you’ll learn in depth in Module 8.

# A pipeline should REFUSE TO LOAD data that fails basic checks.
# These ranges are coarse "could a human possibly have this value?" bounds,
# not clinical reference ranges. A weight of 500 kg is a data error; 90 kg is not.
# This is a lightweight preview of Module 8's data-quality work.
PLAUSIBLE <- list(  # measure -> c(min, max) in SI units
  weight = c(2, 350),
  height = c(30, 250),
  `hemoglobin a1c` = c(3, 20)
)

validate <- function(df) {
  problems <- list()
  for (i in seq_len(nrow(df))) {
    r <- df[i, ]
    rng <- PLAUSIBLE[[r$measure]]  # NULL if we have no range for this measure
    if (!is.null(rng) && !(r$value >= rng[1] && r$value <= rng[2])) {
      problems[[length(problems) + 1]] <- list(patient_id = r$patient_id, measure = r$measure, value = r$value)
    }
  }
  problems
}

issues <- validate(clean)
if (length(issues) == 0) {
  cat("Validation gate: PASS\n")
} else {
  cat("Validation gate: FAIL",
      paste(sapply(issues, function(p) sprintf("('%s', '%s', %s)", p$patient_id, p$measure, p$value)), collapse = ", "),
      "\n")
}

Validation gate: PASS



Milestone 2 - assemble the reusable pipeline
In this section, we’ll assemble all the ETL steps into a single, reusable pipeline function. This function will combine extraction, transformation, cleaning, and validation, ensuring that all data passes through the same process before being loaded for analytics.

# Wrap the steps we already wrote into one reusable function with logging.
# In production this is the function an orchestrator (Airflow, Prefect) would call.
#
# R has no direct analog to Python's logging module for a teaching notebook, so
# these two tiny helpers print timestamp-free, level-tagged lines with cat() —
# same information, same points in the pipeline.
log_info <- function(msg) cat(sprintf("[INFO] %s\n", msg))
log_error <- function(msg) cat(sprintf("[ERROR] %s\n", msg))

run_pipeline <- function(csv_df, fhir_records) {
  log_info("EXTRACT: reading 2 sources")
  a <- extract_source_a(csv_df)
  b <- extract_source_b(fhir_records)
  a$measure <- ifelse(a$measure == "a1c", "hemoglobin a1c", a$measure)
  b$measure <- ifelse(b$measure == "a1c", "hemoglobin a1c", b$measure)
  raw <- bind_rows(a, b)

  log_info(sprintf("TRANSFORM: %d rows -> normalizing units", nrow(raw)))
  df <- normalize_units(raw)
  df <- clean_temporal_and_missing(df)

  log_info("VALIDATE: running plausibility gate")
  if (length(validate(df)) > 0) {
    # Abort rather than load bad data. Module 8 will show a quarantine alternative.
    log_error("LOAD ABORTED: validation failed")
    return(NULL)
  }

  log_info(sprintf("LOAD: %d clean rows ready for analytics", nrow(df)))
  df %>% arrange(patient_id, date)
}

analytics_ready <- run_pipeline(source_a, source_b)

[INFO] EXTRACT: reading 2 sources
[INFO] TRANSFORM: 10 rows -> normalizing units
Dropped 1 row(s) with missing value; 9 remain.
[INFO] VALIDATE: running plausibility gate
[INFO] LOAD: 9 clean rows ready for analytics

title: Module 6: Data Ingestion and ETL Pipelines
text:
6.4 Where orchestration fits
The pipeline function defined above executes the ETL (Extract, Transform, Load) workflow as a single sequence, running each step in order from start to finish within one call. While this linear execution works well in experimental or prototyping environments like notebooks, real-world data systems require additional capabilities to ensure robust, reliable, and manageable data processing.
In a production environment, you typically want to introduce orchestration — the process of managing, monitoring, and automating the execution of data pipelines. Dedicated orchestration tools such as Apache Airflow and Prefect provide features like: - Scheduling: Automatically running pipelines at specified times, such as hourly, daily, or in response to external triggers. - Retries: If a step fails, automatically attempting it again without manual intervention, possibly with configurable backoff and thresholds. - Dependency Management: Defining the precise order in which steps (known as “tasks”) should run based on their dependencies; e.g., not starting a transformation until extraction is complete. - Monitoring and Alerting: Keeping track of the status and health of pipeline runs, and sending notifications or logging errors if something goes wrong.
These tools visualize and control your pipeline as a Directed Acyclic Graph (DAG), where each function or step in your process is represented as a task. The conceptual structure for the pipeline above might look like this:
extract_a ─┐
           ├─> transform ─> validate ─> load
extract_b ─┘
In this DAG, the extract_a and extract_b tasks (which can run independently or in parallel) both feed their outputs into a transform task. The transformed data then passes through validate and load tasks sequentially. The DAG structure allows the orchestrator to know exactly which steps depend on others, and thus handle execution order, error handling, and retries automatically.
The benefit of using an orchestrator is that you do not have to change the logic of your ETL steps—these remain as R functions—but you wrap and schedule them within the orchestrator’s workflow definition. This separation allows you to build robust data pipelines that can handle failures gracefully, rerun specific steps, integrate with business calendars, monitor for issues, and alert you when things deviate from expectations. All of this is essential for reliable, production-grade data engineering.

title: Module 4: Health Data Standards and Formats
text:
Health-Informatics: An R Tutorial
Health Informatics in R · Part I: Foundations · Module 4 of 16
Data that can’t move between systems isn’t much use. Interoperability standards define how a patient record is packaged so a receiving system can understand it. This module walks the ladder from flat files up through HL7 v2, CDA, and FHIR, parsing each in R.

title: Module 4: Health Data Standards and Formats
text:
Learning objectives
By the end of this module you will be able to:

Place the main health-data formats on a spectrum from flat files → HL7 v2 → CDA → FHIR and say when each is used.
Parse an HL7 v2 message and pull structured values out of it.
Parse a CDA document (XML) with xml2.
Construct and serialize FHIR resources as plain nested R lists.
Represent the same patient fact across all three modern standards.

title: Module 4: Health Data Standards and Formats
text:
Dataset
We use small, hand-built sample messages — one HL7 v2 lab result, one CDA fragment, and FHIR resources we construct in code. They all describe the same synthetic patient (Ava Khan, A1c 7.2%) so you can watch one fact change costume.

title: Module 4: Health Data Standards and Formats
text:
4.1 The interoperability ladder









Format
Era / use
Shape
