title: Module 4: Health Data Standards and Formats
text:
4.2 Flat files - the baseline

# A FLAT FILE is the simplest health-data format: rows and columns, like a spreadsheet.
# Easy to parse, but it carries almost no standard meaning - nothing here says
# "this is a LOINC lab" or "this patient matches that hospital's medical-record ID."
#
# read.csv(text = csv) pretends a string is a file, so R can read it
# without writing anything to disk.
library(dplyr)
library(tibble)

csv <- "patient_id,observation,value,unit
P1001,Hemoglobin A1c,7.2,%
P1001,Systolic blood pressure,148,mmHg"

flat <- read.csv(text = csv, stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
cat("Flat file — trivially parsed, but no standard semantics or metadata:\n")

Flat file — trivially parsed, but no standard semantics or metadata:

print(flat, row.names = FALSE)

 patient_id             observation value unit
      P1001          Hemoglobin A1c   7.2    %
      P1001 Systolic blood pressure 148.0 mmHg

title: Module 4: Health Data Standards and Formats
text:
4.3 HL7 v2 - segments and fields
An HL7 v2 message is a set of segments (lines), each split into fields by |, with ^ separating components. MSH is the header, PID the patient, OBX an observation. It looks archaic but it’s everywhere.

# An HL7 v2 message is a text blob hospitals still use for real-time lab results,
# ADT (admit/discharge/transfer) events, and orders. It looks cryptic. Here is
# how to read it:
#
#   Each LINE is a SEGMENT (MSH, PID, OBR, OBX, ...)
#   Fields inside a segment are split by the pipe character |
#   Pieces inside a field are split by ^
#
#   MSH = message header (who sent it, what kind of message, version)
#   PID = patient identification (ID, name, date of birth, sex, address)
#   OBR = order/observation request (which test was ordered)
#   OBX = observation result (the actual lab/vital value)
#
# This sample says: Ava Khan (P1001) has A1c 7.2% (high) and SBP 148 mmHg (high).
hl7_msg <- "MSH|^~\\&|LAB|CENTRAL_HOSP|EHR|CENTRAL_HOSP|20260115093000||ORU^R01|MSG00001|P|2.5
PID|1||P1001^^^HOSP^MR||Khan^Ava^L||19680312|F|||12 Elm St^^Ithaca^NY^14850
OBR|1|||4548-4^Hemoglobin A1c^LN
OBX|1|NM|4548-4^Hemoglobin A1c^LN||7.2|%|4.0-5.6|H|||F
OBX|2|NM|8480-6^Systolic blood pressure^LN||148|mmHg|90-120|H|||F"
cat(hl7_msg, "\n")

MSH|^~\&|LAB|CENTRAL_HOSP|EHR|CENTRAL_HOSP|20260115093000||ORU^R01|MSG00001|P|2.5
PID|1||P1001^^^HOSP^MR||Khan^Ava^L||19680312|F|||12 Elm St^^Ithaca^NY^14850
OBR|1|||4548-4^Hemoglobin A1c^LN
OBX|1|NM|4548-4^Hemoglobin A1c^LN||7.2|%|4.0-5.6|H|||F
OBX|2|NM|8480-6^Systolic blood pressure^LN||148|mmHg|90-120|H|||F 



# There is no CRAN package needed here — this is realistically how HL7 v2 is
# hand-parsed: split the message into segments, then split each segment into
# fields.
#
# Real HL7 v2 messages separate segments with a carriage return (\r), not a
# normal newline (\n). Our sample used newlines so it would display nicely,
# so we convert them before parsing.
raw <- gsub("\n", "\r", hl7_msg)
seg_lines <- strsplit(raw, "\r")[[1]]

# Split each segment line on the pipe character to get its fields.
h <- lapply(seg_lines, function(s) strsplit(s, "\\|")[[1]])

# Each segment's first field is its 3-letter name (MSH, PID, OBR, OBX, ...)
seg_names <- sapply(h, function(s) s[1])
cat("Segments present:", paste(seg_names, collapse = ", "), "\n")

Segments present: MSH, PID, OBR, OBX, OBX 

# get_field(seg, n) returns HL7 field n (1-indexed, per the HL7 spec) from a
# segment vector. Field n sits at R index n + 1, because index 1 holds the
# segment name itself (PID, OBX, ...).
get_field <- function(seg, n) {
  idx <- n + 1
  if (idx <= length(seg)) seg[idx] else ""
}

# the PID (patient identification) segment.
# Fields are numbered from 1 in the spec; get_field() uses the same numbering.
#   PID-5 = patient name (Khan^Ava^L  →  family^given^middle)
#   PID-7 = date of birth (YYYYMMDD)
#   PID-8 = sex
pid <- h[[which(seg_names == "PID")]]
cat("\nPatient name (PID-5):", get_field(pid, 5), "\n")


Patient name (PID-5): Khan^Ava^L 

cat("Patient DOB  (PID-7):", get_field(pid, 7), "\n")

Patient DOB  (PID-7): 19680312 

cat("Patient sex  (PID-8):", get_field(pid, 8), "\n")

Patient sex  (PID-8): F 



Milestone 1 - extract all OBX results into a table

# Walk every segment in the parsed message. When we find an OBX (a result),
# pull out the useful fields and collect them into a tibble.
#
# Inside an OBX, the important field numbers are:
#   OBX-3 = observation identifier  (LOINC^name^coding-system, split by ^)
#   OBX-5 = the value               (e.g. 7.2)
#   OBX-6 = the unit                (e.g. %)
#   OBX-8 = abnormal flag           (H = high, L = low, N = normal)
obx_rows <- list()
for (seg in h) {
  if (seg[1] == "OBX") {
    code_field <- get_field(seg, 3)  # e.g. "4548-4^Hemoglobin A1c^LN"
    # split on ^ : piece 1 is the LOINC code, piece 2 is the display name
    pieces <- strsplit(code_field, "\\^")[[1]]
    loinc <- pieces[1]
    name  <- pieces[2]
    obx_rows[[length(obx_rows) + 1]] <- tibble(
      loinc       = loinc,
      observation = name,
      value       = get_field(seg, 5),
      unit        = get_field(seg, 6),
      flag        = get_field(seg, 8)
    )
  }
}

obx <- bind_rows(obx_rows)
cat("Structured results parsed from HL7 v2 OBX segments:\n")

Structured results parsed from HL7 v2 OBX segments:

print(as.data.frame(obx), row.names = FALSE)

  loinc             observation value unit flag
 4548-4          Hemoglobin A1c   7.2    %    H
 8480-6 Systolic blood pressure   148 mmHg    H

title: Module 4: Health Data Standards and Formats
Module 4: Health Data Standards and Formats
text:
4.5 FHIR - resources and REST
FHIR breaks the record into modular resources (Patient, Observation, Condition, …) exchanged as JSON/XML over a REST API. It is the modern standard and the one you’ll build against most. We construct resources as plain nested R lists — this is how FHIR JSON looks, so a named list is a faithful, dependency-free stand-in — and validate required fields with small hand-written check functions instead of pydantic.

# FHIR breaks the record into modular RESOURCES. A Patient resource is a
# JSON (or XML) object with a defined schema: id, name, gender, birthDate, ...
#
# Here a Patient resource is:
#   1. built as a named R list with the same keys/nesting FHIR JSON uses
#   2. checked against the required fields with a small hand-written validator
#   3. serialized back to JSON with jsonlite for sending over an API
library(jsonlite)

# A small hand-written validator standing in for what fhir.resources checks
# via pydantic in Python: confirm the required fields are present.
validate_patient <- function(p) {
  required <- c("resourceType", "id")
  missing_fields <- setdiff(required, names(p))
  if (length(missing_fields) > 0) {
    stop("Invalid Patient resource, missing required field(s): ",
         paste(missing_fields, collapse = ", "))
  }
  invisible(TRUE)
}

# Build one Patient resource for Ava Khan — the same person as in the HL7/CDA samples.
# name is a list of lists because a person can have several names (official, maiden, nickname).
patient <- list(
  resourceType = "Patient",
  id = "P1001",
  name = list(list(family = "Khan", given = list("Ava"), use = "official")),
  gender = "female",
  birthDate = "1968-03-12"
)
validate_patient(patient)

# toJSON() serializes the list to FHIR JSON (pretty=TRUE for readability;
# auto_unbox=TRUE makes single-element vectors print as scalars, not arrays)
cat(toJSON(patient, auto_unbox = TRUE, pretty = TRUE))

{
  "resourceType": "Patient",
  "id": "P1001",
  "name": [
    {
      "family": "Khan",
      "given": [
        "Ava"
      ],
      "use": "official"
    }
  ],
  "gender": "female",
  "birthDate": "1968-03-12"
}



# An Observation resource is FHIR's version of a lab result or vital sign.
# Notice the same LOINC code (4548-4) and the same 7.2% as in HL7 and CDA —
# the CODE is what makes the three formats talk about the same fact.
validate_observation <- function(o) {
  required <- c("resourceType", "id", "status", "code")
  missing_fields <- setdiff(required, names(o))
  if (length(missing_fields) > 0) {
    stop("Invalid Observation resource, missing required field(s): ",
         paste(missing_fields, collapse = ", "))
  }
  invisible(TRUE)
}

a1c <- list(
  resourceType = "Observation",
  id = "obs-a1c-1",
  status = "final",  # the result is complete, not a preliminary draft
  # code.coding is a list so one observation can be tagged with several systems
  code = list(coding = list(list(system = "http://loinc.org",
                                  code = "4548-4",
                                  display = "Hemoglobin A1c"))),
  # subject.reference points at the Patient resource we built above
  subject = list(reference = "Patient/P1001"),
  # valueQuantity holds the number, the unit, and the UCUM unit system
  valueQuantity = list(value = 7.2, unit = "%",
                       system = "http://unitsofmeasure.org", code = "%")
)
validate_observation(a1c)
cat(toJSON(a1c, auto_unbox = TRUE, pretty = TRUE))

{
  "resourceType": "Observation",
  "id": "obs-a1c-1",
  "status": "final",
  "code": {
    "coding": [
      {
        "system": "http://loinc.org",
        "code": "4548-4",
        "display": "Hemoglobin A1c"
      }
    ]
  },
  "subject": {
    "reference": "Patient/P1001"
  },
  "valueQuantity": {
    "value": 7.2,
    "unit": "%",
    "system": "http://unitsofmeasure.org",
    "code": "%"
  }
}



Milestone 2 - bundle resources for exchange
In FHIR, a Bundle groups multiple resources together, allowing them to be exchanged as a single package between systems (for example, when sending the results of a batch query or submitting multiple records in one API call).

bundle <- list(
  resourceType = "Bundle",
  type = "collection",
  entry = list(
    list(resource = patient, fullUrl = "Patient/P1001"),
    list(resource = a1c,     fullUrl = "Observation/obs-a1c-1")
  )
)
cat("Bundle type:", bundle$type, "\n")

Bundle type: collection 

cat("Entries    :", length(bundle$entry), "\n")

Entries    : 2 

cat("First entry resourceType:", bundle$entry[[1]]$resource$resourceType, "\n")

First entry resourceType: Patient 

cat("\nA FHIR Bundle is what a server returns from a query and what apps POST back.\n")


A FHIR Bundle is what a server returns from a query and what apps POST back.




Milestone 3 - the same fact in three standards
Here we illustrate how a single clinical fact, Ava Khan’s A1c is 7.2%, can be represented using three different healthcare data standards: HL7 v2, CDA (an XML-based standard), and FHIR (a modern JSON-based standard). Although each format has its own structure, they all use the same standardized LOINC code (4548-4) and value to represent the fact, enabling interoperability across systems.

# Same clinical fact — Ava Khan's A1c is 7.2% — in three packaging standards.
# The LOINC code 4548-4 is the glue; only the envelope changes.
cat("HL7 v2 (OBX):\n")

HL7 v2 (OBX):

cat("  OBX|1|NM|4548-4^Hemoglobin A1c^LN||7.2|%|4.0-5.6|H\n")

  OBX|1|NM|4548-4^Hemoglobin A1c^LN||7.2|%|4.0-5.6|H

cat("\nCDA (XML):\n")


CDA (XML):

cat('  <observation><code code="4548-4" .../><value unit="%" value="7.2"/></observation>\n')

  <observation><code code="4548-4" .../><value unit="%" value="7.2"/></observation>

cat("\nFHIR (JSON):\n")


FHIR (JSON):

cat('  {"code":{"coding":[{"system":"http://loinc.org","code":"4548-4"}]},\n')

  {"code":{"coding":[{"system":"http://loinc.org","code":"4548-4"}]},

cat('   "valueQuantity":{"value":7.2,"unit":"%"}}\n')

   "valueQuantity":{"value":7.2,"unit":"%"}}

cat("\nSame LOINC 4548-4, same 7.2% — three packaging standards.\n")


Same LOINC 4548-4, same 7.2% — three packaging standards.

title: Module 4: Health Data Standards and Formats
text:
Exercises

Add a second OBX (heart rate, LOINC 8867-4) to the HL7 message and confirm your parser picks it up without code changes.
Extend the CDA fragment with a second <observation> and adjust the XPath to return a list of all observations.
Build a FHIR Condition resource for hypertension (SNOMED 38341003) and add it to the bundle.

title: Module 4: Health Data Standards and Formats
text:
Key takeaways

Formats climb a ladder: flat file → HL7 v2 → CDA → FHIR, each trading simplicity for richer, more interoperable semantics.
HL7 v2 still dominates live messaging; FHIR is where new work happens — learn both.
The same coded fact travels across all of them; codes (Module 3) are the glue that makes exchange meaningful.


End of Part I — Foundations. Next: Part II — Interoperability and Data Engineering.

title: Module 2: Health Data Types and Structure
text:
Health-Informatics: An R Tutorial
Health Informatics in R · Part I: Foundations · Module 2 of 16
Before you can standardize, exchange, or analyze health data, you have to understand its shape. This module dissects the core entities of an EHR and the difference between structured, unstructured, and semi-structured data.

title: Module 2: Health Data Types and Structure
text:
Learning objectives
By the end of this module you will be able to:

Distinguish structured, unstructured, and semi-structured clinical data.
Identify the core clinical entities: patients, encounters, observations, conditions, medications, procedures.
Work with longitudinal, time-stamped data.
Join the EHR tables into an analysis-ready patient view.
Reshape observations between long and wide formats.

title: Module 2: Health Data Types and Structure
text:
Dataset
We reuse the synthetic EHR from Module 1 — same generator, same seed — so the relational structure is identical. We add a small block of free-text clinical notes to illustrate unstructured data.

# --- Self-contained synthetic EHR generator (no external downloads) ---
# This is the SAME generator from Module 1. We rebuild the fake hospital database
# here so this notebook can run on its own. Nothing here is a real patient.
library(dplyr)
library(tibble)

# This function generates a synthetic electronic health record (EHR) dataset.
# It creates mock tables for patients, encounters, observations, conditions, and medications,
# all with plausible structure, but not referencing any real patients or requiring external data.
make_synthetic_ehr <- function(n_patients = 200, seed = 42) {
  set.seed(seed)  # Ensures reproducibility: same seed => same fake people

  # --- patients table ---
  # Create a tibble with n_patients patients, each with a name, sex, age, and calculated birth_year.
  first <- c("Ava","Liam","Noah","Mia","Zoe","Omar","Ivan","Sara","Leo","Nina",
             "Ruth","Kai","Yara","Theo","Ida","Sam","Ana","Eli","Rex","Uma")
  last  <- c("Khan","Ortiz","Chen","Diaz","Patel","Ali","Brown","Nash","Reed","Vega",
             "Cole","Frost","Grant","Hale","Iqbal","Jain","Kerr","Lund","Mora","Park")
  sexes <- sample(c("male", "female"), size = n_patients, replace = TRUE, prob = c(0.49, 0.51))
  ages  <- sample(18:89, size = n_patients, replace = TRUE)
  # This block creates a tibble called 'patients' with columns representing patient attributes.
  # - "patient_id": Assigns a unique ID to each patient, e.g., "P1000", "P1001", etc.
  # - "given_name": Randomly selects one of the first names for each patient.
  # - "family_name": Randomly selects one of the last names for each patient.
  # - "sex": The pre-generated array of male/female assignments.
  # - "age": The pre-generated ages for each patient.
  # - "birth_year": Calculates the year of birth based on the age, assuming a reference year of 2026.
  patients <- tibble(
    patient_id  = sprintf("P%d", 1000 + (0:(n_patients - 1))),
    given_name  = sample(first, size = n_patients, replace = TRUE),
    family_name = sample(last, size = n_patients, replace = TRUE),
    sex         = sexes,
    age         = ages,
    birth_year  = 2026 - ages
  )

  # --- encounters table ---
  # The following block generates synthetic 'encounters' for each patient:
  # - Each patient has between 1 and 4 encounters (randomly chosen).
  # - Each encounter is assigned a type: 'ambulatory', 'emergency', 'inpatient', or 'wellness'.
  #   The probability of each type is respectively: 55% ambulatory, 15% emergency, 10% inpatient, and 20% wellness.
  # - The encounter's date is randomly set within a 3-year window starting from Jan 1, 2023.
  # - Each encounter receives:
  #     - A unique encounter_id (e.g., E00001, E00002, ...).
  #     - The associated patient_id.
  #     - The randomly assigned type and date.
  enc_rows <- list()
  enc_types <- c("ambulatory", "emergency", "inpatient", "wellness")
  for (pid in patients$patient_id) {
    # Randomly determine how many encounters (between 1 and 4) this patient has
    n_enc <- sample(1:4, 1)
    for (i in seq_len(n_enc)) {
      # For each encounter, pick a random day offset within 3 years (0 to 1094)
      day <- sample(0:(365 * 3 - 1), 1)
      enc_rows[[length(enc_rows) + 1]] <- tibble(
        encounter_id   = sprintf("E%05d", length(enc_rows) + 1),
        patient_id     = pid,
        # Assign encounter type with the specified probabilities
        encounter_type = sample(enc_types, 1, prob = c(0.55, 0.15, 0.10, 0.20)),
        # Calculate the date of the encounter by adding day offset to Jan 1, 2023
        date           = as.Date("2023-01-01") + day
      )
    }
  }
  # Assemble all rows into a tibble
  encounters <- bind_rows(enc_rows)

  # --- observations table ---
  # This block generates synthetic laboratory and vital sign results ("observations") for each encounter.
  #
  # 1. Define a set of different types of observations (e.g., height, blood pressure) with:
  #    - A human-readable name
  #    - The unit of measurement
  #    - A plausible lower and upper bound for values (lo, hi)
  obs_defs <- list(
    list(name = "Body height",              unit = "cm",   lo = 150, hi = 195),
    list(name = "Body weight",               unit = "kg",   lo = 50,  hi = 110),
    list(name = "Systolic blood pressure",   unit = "mmHg", lo = 100, hi = 165),
    list(name = "Heart rate",                unit = "/min", lo = 55,  hi = 100),
    list(name = "Hemoglobin A1c",            unit = "%",    lo = 4.8, hi = 9.5)
  )
  obs_rows <- list()
  # 2. For every encounter (row in the encounters table):
  for (i in seq_len(nrow(encounters))) {
    e <- encounters[i, ]
    # 3. For each defined observation type, with 70% probability:
    for (od in obs_defs) {
      if (runif(1) < 0.7) {  # 70% chance this observation is present in this encounter
        # 4. Generate a random value within the allowed range, rounded to 1 decimal.
        val <- round(runif(1, od$lo, od$hi), 1)
        # 5. Assemble observation fields:
        #    - Unique observation_id (zero-padded)
        #    - encounter_id and patient_id (from the current encounter)
        #    - observation name, value, unit, and date (from the encounter)
        obs_rows[[length(obs_rows) + 1]] <- tibble(
          observation_id = sprintf("O%06d", length(obs_rows) + 1),
          encounter_id   = e$encounter_id,
          patient_id     = e$patient_id,
          observation    = od$name,
          value          = val,
          unit           = od$unit,
          date           = e$date
        )
      }
    }
  }
  # 6. Create a table of all generated observations
  observations <- bind_rows(obs_rows)

  # --- conditions table ---
  # This block generates a table of medical conditions (diagnoses) assigned to each patient.
  #
  # Steps:
  # 1. Define a list of possible conditions (diagnoses) that a patient might have, called cond_pool.
  cond_pool <- c("Essential hypertension", "Type 2 diabetes mellitus", "Asthma",
                 "Acute bronchitis", "Major depressive disorder", "Osteoarthritis",
                 "Chronic kidney disease", "Anemia")
  cond_rows <- list()
  # 2. For every patient, randomly assign them between 0 and 3 unique conditions from the pool.
  for (pid in patients$patient_id) {
    # sample(0:3, 1) generates the number of conditions to assign (0-3),
    # and sample() picks that many unique conditions for that patient.
    n_cond <- sample(0:3, 1)
    if (n_cond > 0) {
      cs <- sample(cond_pool, size = n_cond, replace = FALSE)
      for (c_name in cs) {
        # 3. For each assigned condition, create a row with:
        #   - a unique condition_id (zero-padded)
        #   - the patient_id
        #   - the condition name
        cond_rows[[length(cond_rows) + 1]] <- tibble(
          condition_id = sprintf("C%05d", length(cond_rows) + 1),
          patient_id   = pid,
          condition    = c_name
        )
      }
    }
  }
  # 4. Assemble all condition records into a table.
  conditions <- bind_rows(cond_rows)

  # --- medications table ---
  # This section generates a medications table, which records what medications each patient is taking.
  #
  # Steps:
  # 1. Define a list of possible medications, called med_pool, that could be assigned to any patient.
  med_pool <- c("Lisinopril", "Metformin", "Albuterol", "Atorvastatin",
                "Sertraline", "Amoxicillin", "Ibuprofen", "Hydrochlorothiazide")
  med_rows <- list()
  # 2. For each patient in the patients table:
  for (pid in patients$patient_id) {
    # Randomly assign between 0 and 3 different medications to the patient.
    # sample(0:3, 1) picks how many meds the patient will get (can be zero).
    # sample() picks the medicines without replacement.
    n_med <- sample(0:3, 1)
    if (n_med > 0) {
      ms <- sample(med_pool, size = n_med, replace = FALSE)
      for (m in ms) {
        # 3. For each assigned medication, create a row that includes:
        #   - Unique medication_id (zero-padded)
        #   - patient_id
        #   - medication name
        med_rows[[length(med_rows) + 1]] <- tibble(
          medication_id = sprintf("M%05d", length(med_rows) + 1),
          patient_id    = pid,
          medication    = m
        )
      }
    }
  }
  # 4. Assemble all medication records into a table.
  medications <- bind_rows(med_rows)

  # Return a list containing all generated synthetic EHR tables.
  list(
    patients     = patients,
    encounters   = encounters,
    observations = observations,
    conditions   = conditions,
    medications  = medications
  )
}

# Generate the synthetic EHR data by calling the make_synthetic_ehr() function.
# This returns a list where each element is a table name (e.g., "patients", "encounters")
# and each value is a tibble with the data for that table.
ehr <- make_synthetic_ehr()

# Print out the names of each table along with the number of rows it contains,
# to provide a quick overview of the size of each synthetic EHR table.
cat("Tables:", paste(sprintf("%s (%d rows)", names(ehr), sapply(ehr, nrow)), collapse = ", "), "\n")

Tables: patients (200 rows), encounters (505 rows), observations (1753 rows), conditions (299 rows), medications (312 rows)

title: Module 2: Health Data Types and Structure
text:
2.1 Three kinds of health data









Kind
Example
How it’s stored
How you work with it




Structured
A1c = 7.2 %, coded diagnosis
Rows & columns, coded fields
dplyr, SQL


Unstructured
A progress note, radiology report
Free text
NLP (Module 10)


Semi-structured
HL7 / FHIR / CDA messages
Nested key–value / XML / JSON
Parsers (Module 4)



Roughly 80% of clinical information lives in unstructured text — which is why NLP is such a large part of applied informatics.

# This cell shows the difference between STRUCTURED data and UNSTRUCTURED data.
#
# Structured data lives in tables: every value sits in a named column (patient_id,
# observation, value, unit, date). A computer can count, filter, and join it easily.
#
# Unstructured data is free text — a clinical note. A human can read it, but a
# computer just sees a blob of characters until we use NLP (Module 10).

cat("STRUCTURED — observations table:\n")

STRUCTURED — observations table:

# Pick a few useful columns so the printout is easy to read
display_cols <- c("patient_id", "observation", "value", "unit", "date")
# ehr$observations is the observations tibble from the generator above.
# [, display_cols] keeps only those five columns.
# head(4) means "show the first 4 rows".
# print(..., row.names = FALSE) prints a clean table without row numbers.
print(as.data.frame(head(ehr$observations[, display_cols], 4)), row.names = FALSE)

 patient_id             observation value unit       date
      P1000             Body height 173.6   cm 2024-09-27
      P1000             Body weight 101.6   kg 2024-09-27
      P1000 Systolic blood pressure 118.9 mmHg 2024-09-27
      P1000              Heart rate  68.9 /min 2024-09-27

cat("\nUNSTRUCTURED — a free-text clinical note:\n")


UNSTRUCTURED — a free-text clinical note:

# A fake progress note, written the way a clinician might type it:
# abbreviations (y/o, h/o, HTN, T2DM), mixed facts, no columns.
note <- paste("58 y/o with h/o HTN and T2DM presents for routine follow-up.",
              "BP 148/88, denies chest pain. Continue lisinopril; recheck A1c in 3 months.")
cat(note, "\n")

58 y/o with h/o HTN and T2DM presents for routine follow-up. BP 148/88, denies chest pain. Continue lisinopril; recheck A1c in 3 months.

title: Module 2: Health Data Types and Structure
text:
2.2 The core clinical entities
An EHR is organized around a handful of recurring entities. In our synthetic model:

patients - the person (demographics)
encounters - a contact with the health system (a visit)
observations - measurements: vitals and labs
conditions - diagnoses / problems
medications - drugs prescribed or administered

Real systems add procedures, allergies, immunizations, orders, and results, but these five carry most teaching examples.

# This loop peeks at every EHR table so you can see what each one looks like.
#
# ehr is a list: names are table names, values are tibbles.
# For each table we print:
#   - a header with the table name
#   - the first 2 rows (just enough to see the columns and a sample of values)
for (name in c("patients", "encounters", "observations", "conditions", "medications")) {
  df <- ehr[[name]]  # pull that table out of the list
  cat(sprintf("=== %s ===\n", name))
  print(as.data.frame(head(df, 2)), row.names = FALSE)
  cat("\n")  # blank line between tables so the output is easier to scan
}

=== patients ===
 patient_id given_name family_name  sex age birth_year
      P1000        Eli       Brown male  41       1985
      P1001       Nina        Kerr male  42       1984

=== encounters ===
 encounter_id patient_id encounter_type       date
       E00001      P1000       wellness 2024-09-27
       E00002      P1000      emergency 2024-08-15

=== observations ===
 observation_id encounter_id patient_id observation value unit       date
        O000001       E00001      P1000 Body height 173.6   cm 2024-09-27
        O000002       E00001      P1000 Body weight 101.6   kg 2024-09-27

=== conditions ===
 condition_id patient_id                 condition
       C00001      P1000 Major depressive disorder
       C00002      P1000                    Anemia

=== medications ===
 medication_id patient_id  medication
        M00001      P1000 Amoxicillin
        M00002      P1000  Sertraline



Milestone 1 - the encounter as the hub of activity
In an EHR (Electronic Health Record), the encounter acts as the central point or “hub” of clinical activity. Most events—like measurements, diagnoses, orders, and treatments—are linked to a specific visit or encounter, making it the key connector for organizing and analyzing patient data over time.

# This cell treats the encounter as the "hub" of clinical activity:
# almost every measurement, diagnosis, and order hangs off a visit.
#
# Step 1: pull the encounters table out of the ehr list.
enc <- ehr$encounters

# Step 2: count how many encounters of each type we have.
# table() looks at one column and says "how many times does each value appear?"
# Example output: ambulatory 280, wellness 100, emergency 80, inpatient 51.
cat("Encounter types:\n")

Encounter types:

print(table(enc$encounter_type))


ambulatory  emergency  inpatient   wellness 
       272         69         48        116 

cat("\n")
# Step 3: for each patient, count their encounters, then summarize that distribution.
# group_by(patient_id) + summarise(n = n()) = "how many rows (visits) does each patient have?"
# The custom summary tibble then gives count / mean / min / max of those per-patient counts.
enc_per_patient <- enc |> count(patient_id, name = "n")

enc_summary <- tibble(
  count = nrow(enc_per_patient),
  mean  = mean(enc_per_patient$n),
  std   = sd(enc_per_patient$n),
  min   = min(enc_per_patient$n),
  `25%` = quantile(enc_per_patient$n, 0.25, names = FALSE),
  `50%` = quantile(enc_per_patient$n, 0.50, names = FALSE),
  `75%` = quantile(enc_per_patient$n, 0.75, names = FALSE),
  max   = max(enc_per_patient$n)
) |> mutate(across(everything(), ~ round(.x, 2)))

cat("Encounters per patient (distribution):\n")

Encounters per patient (distribution):

print(enc_summary)

# A tibble: 1 × 8
  count  mean   std   min `25%` `50%` `75%`   max
  <dbl> <dbl> <dbl> <dbl> <dbl> <dbl> <dbl> <dbl>
1   200  2.52  1.08     1     2     3     3     4

title: Module 2: Health Data Types and Structure
text:
2.3 Longitudinal, time-stamped data
Health data is intrinsically tied to time—meaning that many clinical measurements are collected repeatedly for a single patient across different visits or stages of life. This forms a longitudinal record, where values like blood pressure, weight, or lab results are tracked over intervals ranging from days to years. Analyzing these time-stamped data points allows us to observe trends, detect changes (such as improvement or deterioration), and assess how a patient’s health evolves rather than relying on just a single measurement. For example, by following one patient’s sequence of blood pressure readings, we can better understand their cardiovascular risk over time or see the effects of a new medication.

# Health data is time-stamped: the SAME measurement (blood pressure) is taken
# again and again. This cell follows ONE patient's systolic BP over time.
library(lubridate)

# Make a separate copy of the observations table so we can edit it
# without changing the original ehr$observations table.
obs <- ehr$observations

# Dates currently look like 2023-05-12 and are already stored as Date objects.
# as_date() (a no-op here) mirrors pandas' to_datetime() step for parity.
obs$date <- as_date(obs$date)

# Keep only the rows where the observation name is "Systolic blood pressure".
# This is a filter: obs$observation == "..." is TRUE/FALSE for every row;
# dplyr::filter() keeps only the TRUE rows.
sbp <- obs |> filter(observation == "Systolic blood pressure")

# Count how many SBP readings each patient has, then sort highest-first.
# We pick the patient with the MOST readings so the time series is interesting.
counts <- sbp |> count(patient_id, name = "n") |> arrange(desc(n))
pid <- counts$patient_id[1]  # the patient_id at the top of that ranked list

# Pull that one patient's SBP rows and sort them by date (oldest -> newest).
track <- sbp |> filter(patient_id == pid) |> arrange(date)
cat(sprintf("Patient %s — systolic BP over time:\n", pid))

Patient P1000 — systolic BP over time:

print(as.data.frame(track[, c("date", "value", "unit")]), row.names = FALSE)

       date value unit
 2023-10-23 118.5 mmHg
 2024-08-15 141.9 mmHg
 2024-09-27 118.9 mmHg
 2025-05-04 163.1 mmHg



# This code draws a line chart of the one patient's systolic BP over time.
# The shaded bands are a visual reminder of "normal" vs "elevated" ranges —
# they are teaching overlays, not a clinical diagnosis.
library(ggplot2)

band_range <- c(min(track$date), max(track$date))

# Plot date on the x-axis and BP value on the y-axis.
# geom_point puts a dot on each reading so you can see individual visits.
p <- ggplot(track, aes(x = date, y = value)) +
  # geom_rect draws a shaded band between two y-values across the whole x-range.
  # Green band: roughly "normal" systolic BP (<120).
  # Red band: roughly "elevated" (>=130). alpha makes the bands see-through.
  geom_rect(aes(xmin = band_range[1], xmax = band_range[2], ymin = 90, ymax = 120,
                fill = "normal (<120)"), alpha = 0.15, inherit.aes = FALSE) +
  geom_rect(aes(xmin = band_range[1], xmax = band_range[2], ymin = 130, ymax = 180,
                fill = "elevated (>=130)"), alpha = 0.10, inherit.aes = FALSE) +

title: Module 2: Health Data Types and Structure
section: 2.4 Joining tables into an analysis-ready view
text:
2.4 Joining tables into an analysis-ready view
Individual tables answer narrow questions. Real work usually needs them joined around the patient. Below we build a per-patient summary combining demographics, encounter counts, condition counts, and mean A1c.

# Real analysis rarely uses one table at a time. This cell JOINS several tables
# into one "patient view": one row per patient, with extra summary columns.
#
# Think of a join as: "for this patient_id, go look up extra facts in another table
# and glue them on as new columns."

patients <- ehr$patients  # the base table: one row per person

# Count encounters per patient, then name that column "n_encounters"
# so it becomes a column with a clear name after the join.
enc_n <- ehr$encounters |> count(patient_id, name = "n_encounters")

# Same idea for diagnoses: how many condition rows does each patient have?
cond_n <- ehr$conditions |> count(patient_id, name = "n_conditions")

# For A1c: keep only Hemoglobin A1c rows, then average the value per patient.
# round(1) keeps one decimal place (e.g. 7.2).
a1c <- obs |>
  filter(observation == "Hemoglobin A1c") |>
  group_by(patient_id) |>
  summarise(mean_a1c = round(mean(value), 1), .groups = "drop")

# Now glue the summaries onto the patients table.
# left_join keeps EVERY patient, even if they have no A1c / no conditions.
# Patients with no match get a missing value (NA) in that new column.
patient_view <- patients |>
  left_join(enc_n, by = "patient_id") |>
  left_join(cond_n, by = "patient_id") |>
  left_join(a1c, by = "patient_id")

# Missing encounter/condition counts should mean "zero", not "unknown".
# replace_na() turns NA into 0.
patient_view <- patient_view |>
  mutate(n_encounters = tidyr::replace_na(n_encounters, 0),
         n_conditions = tidyr::replace_na(n_conditions, 0))

# Show the first few rows of the combined view
head(patient_view)

# A tibble: 6 × 9
  patient_id given_name family_name sex      age birth_year n_encounters
  <chr>      <chr>      <chr>       <chr>  <int>      <dbl>        <int>
1 P1000      Eli        Brown       male      41       1985            4
2 P1001      Nina       Kerr        male      42       1984            2
3 P1002      Ava        Diaz        female    78       1948            1
4 P1003      Sara       Grant       male      79       1947            4
5 P1004      Uma        Mora        male      31       1995            2
6 P1005      Zoe        Khan        male      51       1975            1
# ℹ 2 more variables: n_conditions <int>, mean_a1c <dbl>



Milestone 2 - a simple cohort question
In this section, we demonstrate how to define a simple cohort—a specific group of patients—based on certain criteria in the data. For example, we can select patients with at least one documented medical condition and a mean Hemoglobin A1c (a key diabetes indicator) of 6.5 or above. This is known as a “cohort question”: identifying which individuals meet a set of rules or clinical thresholds for further study.

# A "cohort" is just a filtered list of patients who meet a rule.
# Here the rule is: mean A1c at or above 6.5 (a common diabetes threshold)
# AND at least one coded condition.
#
# The & means BOTH conditions must be true.
cohort <- patient_view |>
  filter(mean_a1c >= 6.5 & n_conditions >= 1)

# How many people made it through the filter, out of everyone?
cat(sprintf("Cohort size: %d of %d patients\n", nrow(cohort), nrow(patient_view)))

Cohort size: 93 of 200 patients

# Show a few of them, keeping only the columns that explain WHY they qualified
head(cohort[, c("patient_id", "age", "sex", "mean_a1c", "n_conditions")])

  patient_id   age sex    mean_a1c n_conditions

1 P1000         41 male        8.3            3
2 P1002         78 female      8.5            3

5 P1007         49 female      8.4            2
6 P1008         44 male        8.4            1

title: Module 2: Health Data Types and Structure
text:
2.5 Long vs. wide format
In the original data, observations are stored in long format. This means that each individual measurement (such as a patient’s single blood pressure or heart rate reading) occupies its own row in the table, identified by the patient, the type of observation, and the recorded value.
However, many analytic tasks and machine learning models require the data in wide format, where there is only one row per subject (such as a patient or an encounter), and each type of measurement gets its own column. For example, instead of having many rows for a patient with different tests, we would have a single row for that patient, with columns for “Body height”, “Body weight”, “Heart rate”, etc.
Converting between these formats is a common and essential skill in data science—often referred to as “reshaping” or “pivoting” the data. The process of moving from long to wide format is known as “pivoting,” while moving from wide back to long format is called “melting” or “unpivoting.”

# Long -> wide: mean value per patient per observation type
library(tidyr)

wide <- obs |>
  group_by(patient_id, observation) |>
  summarise(value = mean(value), .groups = "drop") |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = observation, values_from = value) |>
  mutate(across(-patient_id, ~ round(.x, 1)))

cat("WIDE format (one row per patient):\n")

WIDE format (one row per patient):

head(wide)

# A tibble: 6 × 6
  patient_id `Body height` `Body weight` `Heart rate` `Hemoglobin A1c`
  <chr>              <dbl>         <dbl>        <dbl>            <dbl>
1 P1000               169           95.3         72.1              8.3
2 P1001               173.         101.          73.9              7  
3 P1002               190.          NA           NA                8.5
4 P1003               174.          71.5         68.5              7.3
5 P1004               178.         101.          84.6              5.6
6 P1005                NA           58.4         90.2              6.9
# ℹ 1 more variable: `Systolic blood pressure` <dbl>



# This cell does the reverse reshape: WIDE -> LONG.
#
# wide already has patient_id as a normal column, which pivot_longer needs.
#
# pivot_longer "unpivots" the table:
#   cols       = columns to unpivot (everything except patient_id)
#   names_to   = name for the column that will hold the old column headers
#                (those observation names become values in a column called "observation")
#   values_to  = name for the column that will hold the numbers
#
# filter(!is.na(...)) drops rows where the value is missing — a patient who never had
# a height recorded should not get a blank height row in the long table.
long_again <- wide |>
  pivot_longer(cols = -patient_id, names_to = "observation", values_to = "mean_value") |>
  filter(!is.na(mean_value))

title: Health Informatics in R
text:
Welcome to Health Informatics in R — a tutorial series for health informatics professionals, clinical data scientists, and graduate students who want to work with health data as it actually exists: coded, standardized, exchanged, governed, and reused.
Health informatics is the discipline concerned with how health information is captured, structured, stored, exchanged, and used. This series starts with that infrastructure — EHRs, terminologies, HL7/FHIR, OMOP — and then applies R to privacy, clinical text, decision support, claims, warehousing, bulk data, and emerging AI.
Modules: 4 parts · 16 notebooks Level: Beginner through advanced · healthcare or public-health background helpful Language: R 4.x · Quarto/knitr-compatible Dataset: Synthetic throughout · no real patients Author: Dr. Zia U. Ahmed · Upatta Analytics

title: Health Informatics in R
text:
Why Health Informatics in R?
Analytics is only as good as the data infrastructure feeding it. This series focuses on the informatics layer that most analytics courses skip:

Representation first — ICD-10, SNOMED CT, LOINC, CPT, and FHIR resources are treated as data types, not footnotes.
Systems that talk to each other — ingestion, ETL, OMOP CDM, data quality, and bulk FHIR are the path from a hospital system to an analysis-ready table.
Use with care — de-identification, clinical NLP, decision support, claims, and warehousing are shown as applied informatics, not isolated algorithms.

title: Module 1: What Health Informatics Is
text:
Health-Informatics: An R Tutorial
Health Informatics in R · Part I: Foundations · Module 1 of 16
Health informatics is the discipline concerned with how health information is captured, structured, stored, exchanged, and used. It sits where information science, computer science, and healthcare meet. This first module builds the mental model for the whole series and gets you working with health data in R right away.
Health informatics is the discipline concerned with how health information is captured, structured, stored, exchanged, and used. It sits at the intersection of information science, computer science, and healthcare. The core questions are about the infrastructure and flow of data: How do we design electronic health record (EHR) systems that clinicians can actually use? How do we standardize medical terminology so a diagnosis recorded in one hospital means the same thing in another (through systems like SNOMED CT, ICD, or LOINC)? How do we make different systems talk to each other (interoperability standards like HL7 and FHIR)? How do we support clinical decision-making at the point of care? Informatics is fundamentally about representation, workflow, and getting the right information to the right person at the right time.
Health analytics is the application of statistical, computational, and machine-learning methods to health data in order to answer questions and drive decisions. Once informatics has captured and organized the data, analytics does something with it: predicting which patients are at risk of readmission, identifying disease clusters across a population, evaluating whether a treatment or program actually worked, forecasting hospital capacity, or estimating causal effects of an intervention. Analytics is about pattern-finding, inference, prediction, and evidence.
A useful way to see the relationship:
In practice the two are deeply interdependent. Analytics is only as good as the data infrastructure feeding it, and informatics systems are increasingly designed with downstream analytics in mind. The line also blurs in areas like clinical decision support, where an informatics system (embedded in the EHR workflow) delivers what is essentially an analytic output (a risk score or alert) to a clinician in real time. Given your work spanning spatial epidemiology and health analytics, you’ve likely lived the dependency from the analytics side — the quality of standardization and coding upstream in the informatics layer largely determines what’s even possible to model downstream.
One more distinction worth noting: informatics as a field also encompasses sub-specialties defined by scale and setting — clinical informatics (individual patient care), public health informatics (populations and surveillance), bioinformatics (molecular and genomic data), and consumer health informatics (patient-facing tools). Analytics tends to be described instead by what it does — descriptive, diagnostic, predictive, and prescriptive analytics.

title: Module 1: What Health Informatics Is
text:
Dataset
This series uses a self-contained synthetic EHR generator — no downloads, no PHI, fully reproducible from a fixed random seed. It produces five linked tables (patients, encounters, observations, conditions, medications) that we thread through every module, so each concept lands on the same data.

Synthetic data means the records are statistically plausible but entirely machine-generated. It is the safest way to learn on realistic-shaped health data without privacy risk, a theme we return to in Module 9.

title: Module 1: What Health Informatics Is
text:
1.1 The information lifecycle in healthcare
Every clinical fact travels a path:
capture → store → exchange → use

Capture - a clinician records a diagnosis; a device emits a vital sign.
Store - the fact lands in an electronic health record (EHR) as structured data.
Exchange - it moves between systems using standards (HL7, FHIR).
Use - it drives care, reporting, research, and analytics.

Informatics is responsible for making that path reliable, standardized, and usable. Analytics (Module-adjacent series) mostly lives in the final use stage.

title: Module 1: What Health Informatics Is
section: 1.4 Load and profile a synthetic EHR
text:
1.4 Load and profile a synthetic EHR
Below is the generator used throughout the series. Read it once now; later modules simply call make_synthetic_ehr().

# --- Self-contained synthetic EHR generator (no external downloads) ---
library(dplyr)
library(tibble)

# This function generates a synthetic electronic health record (EHR) dataset.
# It creates mock tables for patients, encounters, observations, conditions, and medications,
# all with plausible structure, but not referencing any real patients or requiring external data.
make_synthetic_ehr <- function(n_patients = 200, seed = 42) {
  set.seed(seed)  # Ensures reproducibility

  # --- patients table ---
  # Create a tibble with n_patients patients, each with a name, sex, age, and calculated birth_year.
  first <- c("Ava","Liam","Noah","Mia","Zoe","Omar","Ivan","Sara","Leo","Nina",
             "Ruth","Kai","Yara","Theo","Ida","Sam","Ana","Eli","Rex","Uma")
  last  <- c("Khan","Ortiz","Chen","Diaz","Patel","Ali","Brown","Nash","Reed","Vega",
             "Cole","Frost","Grant","Hale","Iqbal","Jain","Kerr","Lund","Mora","Park")
  sexes <- sample(c("male", "female"), size = n_patients, replace = TRUE, prob = c(0.49, 0.51))
  ages  <- sample(18:89, size = n_patients, replace = TRUE)
  # This block creates a tibble called 'patients' with columns representing patient attributes.
  # - "patient_id": Assigns a unique ID to each patient, e.g., "P1000", "P1001", etc.
  # - "given_name": Randomly selects one of the first names for each patient.
  # - "family_name": Randomly selects one of the last names for each patient.
  # - "sex": The pre-generated array of male/female assignments.
  # - "age": The pre-generated ages for each patient.
  # - "birth_year": Calculates the year of birth based on the age, assuming a reference year of 2026.
  patients <- tibble(
    patient_id  = sprintf("P%d", 1000 + (0:(n_patients - 1))),
    given_name  = sample(first, size = n_patients, replace = TRUE),
    family_name = sample(last, size = n_patients, replace = TRUE),
    sex         = sexes,
    age         = ages,
    birth_year  = 2026 - ages
  )

  # --- encounters table ---
  # The following block generates synthetic 'encounters' for each patient:
  # - Each patient has between 1 and 4 encounters (randomly chosen).
  # - Each encounter is assigned a type: 'ambulatory', 'emergency', 'inpatient', or 'wellness'.
  #   The probability of each type is respectively: 55% ambulatory, 15% emergency, 10% inpatient, and 20% wellness.
  # - The encounter's date is randomly set within a 3-year window starting from Jan 1, 2023.
  # - Each encounter receives:
  #     - A unique encounter_id (e.g., E00001, E00002, ...).
  #     - The associated patient_id.
  #     - The randomly assigned type and date.
  enc_rows <- list()
  enc_types <- c("ambulatory", "emergency", "inpatient", "wellness")
  for (pid in patients$patient_id) {
    # Randomly determine how many encounters (between 1 and 4) this patient has
    n_enc <- sample(1:4, 1)
    for (i in seq_len(n_enc)) {
      # For each encounter, pick a random day offset within 3 years (0 to 1094)
      day <- sample(0:(365 * 3 - 1), 1)
      enc_rows[[length(enc_rows) + 1]] <- tibble(
        encounter_id   = sprintf("E%05d", length(enc_rows) + 1),
        patient_id     = pid,
        # Assign encounter type with the specified probabilities
        encounter_type = sample(enc_types, 1, prob = c(0.55, 0.15, 0.10, 0.20)),
        # Calculate the date of the encounter by adding day offset to Jan 1, 2023
        date           = as.Date("2023-01-01") + day
      )
    }
  }
  # Assemble all rows into a tibble
  encounters <- bind_rows(enc_rows)

  # --- observations table ---
  # For each encounter, generate 0 or more plausible laboratory/vital sign results
  # This block generates synthetic laboratory and vital sign results ("observations") for each encounter.
  #
  # 1. Define a set of different types of observations (e.g., height, blood pressure) with:
  #    - A human-readable name
  #    - The unit of measurement
  #    - A plausible lower and upper bound for values (lo, hi)
  obs_defs <- list(
    list(name = "Body height",              unit = "cm",   lo = 150, hi = 195),
    list(name = "Body weight",               unit = "kg",   lo = 50,  hi = 110),
    list(name = "Systolic blood pressure",   unit = "mmHg", lo = 100, hi = 165),
    list(name = "Heart rate",                unit = "/min", lo = 55,  hi = 100),
    list(name = "Hemoglobin A1c",            unit = "%",    lo = 4.8, hi = 9.5)
  )
  obs_rows <- list()
  # 2. For every encounter (row in the encounters table):
  for (i in seq_len(nrow(encounters))) {
    e <- encounters[i, ]
    # 3. For each defined observation type, with 70% probability:
    for (od in obs_defs) {
      if (runif(1) < 0.7) {  # 70% chance this observation is present in this encounter
        # 4. Generate a random value within the allowed range, rounded to 1 decimal.
        val <- round(runif(1, od$lo, od$hi), 1)
        # 5. Assemble observation fields:
        #    - Unique observation_id (zero-padded)
        #    - encounter_id and patient_id (from the current encounter)
        #    - observation name, value, unit, and date (from the encounter)
        obs_rows[[length(obs_rows) + 1]] <- tibble(
          observation_id = sprintf("O%06d", length(obs_rows) + 1),
          encounter_id   = e$encounter_id,
          patient_id     = e$patient_id,
          observation    = od$name,
          value          = val,
          unit           = od$unit,
          date           = e$date
        )
      }
    }
  }
  # 6. Create a table of all generated observations
  observations <- bind_rows(obs_rows)

  # --- conditions table ---
  # This block generates a table of medical conditions (diagnoses) assigned to each patient.
  #
  # Steps:
  # 1. Define a list of possible conditions (diagnoses) that a patient might have, called cond_pool.
  cond_pool <- c("Essential hypertension", "Type 2 diabetes mellitus", "Asthma",
                 "Acute bronchitis", "Major depressive disorder", "Osteoarthritis",
                 "Chronic kidney disease", "Anemia")
  cond_rows <- list()
  # 2. For every patient, randomly assign them between 0 and 3 unique conditions from the pool.
  for (pid in patients$patient_id) {
    # sample(0:3, 1) generates the number of conditions to assign (0-3),
    # and sample() picks that many unique conditions for that patient.
    n_cond <- sample(0:3, 1)
    if (n_cond > 0) {
      cs <- sample(cond_pool, size = n_cond, replace = FALSE)
      for (c_name in cs) {
        # 3. For each assigned condition, create a row with:
        #   - a unique condition_id (zero-padded)
        #   - the patient_id
        #   - the condition name
        cond_rows[[length(cond_rows) + 1]] <- tibble(
          condition_id = sprintf("C%05d", length(cond_rows) + 1),
          patient_id   = pid,
          condition    = c_name
        )
      }
    }
  }
  # 4. Assemble all condition records into a table.
  conditions <- bind_rows(cond_rows)

  # --- medications table ---
  # This section generates a medications table, which records what medications each patient is taking.
  #
  # Steps:
  # 1. Define a list of possible medications, called med_pool, that could be assigned to any patient.
  med_pool <- c("Lisinopril", "Metformin", "Albuterol", "Atorvastatin",
                "Sertraline", "Amoxicillin", "Ibuprofen", "Hydrochlorothiazide")
  med_rows <- list()
  # 2. For each patient in the patients table:
  for (pid in patients$patient_id) {
    # Randomly assign between 0 and 3 different medications to the patient.
    # sample(0:3, 1) picks how many meds the patient will get (can be zero).
    # sample() picks the medicines without replacement.
    n_med <- sample(0:3, 1)
    if (n_med > 0) {
      ms <- sample(med_pool, size = n_med, replace = FALSE)
      for (m in ms) {
        # 3. For each assigned medication, create a row that includes:
        #   - Unique medication_id (zero-padded)
        #   - patient_id
        #   - medication name
        med_rows[[length(med_rows) + 1]] <- tibble(
          medication_id = sprintf("M%05d", length(med_rows) + 1),
          patient_id    = pid,
          medication    = m
        )
      }
    }
  }
  # 4. Assemble all medication records into a table.
  medications <- bind_rows(med_rows)

  # Return a list containing all generated synthetic EHR tables.
  list(
    patients     = patients,
    encounters   = encounters,
    observations = observations,
    conditions   = conditions,
    medications  = medications
  )
}

# Print out the names of each table along with the number of rows it contains,

title: Module 3 : Clinical Terminologies and Coding Systems
text:
Health-Informatics: An R Tutorial
Health Informatics in R · Part I: Foundations · Module 3 of 16
Free-text disease names don’t compute reliably: “high blood pressure”, “hypertension”, and “HTN” are the same concept to a human and three different strings to a machine. Controlled terminologies solve this by giving every clinical concept a stable code. This module is about those code systems and how to work with them in R.

title: Module 3 : Clinical Terminologies and Coding Systems
text:
Learning objectives
By the end of this module you will be able to:

Explain why standardized vocabularies exist and what breaks without them.
Identify the major coding systems, - ICD-10, SNOMED CT, LOINC, RxNorm, CPT, and what each is for.
Map / crosswalk between a local label and standard codes.
Navigate code hierarchies (parent–child relationships).
Define and apply a value set to a clinical dataset.

title: Module 3 : Clinical Terminologies and Coding Systems
text:
Dataset
We use small illustrative code tables built inline. These are real, verifiable codes for common concepts, deliberately kept to a handful per system, a teaching subset, not a complete terminology.

Licensing note. SNOMED CT (via UMLS), CPT (AMA), and others require licenses for production use and bulk distribution. Using individual codes to learn is fine; shipping full code sets is a licensing matter covered in the series appendix.

title: Module 3 : Clinical Terminologies and Coding Systems
text:
3.1 Why controlled vocabularies exist
Without a shared code, the same clinical idea fragments across strings, spellings, and abbreviations — making counting, exchange, and analysis unreliable.

# This cell shows WHY we need codes instead of free-text disease names.
#
# Five clinicians can type the SAME idea five different ways. A computer
# treats those as five different strings, so counts and joins break.
library(dplyr)
library(tibble)

# A vector of strings that all mean "high blood pressure" to a human
free_text <- c("Hypertension", "high blood pressure", "HTN", "htn", "Essential HTN")

# unique(...) keeps only unique values. length(...) counts how many unique strings remain.
# Result: 5 distinct strings for ONE clinical concept.
cat("Distinct strings for ONE concept:", length(unique(free_text)), "\n")

Distinct strings for ONE concept: 5 

cat("A coded system collapses all of these to a single identifier, e.g.\n")

A coded system collapses all of these to a single identifier, e.g.

cat("  ICD-10-CM  I10          (Essential hypertension)\n")

  ICD-10-CM  I10          (Essential hypertension)

cat("  SNOMED CT  38341003     (Hypertensive disorder)\n")

  SNOMED CT  38341003     (Hypertensive disorder)

title: Module 3 : Clinical Terminologies and Coding Systems
text:
3.2 The major coding systems

ICD-10-CM (International Classification of Diseases, 10th Revision, Clinical Modification)

Purpose: Used primarily for diagnoses in billing, epidemiology, and health statistics reporting in the United States.
Governs: Diagnoses (billing/reporting)
Who Maintains: World Health Organization (WHO), with clinical modification by the U.S.
Types of Concepts: Disorders, diseases, injuries, causes of death
Code Example: E11.9 (Type 2 diabetes mellitus without complications)
Notes: Codes are alphanumeric; hierarchical structure; widely required for insurance claims and public health reporting.

SNOMED CT (Systematized Nomenclature of Medicine—Clinical Terms)

Purpose: Comprehensive clinical terminology for recording clinical data in electronic health records (EHRs).
Governs: Clinical concepts (fine-grained)
Who Maintains: SNOMED International
Types of Concepts: Signs, symptoms, diagnoses, procedures, findings, body structures, organisms, substances, etc.
Code Example: 44054006 (Diabetes mellitus type 2)
Notes: Provides full semantic relationships; enables decision support, data analytics, and data exchange internationally; often used within EHRs to capture clinical meaning at the bedside.

LOINC (Logical Observation Identifiers Names and Codes)

Purpose: Universal standard for identifying health measurements, observations, and documents.
Governs: Laboratories, clinical observations, and measurements
Who Maintains: Regenstrief Institute
Types of Concepts: Laboratory tests, clinical measurements, survey panels, vital signs
Code Example: 4548-4 (Hemoglobin A1c in blood)
Notes: Extensively used for reporting lab test results and exchanging clinical data between institutions.

RxNorm

Purpose: Provides normalized names and unique identifiers for medications (clinical drugs), supporting electronic prescribing, pharmacy management, and data exchange.
Governs: Medications (ingredients/products)
Who Maintains: U.S. National Library of Medicine (NLM)
Types of Concepts: Medication ingredients, products, brand names, formulations
Code Example: 6809 (Metformin)
Notes: Connects different drug vocabularies in pharmacy systems and EHRs; facilitates e-prescribing and clinical decision support.

CPT (Current Procedural Terminology) / HCPCS (Healthcare Common Procedure Coding System)

Purpose: Standardized codes for medical procedures, diagnostic services, and supplies; used mainly for billing and insurance claims in the U.S.
Governs: Procedures and services
Who Maintains: CPT: American Medical Association (AMA); HCPCS: Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services (CMS)
Types of Concepts: Office visits, surgeries, radiology, lab tests, durable medical equipment, ambulance services
Code Example: 99213 (Office or other outpatient visit for the evaluation and management of an established patient)
Notes: CPT is widely used for medical billing; HCPCS extends CPT to cover Medicare, Medicaid, and supplies not included in CPT.

title: Module 3 : Clinical Terminologies and Coding Systems
section: 3.3 Crosswalking a local label to standard codes
text:
3.3 Crosswalking a local label to standard codes
In most real-world scenarios, data collected from clinical sources such as electronic health records (EHRs) is not already standardized with codes; instead, diagnoses and conditions are often recorded as free-text descriptions or local hospital-specific labels. The initial step in preparing this data for broader use is to “map” or “crosswalk” these local strings to universal standard code systems—such as ICD-10 for diagnoses or SNOMED CT for clinical concepts. This mapping process creates a bridge (the crosswalk) from each local term to the appropriate code(s) so that the information can be shared, analyzed, and compared in a consistent way across different organizations. In the example below, we demonstrate how to build such a crosswalk for a set of synthetic clinical condition names, linking each local label to its corresponding ICD-10 and SNOMED CT codes.

# A "crosswalk" is a mapping table: local hospital label -> standard codes.
# Real EHR data often arrives as local strings ("Essential hypertension").
# We need to attach the ICD-10 and SNOMED codes that the rest of the world uses.

# Each row: one local name, its ICD-10 code, and its SNOMED code
crosswalk <- tribble(
  ~local_label,                 ~icd10,    ~snomed,
  "Essential hypertension",     "I10",     "38341003",
  "Type 2 diabetes mellitus",   "E11.9",   "44054006",
  "Asthma",                     "J45.909", "195967001",
  "Acute bronchitis",           "J20.9",   "10509002",
  "Major depressive disorder",  "F32.9",   "370143000"
)

# Now we JOIN the human-readable displays onto those codes so the table is readable.
# rename(...) first so the join keys match:
#   icd10$code    becomes icd10$icd10       — then we merge on "icd10"
#   snomed$code   becomes snomed$snomed     — then we merge on "snomed"
# After the joins, each row has both codes AND both display names.
mapped <- crosswalk |>
  inner_join(icd10 |> rename(icd10 = code, icd10_display = display), by = "icd10") |>
  inner_join(snomed |> rename(snomed = code, snomed_display = display), by = "snomed")
mapped

# A tibble: 5 × 5
  local_label               icd10   snomed    icd10_display       snomed_display
  <chr>                     <chr>   <chr>     <chr>               <chr>         
1 Essential hypertension    I10     38341003  Essential (primary… Hypertensive …
2 Type 2 diabetes mellitus  E11.9   44054006  Type 2 diabetes me… Diabetes mell…
3 Asthma                    J45.909 195967001 Unspecified asthma… Asthma        
4 Acute bronchitis          J20.9   10509002  Acute bronchitis, … Acute bronchi…
5 Major depressive disorder F32.9   370143000 Major depressive d… Major depress…



Milestone 1 - apply the crosswalk to EHR conditions
To apply the crosswalk to EHR conditions, we start with a dataset of condition records from an EHR, where diagnoses are recorded as local human-readable strings (such as “Essential hypertension” or “Asthma”). The crosswalk table we built maps each local label to the appropriate standard codes (ICD-10 and SNOMED). We use a LEFT JOIN to merge the EHR conditions with the crosswalk: - For each EHR record, dplyr searches for a matching local label in the crosswalk. - If it finds one, it attaches the corresponding ICD-10 and SNOMED codes. - If it does not find a match, the standard code fields will be empty (NA), revealing any unmatched/unmapped data. This process simulates the real-world workflow in data integration projects, where standardized coding is essential for interoperability, research, and analytics.

# Apply the crosswalk to a small fake "conditions" table — the same idea as
# taking a hospital's diagnosis list and stamping standard codes onto it.
set.seed(42)  # fixed seed so everyone gets the same fake patients

# pool = the local labels we know how to map (from the crosswalk table above)
pool <- crosswalk$local_label

# Build 30 fake condition rows:
#   patient_id: random IDs from P1000 to P1119
#   condition:  a random local label from the pool
cond <- tibble(
  patient_id = sprintf("P%d", 1000 + sample(0:119, size = 30, replace = TRUE)),
  condition  = sample(pool, size = 30, replace = TRUE)
)

# LEFT join: keep every condition row; if a label has no match in the crosswalk,
# the icd10 / snomed columns will be empty (NA). That is how you find unmapped data.
coded <- cond |> left_join(crosswalk, by = c("condition" = "local_label"))

cat("Coded conditions (first 8):\n")

Coded conditions (first 8):

print(as.data.frame(head(coded[, c("patient_id", "condition", "icd10", "snomed")], 8)), row.names = FALSE)

 patient_id                condition   icd10    snomed
      P1048         Acute bronchitis   J20.9  10509002
      P1100                   Asthma J45.909 195967001
      P1064 Type 2 diabetes mellitus   E11.9  44054006
      P1024   Essential hypertension     I10  38341003
      P1073 Type 2 diabetes mellitus   E11.9  44054006
      P1099                   Asthma J45.909 195967001
      P1017 Type 2 diabetes mellitus   E11.9  44054006
      P1048         Acute bronchitis   J20.9  10509002

# sum(is.na(...)) counts how many rows failed to get an ICD-10 code.
# 0 unmapped rows means every local label was in the crosswalk.
cat("\nUnmapped rows:", sum(is.na(coded$icd10)), "\n")


Unmapped rows: 0

title: Module 3 : Clinical Terminologies and Coding Systems
text:
3.4 Code hierarchies
Clinical terminologies are organized as hierarchical structures rather than simple flat lists. This means that each individual diagnosis or concept is part of a larger, nested system of groupings.
For example, in the ICD-10 coding system, the hierarchy consists of several levels: - At the highest level are chapters, which encompass broad classes of conditions (such as “Diseases of the circulatory system”). - Within each chapter are blocks or ranges, which group together related categories (e.g., all types of diabetes-related conditions). - Each block contains multiple categories, which correspond to more specific disease groupings (e.g., Type 2 diabetes). - Finally, the lowest level includes the actual detailed codes that are recorded for patient diagnoses.
SNOMED CT, another widely used terminology, also employs a hierarchy, but it is structured using is-a relationships. In this system, every specific medical concept is connected “upward” to a more general parent concept (for example, “Type 2 diabetes mellitus” is a type of “Diabetes mellitus”, which itself is a type of “Endocrine disorder”, and so on).
These hierarchical relationships are powerful because they allow us to “roll up” or aggregate more specific codes into broader categories. This is essential for analyzing clinical data, creating reports (such as counts by chapter or disease group), and building value sets to identify all diagnoses that fall within a certain domain without needing to list every individual code.

# Terminologies are trees, not flat lists. This tiny table shows one ICD-10
# "family tree" fragment for a few of our codes:
#
#   code     = the specific diagnosis (what was recorded)
#   category = a slightly broader bucket (e.g. E11 = type 2 diabetes)
#   block    = a range of related categories
#   chapter  = the high-level grouping used in reports (e.g. "Circulatory")
#
# Rolling specific codes UP the tree is how you produce chapter-level counts
# without writing a separate rule for every detailed code.
icd_hier <- tribble(
  ~code,      ~category, ~block,                                  ~chapter,
  "E11.9",    "E11",     "E08-E13 (Diabetes mellitus)",           "Ch.IV Endocrine/metabolic",
  "I10",      "I10",     "I10-I16 (Hypertensive diseases)",       "Ch.IX Circulatory",
  "J45.909",  "J45",     "J40-J4A (Chronic lower respiratory)",   "Ch.X Respiratory",
  "J20.9",    "J20",     "J00-J06/J20-J22 (Acute respiratory)",   "Ch.X Respiratory"
)
icd_hier

# A tibble: 4 × 4
  code    category block                               chapter                  
  <chr>   <chr>    <chr>                               <chr>                    
1 E11.9   E11      E08-E13 (Diabetes mellitus)         Ch.IV Endocrine/metabolic
2 I10     I10      I10-I16 (Hypertensive diseases)     Ch.IX Circulatory        
3 J45.909 J45      J40-J4A (Chronic lower respiratory) Ch.X Respiratory         
4 J20.9   J20      J00-J06/J20-J22 (Acute respiratory) Ch.X Respiratory         



# Use the hierarchy to ROLL UP coded diagnoses to chapter level for a report.
#
# 1. Join our coded EHR rows with the hierarchy table, matching on ICD-10 code.
#    "icd10" is the column in `coded`; "code" is the column in icd_hier.
# 2. count(chapter) counts how many diagnosis rows fall in each chapter.
report <- coded |>
  left_join(icd_hier[, c("code", "chapter")], by = c("icd10" = "code")) |>
  count(chapter, name = "n")

cat("Diagnoses grouped by ICD-10 chapter:\n")

Diagnoses grouped by ICD-10 chapter:

print(as.data.frame(report), row.names = FALSE)

                   chapter  n
 Ch.IV Endocrine/metabolic 12
         Ch.IX Circulatory  3
          Ch.X Respiratory 10
                      <NA>  5



Milestone 2 - a SNOMED is-a walk
One of SNOMED CT’s core strengths is its use of a subsumption (or “is-a”) hierarchy. In this structure, every specific medical concept (like “Diabetes mellitus type 2”) is linked upward to increasingly broader concepts (such as “Diabetes mellitus”, then “Disorder of endocrine system”, ultimately up to “Disease” and then to the topmost root concept). This allows us to reason about clinical data at different levels of specificity: for example, we can easily group diagnoses by parent concept to answer questions like “how many patients have any kind of diabetes or endocrine disorder?” The code fragment below demonstrates a small, hand-constructed example of this hierarchical chaining.

# A named vector: each SNOMED code points to its immediate parent code.
isa <- c(
  "44054006"  = "73211009",   # Diabetes mellitus type 2 IS-A Diabetes mellitus
  "73211009"  = "362969004",  # Diabetes mellitus IS-A Disorder of endocrine system
  "362969004" = "64572001"    # ... IS-A Disease
)
labels <- c(
  "44054006"  = "Diabetes mellitus type 2",
  "73211009"  = "Diabetes mellitus",
  "362969004" = "Disorder of endocrine system",
  "64572001"  = "Disease"
)

walk_up <- function(code) {
  path <- code
  while (code %in% names(isa)) {
    code <- isa[[code]]
    path <- c(path, code)
  }
  path
}

for (c_code in walk_up("44054006")) {
  cat(sprintf("%-12s %s\n", c_code, labels[[c_code]]))
}

44054006     Diabetes mellitus type 2
73211009     Diabetes mellitus
362969004    Disorder of endocrine system
64572001     Disease

title: Module 3 : Clinical Terminologies and Coding Systems
text:
3.5 Value sets
A value set is a named, reusable list of codes that defines a clinical idea for a specific purpose - e.g. “all codes that count as diabetes.” Value sets power cohort definitions, quality measures, and decision-support rules.

# A VALUE SET is a named list of codes that means "this clinical idea"
# for a specific purpose (a quality measure, a cohort, an alert).
#
# Real diabetes value sets include hundreds of ICD and SNOMED codes.
# Ours is tiny on purpose: one ICD code and two SNOMED codes.
diabetes_valueset <- list(
  "ICD-10-CM" = c("E11.9"),                 # (real sets include E08-E13.*)
  "SNOMED CT" = c("44054006", "73211009")   # type 2 diabetes + parent "diabetes mellitus"
)
cat("Value set: Diabetes\n")

Value set: Diabetes

for (system in names(diabetes_valueset)) {
  cat(sprintf("  %s: %s\n", system, paste(diabetes_valueset[[system]], collapse = ", ")))
}

  ICD-10-CM: E11.9
  SNOMED CT: 44054006, 73211009

# Apply it to our coded EHR rows:
# %in% keeps rows whose icd10 value is in the ICD list of the value set.
in_set <- coded |> filter(icd10 %in% diabetes_valueset[["ICD-10-CM"]])
cat(sprintf("\nEHR condition rows matching the Diabetes value set: %d\n", nrow(in_set)))


EHR condition rows matching the Diabetes value set: 12

# length(unique(...)) counts distinct patient IDs (one patient can have several matching rows)
cat("Distinct patients:", length(unique(in_set$patient_id)), "\n")

Distinct patients: 12

title: Module 3 : Clinical Terminologies and Coding Systems
text:
Key takeaways

Controlled vocabularies replace ambiguous strings with stable codes.
Each system has a job: ICD (billing dx), SNOMED (clinical meaning), LOINC (measurements), RxNorm (drugs), CPT (procedures).
Crosswalks, hierarchies, and value sets are the three moves you’ll repeat constantly.


Next: Module 4 - Health Data Standards and Formats.

text:
Health-Informatics: An R Tutorial
Health Informatics in R · Part II: Interoperability & Data Engineering · Module 5 of 16
FHIR (Fast Healthcare Interoperability Resources) is a standard describing data formats and elements (known as “resources”) and an API for exchanging electronic health records. the backbone of modern health-data exchange, so this module goes deep: the resource model, references that link resources, bundles that package them, search, and the SMART on FHIR authorization pattern that lets apps read from an EHR.

text:
Learning objectives
By the end of this module you will be able to:

Explain the FHIR resource model and how references stitch resources together.
Build and validate Patient, Observation, and Condition resources from tabular data.
Assemble the three bundle types you meet in practice: collection, transaction, searchset.
Perform a FHIR search (simulated locally) and read a real server with a graceful fallback.
Describe profiles/validation and the SMART on FHIR launch/authorization flow.


Note on version. The FHIR resources in this notebook are represented as plain R lists modeling FHIR R5 JSON. The concepts — resources, references, bundles, search — are identical in R4, which you’ll see most often in the wild.

href: Notebooks/Part II -  Interoperability and Data Engineering (Intermediate)/05_fhir_in_depth.html#dataset
title: Module 5: FHIR in Depth
text:
Dataset
We reuse the synthetic EHR generator (identical to Part I) and turn a slice of it into real FHIR resources. Live-server calls target public sandboxes but fall back to local resources so the notebook always runs.

# --- Self-contained synthetic EHR generator (identical to Part I) ---
# This is the SAME generator from Module 1. We rebuild the fake hospital database
# here so this notebook can run on its own. Nothing here is a real patient.
library(dplyr)
library(tibble)

# This function generates a synthetic electronic health record (EHR) dataset.
# It creates mock tables for patients, encounters, observations, conditions, and medications,
# all with plausible structure, but not referencing any real patients or requiring external data.
make_synthetic_ehr <- function(n_patients = 200, seed = 42) {
  # Generate a small, internally-consistent synthetic EHR dataset.
  # Returns a list of linked tibbles: patients, encounters, observations,
  # conditions, and medications. This is for illustrative, educational use.
  set.seed(seed)  # same seed => same fake people every run

  # --- patients table ---
  # Create a tibble with n_patients patients, each with a name, sex, age, and birth year.
  first <- c("Ava","Liam","Noah","Mia","Zoe","Omar","Ivan","Sara","Leo","Nina",
             "Ruth","Kai","Yara","Theo","Ida","Sam","Ana","Eli","Rex","Uma")
  last  <- c("Khan","Ortiz","Chen","Diaz","Patel","Ali","Brown","Nash","Reed","Vega",
             "Cole","Frost","Grant","Hale","Iqbal","Jain","Kerr","Lund","Mora","Park")
  sexes <- sample(c("male", "female"), size = n_patients, replace = TRUE, prob = c(0.49, 0.51))
  ages  <- sample(18:89, size = n_patients, replace = TRUE)
  # Columns:
  #   patient_id  — unique ID, e.g. "P1000", "P1001"
  #   given_name / family_name — randomly chosen from the name lists
  #   sex, age — pre-generated vectors
  #   birth_year — derived from age, assuming the reference year 2026
  patients <- tibble(
    patient_id  = sprintf("P%d", 1000 + (0:(n_patients - 1))),
    given_name  = sample(first, size = n_patients, replace = TRUE),
    family_name = sample(last,  size = n_patients, replace = TRUE),
    sex         = sexes,
    age         = ages,
    birth_year  = 2026 - ages
  )

  # --- encounters table ---
  # Each patient gets 1–4 visits. Types and dates are random but internally consistent.
  #   encounter_id    — unique, zero-padded (E00001, E00002, ...)
  #   encounter_type  — ambulatory 55%, emergency 15%, inpatient 10%, wellness 20%
  #   date            — a random day in a 3-year window starting 2023-01-01
  enc_types <- c("ambulatory", "emergency", "inpatient", "wellness")
  enc_list <- vector("list", 0)
  n <- 0
  for (pid in patients$patient_id) {
    n_visits <- sample.int(4, 1)  # 1 to 4 encounters per patient
    for (j in seq_len(n_visits)) {
      n <- n + 1
      day <- sample(0:(365 * 3 - 1), 1)  # offset within 3 years
      enc_list[[n]] <- tibble(
        encounter_id = sprintf("E%05d", n),
        patient_id = pid,
        encounter_type = sample(enc_types, 1, prob = c(0.55, 0.15, 0.10, 0.20)),
        date = as.Date("2023-01-01") + day
      )
    }
  }
  encounters <- bind_rows(enc_list)

  # --- observations table ---
  # Labs and vitals attached to encounters. Each row is (name, unit, lo, hi).
  # A value is drawn uniformly in [lo, hi]; 70% of (encounter, measure) pairs exist
  # so the table looks sparse the way a real EHR does.
  obs_defs <- tribble(
    ~name, ~unit, ~lo, ~hi,
    "Body height", "cm", 150, 195,
    "Body weight", "kg", 50, 110,
    "Systolic blood pressure", "mmHg", 100, 165,
    "Heart rate", "/min", 55, 100,
    "Hemoglobin A1c", "%", 4.8, 9.5
  )
  obs_list <- vector("list", 0)
  m <- 0
  for (i in seq_len(nrow(encounters))) {
    e <- encounters[i, ]
    for (k in seq_len(nrow(obs_defs))) {
      if (runif(1) < 0.7) {
        m <- m + 1
        obs_list[[m]] <- tibble(
          observation_id = sprintf("O%06d", m),
          encounter_id = e$encounter_id,
          patient_id = e$patient_id,
          observation = obs_defs$name[k],
          value = round(runif(1, obs_defs$lo[k], obs_defs$hi[k]), 1),
          unit = obs_defs$unit[k],
          date = e$date
        )
      }
    }
  }
  observations <- bind_rows(obs_list)

  # --- conditions table ---
  # Each patient is assigned 0–3 unique diagnoses from a small pool.
  cond_pool <- c("Essential hypertension", "Type 2 diabetes mellitus", "Asthma",
                 "Acute bronchitis", "Major depressive disorder", "Osteoarthritis",
                 "Chronic kidney disease", "Anemia")
  cond_list <- vector("list", 0)
  cn <- 0
  for (pid in patients$patient_id) {
    n_cond <- sample(0:3, 1)
    if (n_cond > 0) {
      chosen <- sample(cond_pool, size = n_cond, replace = FALSE)
      for (cc in chosen) {
        cn <- cn + 1
        cond_list[[cn]] <- tibble(condition_id = sprintf("C%05d", cn), patient_id = pid, condition = cc)
      }
    }
  }
  conditions <- bind_rows(cond_list)

  # --- medications table ---
  # Same pattern as conditions: 0–3 unique drugs per patient.
  med_pool <- c("Lisinopril", "Metformin", "Albuterol", "Atorvastatin",
                "Sertraline", "Amoxicillin", "Ibuprofen", "Hydrochlorothiazide")
  med_list <- vector("list", 0)
  mn <- 0
  for (pid in patients$patient_id) {
    n_med <- sample(0:3, 1)
    if (n_med > 0) {
      chosen <- sample(med_pool, size = n_med, replace = FALSE)
      for (mm in chosen) {
        mn <- mn + 1
        med_list[[mn]] <- tibble(medication_id = sprintf("M%05d", mn), patient_id = pid, medication = mm)
      }
    }
  }
  medications <- bind_rows(med_list)

  list(
    patients = patients,
    encounters = encounters,
    observations = observations,
    conditions = conditions,
    medications = medications
  )
}

# Generate the five linked tables. Each notebook in this series starts from here.
ehr <- make_synthetic_ehr()
cat("Tables:", paste(sprintf("%s (%d rows)", names(ehr), sapply(ehr, nrow)), collapse = ", "), "\n")

Tables: patients (200 rows), encounters (505 rows), observations (1753 rows), conditions (299 rows), medications (312 rows)
