title: Module 5: FHIR in Depth
text:
5.1 The resource model and references
In FHIR, information is separated into distinct building blocks called resources. These resources do not contain other resources directly; instead, they are linked by references using the pattern ResourceType/id. For example, an Observation resource links to its associated patient through a reference like subject: Patient/P1001. This referencing mechanism enables systems to piece together a complete health record from separately stored resources, rather than relying on deeply nested or monolithic data structures.

# A FHIR resource is a JSON (or XML) object with a defined schema: resourceType,
# id, name, gender, birthDate, ...  We represent it as a plain nested named list
# in R — this *is* how FHIR JSON looks, so a named list is a faithful,
# dependency-free stand-in for a schema-validating library like Python's
# fhir.resources. We build one from a row in our table.
library(jsonlite)

# Pick a patient with a Hemoglobin A1c reading among their observations, so the
# examples below (and the search demo in 5.3) have something to find.
pid_with_a1c <- ehr$observations %>%
  filter(observation == "Hemoglobin A1c") %>%
  pull(patient_id) %>%
  unique() %>%
  .[1]

row <- ehr$patients %>% filter(patient_id == pid_with_a1c) %>% slice(1)

# Build a Patient resource from that row.
# name is a list of lists because a person can have several names (official, maiden, nickname).
# given is also a list: some people have more than one given name.
# birthDate uses YYYY-MM-DD; we only know the year, so we use January 1 as a stand-in.
patient <- list(
  resourceType = "Patient",
  id = row$patient_id,
  name = list(list(use = "official",
                    family = row$family_name,
                    given = list(row$given_name))),
  gender = row$sex,
  birthDate = sprintf("%d-01-01", row$birth_year)
)

# toJSON() serializes the list to FHIR JSON (pretty = TRUE makes it readable)
cat(toJSON(patient, auto_unbox = TRUE, pretty = TRUE))

{
  "resourceType": "Patient",
  "id": "P1000",
  "name": [
    {
      "use": "official",
      "family": "Brown",
      "given": [
        "Eli"
      ]
    }
  ],
  "gender": "male",
  "birthDate": "1985-01-01"
}



Milestone 1 - convert tabular observations to referenced Observation resources

# An Observation resource is FHIR's version of a lab result or vital sign.
# The CODE (LOINC) is what makes the observation interoperable — the same
# 4548-4 means "Hemoglobin A1c" in every FHIR system, not just ours.
#
# LOINC maps our human-readable observation names to official codes.
LOINC <- c(
  "Hemoglobin A1c" = "4548-4",
  "Systolic blood pressure" = "8480-6",
  "Heart rate" = "8867-4",
  "Body weight" = "29463-7",
  "Body height" = "8302-2"
)

pid <- row$patient_id  # e.g. "P1000" — the same person as the Patient above

# filter() keeps only this patient's observations. We order so the Hemoglobin
# A1c reading (guaranteed to exist for this patient) sorts first, then keep
# the first four rows so the example stays small.
pt_obs <- ehr$observations %>%
  filter(patient_id == pid) %>%
  arrange(desc(observation == "Hemoglobin A1c")) %>%
  head(4)

obs_resources <- vector("list", nrow(pt_obs))
for (i in seq_len(nrow(pt_obs))) {  # walk each observation row
  o <- pt_obs[i, ]
  obs_resources[[i]] <- list(
    resourceType = "Observation",
    status = "final",  # the result is complete, not a preliminary draft
    # code.coding is a list so one observation can be tagged with several systems
    code = list(coding = list(list(system = "http://loinc.org",
                                    code = unname(LOINC[o$observation]),
                                    display = o$observation))),
    # subject.reference points at the Patient resource we built above.
    # The pattern is always ResourceType/id — that is the FHIR "pointer".
    subject = list(reference = sprintf("Patient/%s", pid)),
    effectiveDateTime = as.character(o$date),  # when the measurement was taken
    # valueQuantity holds the number and the unit
    valueQuantity = list(value = o$value, unit = o$unit)
  )
}

cat(sprintf("Built %d Observation resources, all referencing Patient/%s\n", length(obs_resources), pid))

Built 4 Observation resources, all referencing Patient/P1000

cat("\nExample subject reference:", obs_resources[[1]]$subject$reference, "\n")


Example subject reference: Patient/P1000

title: Module 5: FHIR in Depth
text:
5.2 Bundles: collection, transaction, searchset
A Bundle in FHIR is a resource that groups together multiple other resources into a single package. The meaning of a Bundle depends on its type field, which defines how its contents should be interpreted:

collection: Represents a simple group of resources bundled together, such as a set of related documents or a snapshot of information.
transaction: Specifies a batch of operations that should be performed together in a single, atomic action on a FHIR server—meaning either all succeed or none are applied. Each item in the bundle includes instructions on what to do (in a request field).
searchset: Represents the results from a FHIR server search query. When you ask a FHIR server to search for resources, it responds with a Bundle of type searchset containing the matching resources.


# A Bundle packages several resources into one payload.
# type="transaction" means: apply every entry as a write, all-or-nothing.
# If any entry fails on the server, none of them should be saved.
#
# Each entry needs two pieces:
#   resource  — the FHIR resource itself
#   request   — the HTTP method and URL the server should execute

# PUT Patient/{id} → create-or-replace this patient (idempotent: same id, same result)
tx_entries <- list(
  list(resource = patient, request = list(method = "PUT", url = sprintf("Patient/%s", pid)))
)

# POST Observation → create a new observation; the server assigns the id
for (obs in obs_resources) {
  tx_entries[[length(tx_entries) + 1]] <- list(resource = obs,
                                                request = list(method = "POST", url = "Observation"))
}

transaction <- list(resourceType = "Bundle", type = "transaction", entry = tx_entries)

cat("Transaction bundle:\n")

Transaction bundle:

cat("  entries:", length(transaction$entry), "\n")

  entries: 5 

cat("  first request:", transaction$entry[[1]]$request$method, transaction$entry[[1]]$request$url, "\n")

  first request: PUT Patient/P1000 

cat("  this is what an app POSTs to [base]/ to write atomically\n")

  this is what an app POSTs to [base]/ to write atomically

href: Notebooks/Part II -  Interoperability and Data Engineering (Intermediate)/05_fhir_in_depth.html#fhir-search---simulated-locally
title: Module 5: FHIR in Depth
text:
5.3 FHIR search - simulated locally
In FHIR, performing a search typically involves making an HTTP GET request such as: [base]/Observation?subject=Patient/P1001&code=4548-4 This instructs the FHIR server to return all Observation resources associated with subject Patient/P1001 and the specific code 4548-4. The server responds with a Bundle of type searchset, which contains the results matching the search criteria. In this example, we mimic this search functionality locally by iterating through our in-memory resources, allowing you to understand how FHIR servers process searches without requiring a live server connection.

# A real FHIR search is an HTTP GET like:
#   [base]/Observation?subject=Patient/P1001&code=4548-4
# The server returns a Bundle with type="searchset".
#
# We don't need a live server to see the mechanics. This function walks an
# in-memory list of resources and applies the same two filters a server would:
#   subject  — whose record is this?  (Patient/P1001)
#   code     — which LOINC (or other) code?
fhir_search <- function(resources, resource_type, subject = NULL, code = NULL) {
  # Minimal FHIR-style search over in-memory resources -> searchset Bundle.
  hits <- list()
  for (r in resources) {
    # Skip anything that isn't the requested resource type (Patient vs Observation)
    if (r$resourceType != resource_type) next
    ok <- TRUE
    # subject filter: Observation.subject.reference must match exactly
    if (!is.null(subject)) {
      ok <- ok && (!is.null(r$subject) && identical(r$subject$reference, subject))
    }
    # code filter: look inside code.coding[] for the requested code
    if (!is.null(code)) {
      codes <- if (!is.null(r$code)) sapply(r$code$coding, function(c) c$code) else character(0)
      ok <- ok && (code %in% codes)
    }
    if (ok) hits[[length(hits) + 1]] <- r
  }
  # A searchset Bundle carries the matching resources plus a total count
  list(resourceType = "Bundle", type = "searchset", total = length(hits),
       entry = lapply(hits, function(h) list(resource = h)))
}

# Search the patient + their observations as if they were a tiny FHIR server
pool <- c(list(patient), obs_resources)
result <- fhir_search(pool, "Observation", subject = sprintf("Patient/%s", pid), code = "4548-4")

cat(sprintf("GET [base]/Observation?subject=Patient/%s&code=4548-4\n", pid))

GET [base]/Observation?subject=Patient/P1000&code=4548-4

cat("searchset total:", result$total, "\n")

searchset total: 3 

for (e in result$entry) {
  q <- e$resource$valueQuantity
  cat(sprintf("  -> %s: %s %s\n", e$resource$code$coding[[1]]$display, q$value, q$unit))
}

  -> Hemoglobin A1c: 7.4 %
  -> Hemoglobin A1c: 9.1 %
  -> Hemoglobin A1c: 8.5 %

title: Module 5: FHIR in Depth
section: 5.4 Reading from a real server — with a fallback explained
text:
5.4 Reading from a real server — with a fallback explained
In the context of FHIR and real-world notebooks: when fetching resources from public sandboxes (such as HAPI), you would typically use the httr package for HTTP calls. However, notebooks are sometimes unable to access external servers, which could cause code to fail. To prevent this, well-designed tutorial code uses “graceful degradation”: if a live server can’t be reached, it falls back to using local data, ensuring the notebook still works and doesn’t crash.

# Against a public sandbox (e.g. HAPI FHIR) you read a resource with HTTP GET:
#   GET https://hapi.fhir.org/baseR5/Patient/P1001
#   Accept: application/fhir+json
#
# Tutorial notebooks often can't reach the internet, so this function
# degrades gracefully: try the live server, and if anything fails (timeout,
# DNS, non-200, ...), return the local Patient we already built.
library(httr)

get_patient_live <- function(base, pid, timeout_s = 5) {
  # Try a live FHIR read; fall back to the local resource on any failure.
  tryCatch({
    r <- GET(
      sprintf("%s/Patient/%s", base, pid),
      add_headers(Accept = "application/fhir+json"),  # ask for FHIR JSON, not HTML
      timeout(timeout_s)  # don't hang forever if the sandbox is down
    )
    if (status_code(r) == 200) {  # 200 = the resource was found
      list(source = "live", data = content(r, as = "parsed", type = "application/json"))
    } else {
      stop("non-200 response")  # fall through to local data via the error handler
    }
  }, error = function(e) {
    # network error, timeout, non-200, etc. — fall back to the local resource.
    # `patient` here is the dict-like list form of our local Patient (same
    # shape as live JSON) built earlier in the notebook.
    list(source = "fallback", data = patient)
  })
}

res <- get_patient_live("https://hapi.fhir.org/baseR5", pid)
cat(sprintf("source: %s\n", res$source))

source: fallback

cat("patient family name:", res$data$name[[1]]$family, "\n")

patient family name: Brown 

cat("\n(The REST pattern is identical against any FHIR server; only the base URL changes.)\n")


(The REST pattern is identical against any FHIR server; only the base URL changes.)

section: 5.6 What is SMART on FHIR? How do apps connect?
text:
5.6 What is SMART on FHIR? How do apps connect?
SMART on FHIR is a specification that allows third-party applications to securely connect to electronic health record (EHR) systems. It does this by combining FHIR (for accessing health data) with OAuth2 (for authorization and user consent).
Here’s how the SMART on FHIR authorization process typically works:

Launch – The EHR launches an app, providing both a launch token and the FHIR server’s base URL.
Authorize – The app redirects the user to the EHR’s OAuth2 authorization page, asking for specific “scopes” (permissions), for example, the ability to read a patient’s Observations (patient/Observation.read).
Token – After the user approves, the app receives an authorization code, which it exchanges with the EHR for an access token.
Call – The app makes FHIR API requests to the server, including Authorization: Bearer <token> in the HTTP header; this proves the app’s identity and defines which data it is allowed to access.


# SMART on FHIR's last step is an ordinary FHIR search with an extra header:
#   Authorization: Bearer <access_token>
# The token is what the EHR issued after the user authorized the app.
# Scopes on that token (e.g. patient/Observation.read) decide what the
# server will actually return.
#
# We don't make a live call here — we just show the request you would send.
authorized_search <- function(base, token, path) {
  headers <- list(
    Authorization = sprintf("Bearer %s", token),  # proves the app is allowed to read
    Accept = "application/fhir+json"
  )
  # Live version would be: httr::GET(sprintf("%s/%s", base, path), add_headers(...))
  sprintf("GET %s/%s  [Authorization: Bearer <token>]", base, path)
}

cat(authorized_search(
  "https://ehr.example/fhir",
  "TOKEN",
  sprintf("Observation?patient=%s&code=4548-4", pid)
))

GET https://ehr.example/fhir/Observation?patient=P1000&code=4548-4  [Authorization: Bearer <token>]

text:
Key takeaways

FHIR records are modular resources linked by references, not one big blob.
Bundle type (collection/transaction/searchset) determines what the bundle does.
Search is HTTP; the returned searchset bundle is the unit of exchange.
Schema validation is free with a small hand-written check function; SMART on FHIR is how apps obtain scoped access.

text:
Health-Informatics: An R Tutorial
Health Informatics in R · Part II: Interoperability & Data Engineering · Module 7 of 16
Every health system stores data differently. A Common Data Model (CDM) solves this by defining one standardized schema and vocabulary, so the same analysis code runs unchanged across many institutions. The OMOP CDM (from the OHDSI community) is the most widely used for observational research. This module maps our synthetic EHR into OMOP.

title: Module 7: Common Data Models (OMOP CDM)
text:
Dataset
We reuse the synthetic EHR and transform it into a miniature OMOP CDM. The concept IDs shown are illustrative standard concepts (the real OMOP vocabulary lives in OHDSI Athena); a couple — gender and common conditions — match real standard concept IDs, but treat the table as a teaching stand-in, not the source of truth.

# --- Self-contained synthetic EHR generator (identical to Part I) ---
# This is the SAME generator from Module 1. We rebuild the fake hospital database
# here so this notebook can run on its own. Nothing here is a real patient.
library(dplyr)
library(tibble)

# This function generates a synthetic electronic health record (EHR) dataset.
# It creates mock tables for patients, encounters, observations, conditions, and medications,
# all with plausible structure, but not referencing any real patients or requiring external data.
make_synthetic_ehr <- function(n_patients = 200, seed = 42) {
  # Generate a small, internally-consistent synthetic EHR dataset.
  # Returns a list of linked tibbles: patients, encounters, observations,
  # conditions, and medications. This is for illustrative, educational use.
  set.seed(seed)  # same seed => same fake people every run

  # --- patients table ---
  # Create a tibble with n_patients patients, each with a name, sex, age, and birth year.
  first <- c("Ava","Liam","Noah","Mia","Zoe","Omar","Ivan","Sara","Leo","Nina",
             "Ruth","Kai","Yara","Theo","Ida","Sam","Ana","Eli","Rex","Uma")
  last  <- c("Khan","Ortiz","Chen","Diaz","Patel","Ali","Brown","Nash","Reed","Vega",
             "Cole","Frost","Grant","Hale","Iqbal","Jain","Kerr","Lund","Mora","Park")
  sexes <- sample(c("male", "female"), size = n_patients, replace = TRUE, prob = c(0.49, 0.51))
  ages  <- sample(18:89, size = n_patients, replace = TRUE)
  # Columns:
  #   patient_id  — unique ID, e.g. "P1000", "P1001"
  #   given_name / family_name — randomly chosen from the name lists
  #   sex, age — pre-generated vectors
  #   birth_year — derived from age, assuming the reference year 2026
  patients <- tibble(
    patient_id  = sprintf("P%d", 1000 + (0:(n_patients - 1))),
    given_name  = sample(first, size = n_patients, replace = TRUE),
    family_name = sample(last,  size = n_patients, replace = TRUE),
    sex         = sexes,
    age         = ages,
    birth_year  = 2026 - ages
  )

  # --- encounters table ---
  # Each patient gets 1–4 visits. Types and dates are random but internally consistent.
  #   encounter_id    — unique, zero-padded (E00001, E00002, ...)
  #   encounter_type  — ambulatory 55%, emergency 15%, inpatient 10%, wellness 20%
  #   date            — a random day in a 3-year window starting 2023-01-01
  enc_types <- c("ambulatory", "emergency", "inpatient", "wellness")
  enc_list <- vector("list", 0)
  n <- 0
  for (pid in patients$patient_id) {
    n_visits <- sample.int(4, 1)  # 1 to 4 encounters per patient
    for (j in seq_len(n_visits)) {
      n <- n + 1
      day <- sample(0:(365 * 3 - 1), 1)  # offset within 3 years
      enc_list[[n]] <- tibble(
        encounter_id = sprintf("E%05d", n),
        patient_id = pid,
        encounter_type = sample(enc_types, 1, prob = c(0.55, 0.15, 0.10, 0.20)),
        date = as.Date("2023-01-01") + day
      )
    }
  }
  encounters <- bind_rows(enc_list)

  # --- observations table ---
  # Labs and vitals attached to encounters. Each row is (name, unit, lo, hi).
  # A value is drawn uniformly in [lo, hi]; 70% of (encounter, measure) pairs exist
  # so the table looks sparse the way a real EHR does.
  obs_defs <- tribble(
    ~name, ~unit, ~lo, ~hi,
    "Body height", "cm", 150, 195,
    "Body weight", "kg", 50, 110,
    "Systolic blood pressure", "mmHg", 100, 165,
    "Heart rate", "/min", 55, 100,
    "Hemoglobin A1c", "%", 4.8, 9.5
  )
  obs_list <- vector("list", 0)
  m <- 0
  for (i in seq_len(nrow(encounters))) {
    e <- encounters[i, ]
    for (k in seq_len(nrow(obs_defs))) {
      if (runif(1) < 0.7) {
        m <- m + 1
        obs_list[[m]] <- tibble(
          observation_id = sprintf("O%06d", m),
          encounter_id = e$encounter_id,
          patient_id = e$patient_id,
          observation = obs_defs$name[k],
          value = round(runif(1, obs_defs$lo[k], obs_defs$hi[k]), 1),
          unit = obs_defs$unit[k],
          date = e$date
        )
      }
    }
  }
  observations <- bind_rows(obs_list)

  # --- conditions table ---
  # Each patient is assigned 0–3 unique diagnoses from a small pool.
  cond_pool <- c("Essential hypertension", "Type 2 diabetes mellitus", "Asthma",
                 "Acute bronchitis", "Major depressive disorder", "Osteoarthritis",
                 "Chronic kidney disease", "Anemia")
  cond_list <- vector("list", 0)
  cn <- 0
  for (pid in patients$patient_id) {
    n_cond <- sample(0:3, 1)
    if (n_cond > 0) {
      chosen <- sample(cond_pool, size = n_cond, replace = FALSE)
      for (cc in chosen) {
        cn <- cn + 1
        cond_list[[cn]] <- tibble(condition_id = sprintf("C%05d", cn), patient_id = pid, condition = cc)
      }
    }
  }
  conditions <- bind_rows(cond_list)

  # --- medications table ---
  # Same pattern as conditions: 0–3 unique drugs per patient.
  med_pool <- c("Lisinopril", "Metformin", "Albuterol", "Atorvastatin",
                "Sertraline", "Amoxicillin", "Ibuprofen", "Hydrochlorothiazide")
  med_list <- vector("list", 0)
  mn <- 0
  for (pid in patients$patient_id) {
    n_med <- sample(0:3, 1)
    if (n_med > 0) {
      chosen <- sample(med_pool, size = n_med, replace = FALSE)
      for (mm in chosen) {
        mn <- mn + 1
        med_list[[mn]] <- tibble(medication_id = sprintf("M%05d", mn), patient_id = pid, medication = mm)
      }
    }
  }
  medications <- bind_rows(med_list)

  list(
    patients = patients,
    encounters = encounters,
    observations = observations,
    conditions = conditions,
    medications = medications
  )
}

# Generate the five linked tables. Each notebook in this series starts from here.
ehr <- make_synthetic_ehr()
cat("Tables:", paste(sprintf("%s (%d rows)", names(ehr), sapply(ehr, nrow)), collapse = ", "), "\n")

Tables: patients (200 rows), encounters (505 rows), observations (1753 rows), conditions (299 rows), medications (312 rows)

title: Module 7: Common Data Models (OMOP CDM)
text:
7.1 Why a common data model
A Common Data Model (CDM) standardizes database structure across multiple sites. Without a CDM, each institution in a multi-site study needs to write its own custom data extraction code, creating duplication and inconsistency. With a CDM, every site converts its local data into the same format just one time. After this initial mapping, the same analytical tools and scripts can be used everywhere, greatly simplifying multicenter research. This is the approach used by OHDSI network studies: map once, then share analyses.
The initial investment in mapping enables efficient, reusable, and shareable analytics across sites.

title: Module 7: Common Data Models (OMOP CDM)
text:
7.2 The OMOP vocabulary (concept)
At the heart of the OMOP Common Data Model (CDM) lies a standardized vocabulary, which plays a crucial role in harmonizing clinical data from diverse sources. In OMOP, every meaningful clinical entity—whether it pertains to a diagnosis, measurement, medication, or demographic attribute—is represented by a numeric identifier called a concept_id.
This approach ensures that every clinical fact stored in an OMOP database is linked to a specific, well-defined concept. Instead of storing local or proprietary codes (such as ICD-10 for diagnoses, SNOMED for conditions, LOINC for lab tests, or RxNorm for medications), OMOP requires that all source codes be mapped to standard concepts from its extensive vocabulary. Each standard concept is assigned a unique concept_id and grouped into meaningful domains (e.g., Condition, Measurement, Drug, Gender).
By forcing every participating organization to translate its source data into this shared vocabulary, OMOP enables seamless data integration and cross-site analytics. Analysts and researchers can write a single query or analysis pipeline that runs unmodified on any OMOP-mapped dataset, regardless of local idiosyncrasies or coding systems. This shared language eliminates ambiguity, fosters reproducibility, and is the foundation for interoperable, multi-center observational research across the international OHDSI community.

# At OMOP's center is a CONCEPT table: every clinical fact is a concept_id.
# Source codes (ICD, SNOMED, LOINC, RxNorm) map to these standard IDs so every
# site speaks the same language.
#
# Columns:
#   concept_id     — the integer that other OMOP tables store as a foreign key
#   concept_name   — human-readable label
#   domain_id      — which OMOP table this concept belongs in
#                    (Gender -> person, Condition -> condition_occurrence, ...)
#   vocabulary_id  — which coding system it came from
#
# These IDs are ILLUSTRATIVE. Gender 8507/8532 and a few conditions match real
# OHDSI Athena IDs; treat the rest as a teaching stand-in, not the source of truth.
concept <- tribble(
  ~concept_id, ~concept_name,               ~domain_id,    ~vocabulary_id,
  8507,        "MALE",                      "Gender",      "Gender",
  8532,        "FEMALE",                    "Gender",      "Gender",
  320128,      "Essential hypertension",    "Condition",   "SNOMED",
  201826,      "Type 2 diabetes mellitus",  "Condition",   "SNOMED",
  317009,      "Asthma",                    "Condition",   "SNOMED",
  3004410,     "Hemoglobin A1c",            "Measurement", "LOINC",
  3004249,     "Systolic blood pressure",   "Measurement", "LOINC",
  3025315,     "Body weight",               "Measurement", "LOINC",
  1308216,     "Lisinopril",                "Drug",        "RxNorm",
  1503297,     "Metformin",                 "Drug",        "RxNorm"
)
concept

title: Module 7: Common Data Models (OMOP CDM)
text:
7.3 Building the OMOP tables
At this stage, we translate our original source tables into the standardized OMOP tables. String-based IDs from the source data (like patient or visit codes) are converted into OMOP-compliant integer foreign keys—such as person_id and visit_occurrence_id. This harmonization enables reliable joins between tables and consistency across datasets.

Milestone 1 - PERSON
PERSON: This OMOP table standardizes patient identities for all subsequent data integration. Each patient from the source data is assigned a unique integer person_id, replacing any non-standard string IDs. The table also stores their gender as a standard concept ID (from the CONCEPT table), year of birth, and the original source identifier for traceability.

# PERSON is OMOP's patient table. Source string IDs (P1000, P1001, ...) become
# integer person_id values. Everything else in the CDM will join on person_id.
patients <- ehr$patients
patients$person_id <- seq_len(nrow(patients))  # 1, 2, 3, ... n

# id_map lets later tables translate "P1000" -> 1 without looking up patients again.
id_map <- setNames(patients$person_id, patients$patient_id)

# sex strings -> standard gender concept_ids from the CONCEPT table above
gender_concept <- c(male = 8507, female = 8532)

person <- tibble(
  person_id = patients$person_id,
  gender_concept_id = unname(gender_concept[patients$sex]),  # 8507 or 8532
  year_of_birth = patients$birth_year,
  # person_source_value keeps the original ID so you can audit the mapping
  person_source_value = patients$patient_id
)
cat("PERSON table:\n")

PERSON table:

head(person)

# A tibble: 6 × 4
  person_id gender_concept_id year_of_birth person_source_value
      <int>             <dbl>         <dbl> <chr>              
1         1              8507          1985 P1000              
2         2              8507          1984 P1001              
3         3              8532          1948 P1002              
4         4              8507          1947 P1003              
5         5              8507          1995 P1004              
6         6              8507          1975 P1005              




Milestone 2 - VISIT_OCCURRENCE, CONDITION_OCCURRENCE, and MEASUREMENT
VISIT_OCCURRENCE: This OMOP table captures information about each patient encounter or visit. Each encounter from the source data is assigned a unique integer visit_occurrence_id. The type of visit is mapped to a standard visit_concept_id (e.g., inpatient, outpatient, emergency) for interoperability. Each row links the visit back to the patient (person_id) and records the start date.
CONDITION_OCCURRENCE: This OMOP table standardizes diagnoses for patients based on their encounters. Each condition from the source data is mapped to a standard OMOP concept_id, whenever possible. Only diagnoses with a recognized standard concept are retained, and the original label is kept for traceability. Each row links the condition to the patient (person_id).
MEASUREMENT: This OMOP table holds quantitative labs and vitals (A1c, blood pressure, weight). Source observation labels are mapped to standard concept IDs. Measures that are not in our tiny vocabulary (heart rate, height) are dropped — the same unmapped-rate signal as for conditions.

# VISIT_OCCURRENCE is OMOP's encounter table.
# visit_concept_id uses standard OMOP visit concepts:
#   9201 inpatient, 9202 outpatient/ambulatory/wellness, 9203 emergency
visit_concept <- c(ambulatory = 9202, emergency = 9203, inpatient = 9201, wellness = 9202)

enc <- ehr$encounters
enc$visit_occurrence_id <- seq_len(nrow(enc))
enc$person_id <- unname(id_map[enc$patient_id])  # P1000 -> 1, via the map from PERSON

visit_occurrence <- tibble(
  visit_occurrence_id = enc$visit_occurrence_id,
  person_id = enc$person_id,
  visit_concept_id = unname(visit_concept[enc$encounter_type]),
  visit_start_date = as.Date(enc$date)
)

# CONDITION_OCCURRENCE: source diagnosis labels -> standard concept_ids.
# Only three conditions are in our tiny vocabulary; the rest will map to NA
# and drop out. That drop is itself a data-quality signal (unmapped rate).
cond_to_concept <- c(
  "Essential hypertension" = 320128,
  "Type 2 diabetes mellitus" = 201826,
  "Asthma" = 317009
)
cond <- ehr$conditions
cond$person_id <- unname(id_map[cond$patient_id])
cond$condition_concept_id <- unname(cond_to_concept[cond$condition])  # unmapped -> NA

condition_occurrence <- cond %>%
  filter(!is.na(condition_concept_id)) %>%  # keep only mapped diagnoses
  mutate(condition_concept_id = as.integer(condition_concept_id)) %>%
  select(person_id, condition_concept_id, condition_source_value = condition)  # provenance

# MEASUREMENT holds quantitative labs and vitals (A1c, blood pressure, weight).
# Heart rate and height are in the source observations but not in our tiny
# concept table, so they are filtered out — same unmapped pattern as conditions.
meas_to_concept <- c(
  "Hemoglobin A1c" = 3004410,
  "Systolic blood pressure" = 3004249,
  "Body weight" = 3025315
)
obs <- ehr$observations
obs$person_id <- unname(id_map[obs$patient_id])

measurement <- obs %>%
  filter(observation %in% names(meas_to_concept)) %>%  # keep only mapped measures
  mutate(measurement_concept_id = unname(meas_to_concept[observation])) %>%
  select(person_id, measurement_concept_id,
         value_as_number = value,          # OMOP's numeric-value column
         unit,
         measurement_date = date,
         measurement_source_value = observation)  # provenance: original label

cat("VISIT_OCCURRENCE:", nrow(visit_occurrence), "rows,", ncol(visit_occurrence), "cols",
    "| CONDITION_OCCURRENCE:", nrow(condition_occurrence), "rows,", ncol(condition_occurrence), "cols",
    "| MEASUREMENT:", nrow(measurement), "rows,", ncol(measurement), "cols\n")

# condition_occurrence. Inspect a few rows: each lab/vital is stored as a
# measurement_concept_id, not as a free-text label.

title: Module 7: Common Data Models (OMOP CDM)
text:
7.4 A standardized analytic query
Now that our data has been transformed into the OMOP Common Data Model (CDM), we can take advantage of its standardized structure to perform analyses that will work at any OMOP-compliant site, without needing to adjust the code for differences in local data tables or variable naming conventions.
For example, if we want to calculate the prevalence of each medical condition represented in our dataset, we can write a query using OMOP’s standard fields and concepts. Specifically, we are interested in the prevalence of each mapped condition (e.g., asthma, hypertension, diabetes). The query groups patients by their standardized OMOP concept ID for each condition, counts the number of unique persons with each condition, and then joins this with the OMOP “concept” table. The concept table provides the human-readable names corresponding to each standardized concept ID.
By using standardized concept IDs rather than site-specific strings (such as “Essential hypertension” or “asthma”), our query is robust to differences in how conditions might be labeled or coded at different institutions. This ensures consistent, reproducible, and portable analyses: the code will work “as is” at any site using OMOP, and will always report well-defined concepts with their proper clinical names, regardless of the specific way the local site originally recorded them.

# Because the data is now in OMOP, this query would run UNCHANGED at any OMOP site.
# We count distinct persons per condition_concept_id, then join CONCEPT to get
# human-readable names. The analysis never mentions "Essential hypertension" as
# a string — only the integer 320128 — so site-specific labels cannot break it.
prevalence <- condition_occurrence %>%
  group_by(condition_concept_id) %>%
  summarise(n_persons = n_distinct(person_id), .groups = "drop") %>%  # unique patients, not rows
  inner_join(
    concept %>% select(concept_id, concept_name),
    by = c("condition_concept_id" = "concept_id")
  )

prevalence$pct <- round(100 * prevalence$n_persons / nrow(person), 1)

cat("Standardized prevalence query (portable across OMOP sites):\n")

Standardized prevalence query (portable across OMOP sites):

print(as.data.frame(prevalence[, c("concept_name", "n_persons", "pct")]), row.names = FALSE)

             concept_name n_persons  pct
 Type 2 diabetes mellitus        53 26.5
                   Asthma        34 17.0
   Essential hypertension        32 16.0



# Same idea for a lab: look up A1c by its concept_id, not by the string "Hemoglobin A1c".
# If another site stored the label as "HbA1c" or "glycohemoglobin", this still works.
a1c_id <- 3004410
mean_a1c <- mean(measurement$value_as_number[measurement$measurement_concept_id == a1c_id], na.rm = TRUE)
name <- concept$concept_name[concept$concept_id == a1c_id][1]
cat(sprintf("Mean %s across cohort: %.2f %%\n", name, mean_a1c))

Mean Hemoglobin A1c across cohort: 7.17 %

title: Module 7: Common Data Models (OMOP CDM)
text:
7.5 Other common data models
OMOP is dominant for observational research, but you’ll meet others:








CDM
Origin
Typical use




OMOP
OHDSI
Observational research networks, large-scale analytics


i2b2
Partners/Harvard
Cohort discovery, local data warehouses


PCORnet
PCORI
Patient-centered outcomes research


Sentinel
FDA
Drug/device safety surveillance



They share the same core idea: map once, analyze everywhere.

1. OMOP (Observational Medical Outcomes Partnership)

Origin: Developed by OHDSI (Observational Health Data Sciences and Informatics)
Typical Use: Large-scale observational research and analytics; multi-site studies.
Core Idea: Uses a fixed schema (person, visit_occurrence, condition_occurrence, measurement, drug_exposure, etc.) and common vocabulary (concept_id).
R Example: Query prevalence of a condition standardized by concept_id.


# Find prevalence of 'Asthma' (concept_id = 317009) in a cohort
asthma_id <- 317009
asthma_patients <- n_distinct(condition_occurrence$person_id[condition_occurrence$condition_concept_id == asthma_id])
total_patients <- n_distinct(person$person_id)
cat(sprintf("Asthma prevalence: %.1f%%\n", 100 * asthma_patients / total_patients))

Asthma prevalence: 17.0%




2. i2b2 (Informatics for Integrating Biology and the Bedside)

Origin: Partners HealthCare / Harvard
Typical Use: Cohort discovery, local clinical data warehouse queries, self-service exploration.
Core Idea: Uses a flexible, hierarchical “star schema” model (fact table + ontology), allowing for fast, ad-hoc queries.
R Example: Pull encounter counts of patients by sub-tree (e.g., diagnoses starting with ‘E11’ for diabetes).


# Example stub: i2b2 query for all 'E11%' ICD-10 codes (Type 2 Diabetes)
diagnoses <- tibble(code = c("E11.9", "I10"), person_id = c(1, 2))
diabetes_patients <- n_distinct(diagnoses$person_id[startsWith(diagnoses$code, "E11")])
cat(sprintf("Type 2 diabetes patients (i2b2): %d\n", diabetes_patients))

Type 2 diabetes patients (i2b2): 1




3. PCORnet (Patient-Centered Outcomes Research Network)

Origin: PCORI (Patient-Centered Outcomes Research Institute)
Typical Use: National-scale, multi-system patient-centered outcomes research.
Core Idea: Wide tables, common vocabulary mappings, supports pragmatic clinical trial and observational studies.


# Example stub: PCORnet procedure table analysis
procedures <- tibble(px_code = c("93000", "80050"), person_id = c(3, 4))
ecg_count <- n_distinct(procedures$person_id[procedures$px_code == "93000"])
cat(sprintf("Patients with ECG procedure (PCORnet): %d\n", ecg_count))

Patients with ECG procedure (PCORnet): 1




4. Sentinel

Origin: FDA
Typical Use: Drug and device safety surveillance, regulatory queries.
Core Idea: Designed for regulatory queries at scale, federated querying across data partners, focused tables (dispensing, enrollment, etc.).


dispensing <- tibble(ndc = c("00093754456", "00591088810"), person_id = c(5, 6))
drug_count <- n_distinct(dispensing$person_id[dispensing$ndc == "00093754456"])
cat(sprintf("Patients dispensed statins (Sentinel): %d\n", drug_count))

Patients dispensed statins (Sentinel): 1

href: Notebooks/Part II -  Interoperability and Data Engineering (Intermediate)/07_omop_common_data_model.html#key-takeaways
title: Module 7: Common Data Models (OMOP CDM)
text:
Key takeaways

A CDM turns N bespoke extractions into one mapping + one analysis.
OMOP’s core is the standardized vocabulary (concept_id) plus a fixed schema (person, visit_occurrence, condition_occurrence, measurement, drug_exposure).
Provenance (*_source_value) is preserved so mappings stay auditable.

Health Informatics in R · Part III: Privacy, Text & Applied Informatics · Module 9 of 16
Health data is among the most sensitive data there is, and its use is governed by law. Before data can be shared for research or analytics, protected health information (PHI) usually has to be removed. This module covers the HIPAA de-identification standards and implements de-identification for both structured tables and free text.

By the end of this module you will be able to:

Distinguish HIPAA Safe Harbor (the 18 identifiers) from Expert Determination.
De-identify structured data by suppressing, generalizing, and hashing identifiers.
De-identify free text using regex plus rule-based named-entity matching.
Measure k-anonymity over quasi-identifiers and generalize to reach a target k.
Explain synthetic data and governance controls (IRB, DUA, minimum necessary).

Dataset
The synthetic EHR plus two fabricated clinical notes seeded with PHI-shaped tokens (names, MRNs, dates, phone, email, address) so the de-identification code has realistic targets.

# --- Self-contained synthetic EHR generator (identical to Parts I-II) ---
library(dplyr)
library(tibble)

make_synthetic_ehr <- function(n_patients = 200, seed = 42) {
  set.seed(seed)
  first <- c("Ava","Liam","Noah","Mia","Zoe","Omar","Ivan","Sara","Leo","Nina",
             "Ruth","Kai","Yara","Theo","Ida","Sam","Ana","Eli","Rex","Uma")
  last  <- c("Khan","Ortiz","Chen","Diaz","Patel","Ali","Brown","Nash","Reed","Vega",
             "Cole","Frost","Grant","Hale","Iqbal","Jain","Kerr","Lund","Mora","Park")
  ages <- sample(18:89, size = n_patients, replace = TRUE)
  patients <- tibble(
    patient_id = sprintf("P%d", 1000 + 0:(n_patients - 1)),
    given_name = sample(first, size = n_patients, replace = TRUE),
    family_name = sample(last, size = n_patients, replace = TRUE),
    sex = sample(c("male", "female"), size = n_patients, replace = TRUE, prob = c(0.49, 0.51)),
    age = ages,
    birth_year = 2026 - ages
  )

  enc_types <- c("ambulatory", "emergency", "inpatient", "wellness")
  enc_rows <- list()
  for (pid in patients$patient_id) {
    n_enc <- sample(1:4, 1)
    for (i in seq_len(n_enc)) {
      day <- sample(0:(365 * 3 - 1), 1)
      enc_rows[[length(enc_rows) + 1]] <- tibble(
        encounter_id = sprintf("E%05d", length(enc_rows) + 1),
        patient_id = pid,
        encounter_type = sample(enc_types, 1, prob = c(0.55, 0.15, 0.10, 0.20)),
        date = as.Date("2023-01-01") + day
      )
    }
  }
  encounters <- bind_rows(enc_rows)

  obs_defs <- list(
    list(name = "Body height", unit = "cm", lo = 150, hi = 195),
    list(name = "Body weight", unit = "kg", lo = 50, hi = 110),
    list(name = "Systolic blood pressure", unit = "mmHg", lo = 100, hi = 165),
    list(name = "Heart rate", unit = "/min", lo = 55, hi = 100),
    list(name = "Hemoglobin A1c", unit = "%", lo = 4.8, hi = 9.5)
  )
  obs_rows <- list()
  for (i in seq_len(nrow(encounters))) {
    e <- encounters[i, ]
    for (od in obs_defs) {
      if (runif(1) < 0.7) {
        obs_rows[[length(obs_rows) + 1]] <- tibble(
          observation_id = sprintf("O%06d", length(obs_rows) + 1),
          encounter_id = e$encounter_id,
          patient_id = e$patient_id,
          observation = od$name,
          value = round(runif(1, od$lo, od$hi), 1),
          unit = od$unit,
          date = e$date
        )
      }
    }
  }
  observations <- bind_rows(obs_rows)

  cond_pool <- c("Essential hypertension", "Type 2 diabetes mellitus", "Asthma",
                 "Acute bronchitis", "Major depressive disorder", "Osteoarthritis",
                 "Chronic kidney disease", "Anemia")
  cond_rows <- list()
  for (pid in patients$patient_id) {
    n_cond <- sample(0:3, 1)
    if (n_cond > 0) {
      cs <- sample(cond_pool, size = n_cond, replace = FALSE)
      for (c in cs) {
        cond_rows[[length(cond_rows) + 1]] <- tibble(
          condition_id = sprintf("C%05d", length(cond_rows) + 1),
          patient_id = pid, condition = c
        )
      }
    }
  }
  conditions <- bind_rows(cond_rows)

  med_pool <- c("Lisinopril", "Metformin", "Albuterol", "Atorvastatin", "Sertraline",
                "Amoxicillin", "Ibuprofen", "Hydrochlorothiazide")
  med_rows <- list()
  for (pid in patients$patient_id) {
    n_med <- sample(0:3, 1)
    if (n_med > 0) {
      ms <- sample(med_pool, size = n_med, replace = FALSE)
      for (m in ms) {
        med_rows[[length(med_rows) + 1]] <- tibble(
          medication_id = sprintf("M%05d", length(med_rows) + 1),
          patient_id = pid, medication = m
        )
      }
    }
  }
  medications <- bind_rows(med_rows)

  list(patients = patients, encounters = encounters, observations = observations,
       conditions = conditions, medications = medications)
}

ehr <- make_synthetic_ehr()
cat("Tables:", paste(sprintf("%s (%d)", names(ehr), sapply(ehr, nrow)), collapse = ", "), "\n")

Tables: patients (200), encounters (505), observations (1750), conditions (305), medications (314)

title: Module 9: Privacy, De-identification, and Governance
text:
9.1 The two HIPAA de-identification standards








Standard
How it works
Trade-off




Safe Harbor
Remove 18 specific identifiers named by HIPAA regulations from all data.
Straightforward, rule-based; may remove useful data along with identifiers.


Expert Determination
An expert assesses and documents that the risk of re-identification is “very small,” allowing custom methods to reduce such risk.
Allows more data utility and context sensitivity; requires specialized knowledge and thorough documentation.



Safe Harbor: Relies on a strict list of 18 personal identifiers (such as names, addresses smaller than state, full dates, and contact info) that must be removed to consider data de-identified. This method is relatively easy to apply and does not require specialized statistical or privacy expertise. However, it can inadvertently remove more information than strictly necessary for privacy, potentially harming research utility.
Expert Determination: Involves hiring or relying on a qualified expert in statistical and scientific methods who will identify direct and indirect identifiers in the dataset and certify that the likelihood of someone being re-identified from the data is very small. This approach allows for nuanced balancing between privacy and information loss, accommodating unique data situations, but it is more complex and requires expert oversight and documentation.
18 Safe Harbor identifiers (must be removed or generalized): names, any small-area geographic indicator (smaller than a state, e.g. city, zip code except for the initial 3 digits in some cases), all dates directly related to an individual (other than year), ages over 89, phone/fax numbers, emails, social security numbers, medical record/account/license numbers, vehicle/device identifiers, URLs, IP addresses, biometric identifiers, full-face photographs/images, and any other unique identifying code or characteristic.

SAFE_HARBOR_18 <- c(
  "Names", "Geographic subdivisions < state", "Dates (finer than year); ages > 89",
  "Telephone numbers", "Fax numbers", "Email addresses", "Social Security numbers",
  "Medical record numbers", "Health plan beneficiary numbers", "Account numbers",
  "Certificate/license numbers", "Vehicle identifiers", "Device identifiers",
  "Web URLs", "IP addresses", "Biometric identifiers", "Full-face photos",
  "Any other unique identifying number/characteristic/code"
)
cat(sprintf("HIPAA Safe Harbor identifiers (%d):\n", length(SAFE_HARBOR_18)))

HIPAA Safe Harbor identifiers (18):

for (i in seq_along(SAFE_HARBOR_18)) {
  cat(sprintf("%2d. %s\n", i, SAFE_HARBOR_18[i]))
}

text:
9.2 De-identifying structured data
When working with structured (tabular) data, removing identifiers is a column-by-column process. Each column containing an identifier should have an appropriate de-identification strategy assigned to it. Common strategies include: - Suppress (drop): Remove the column entirely if it directly identifies a person (e.g., name). - Generalize (reduce precision): Broaden the information so it’s less specific, such as reporting age groups instead of exact ages, or using birth year instead of full birth date. - Pseudonymize (hash to a consistent token): Replace an identifier, like a patient ID, with a generated code (using a hash function and possibly a secret salt) that is stable within the dataset but cannot be used to recover the original value. This approach balances privacy protection with the need to retain useful, analyzable data.

library(digest)
patients <- ehr$patients

pseudonymize <- function(value, salt = "study-2026") {
  paste0("PT-", substr(vapply(value, function(v) digest(paste0(salt, v), algo = "sha256"), character(1)), 1, 10))
}

deid <- tibble(
  # pseudonymize the direct identifier (stable across the dataset, not reversible without salt)
  study_id = pseudonymize(patients$patient_id),
  # suppress names entirely
  # generalize: age > 89 collapses to '90+' per Safe Harbor; keep birth YEAR only
  age_group = cut(patients$age, breaks = c(0, 18, 40, 65, 89, 200),
                   labels = c("<18", "18-39", "40-64", "65-89", "90+")),
  sex = patients$sex
)
cat("De-identified structured table (names suppressed, id hashed, age generalized):\n")

title: Module 9: Privacy, De-identification, and Governance
text:
9.3 De-identifying free text
De-identifying free text is more complex than structured data because personal identifiers may appear anywhere within unstructured prose. To address this, we use a combination of: - Regular expressions (regex): These can reliably detect well-defined patterns such as Medical Record Numbers (MRNs), phone numbers, emails, dates, and similar structured strings. - Rule-based name/place matching: A small dictionary of known name and place tokens detects proper nouns (like “Ava Khan” or “Ithaca”) in natural language, standing in for a full named-entity-recognition model.
For maximum portability, the code below is entirely dependency-free — a production R pipeline for this step would typically reach for spacyr (a reticulate bridge to spaCy) or a dedicated NER package, but the rule/dictionary approach here needs no external model and always runs.

library(stringr)

PATTERNS <- list(
  MRN   = regex("\\bMRN\\s*\\d{5,}\\b", ignore_case = TRUE),
  PHONE = regex("\\b\\d{3}-\\d{3}-\\d{4}\\b"),
  EMAIL = regex("\\b[\\w.]+@[\\w.]+\\.\\w+\\b"),
  DATE  = regex("\\b\\d{1,2}/\\d{1,2}/\\d{2,4}\\b"),
  SSN   = regex("\\b\\d{3}-\\d{2}-\\d{4}\\b")
)

# Small dictionary standing in for NER: known person names and place names
# from the fabricated notes (a production system would use a trained NER model instead).
NAME_TERMS  <- c("Ava Khan", "Liam Ortiz")
PLACE_TERMS <- c("12 Elm St", "Ithaca")

find_matches <- function(text, pattern, tag) {
  m <- gregexpr(pattern, text, perl = TRUE)[[1]]
  if (m[1] == -1) return(tibble(start = integer(0), end = integer(0), tag = character(0)))
  len <- attr(m, "match.length")
  tibble(start = as.integer(m), end = as.integer(m) + len, tag = tag)
}

deidentify_text <- function(text) {
  redactions <- list()
  # 1) regex-based structured identifiers
  for (tag in names(PATTERNS)) {
    redactions[[length(redactions) + 1]] <- find_matches(text, PATTERNS[[tag]], tag)
  }
  # 2) dictionary-based names and places (stand-in for spaCy NER)
  for (nm in NAME_TERMS) {
    redactions[[length(redactions) + 1]] <- find_matches(text, fixed(nm), "PERSON")
  }
  for (pl in PLACE_TERMS) {
    redactions[[length(redactions) + 1]] <- find_matches(text, fixed(pl), "FAC")
  }
  red <- bind_rows(redactions)
  if (nrow(red) == 0) return(text)
  # apply right-to-left so offsets stay valid
  red <- red[order(-red$start), ]
  out <- text
  for (i in seq_len(nrow(red))) {
    start <- red$start[i]; end <- red$end[i]; tag <- red$tag[i]
    out <- paste0(substr(out, 1, start - 1), "[", tag, "]", substr(out, end, nchar(out)))
  }
  out
}


Milestone 1 - redact a clinical note

original <- notes[[1]]$text
redacted <- deidentify_text(original)
cat("ORIGINAL:\n", original, "\n")

ORIGINAL:

cat("\nDE-IDENTIFIED:\n", redacted, "\n")


DE-IDENTIFIED:

for (token in c("4471982", "607-555-0148", "03/12/2024", "Ava", "Ithaca")) {
  cat(sprintf("  %-14s redacted: %s\n", token, !str_detect(redacted, fixed(token))))
}

title: Module 9: Privacy, De-identification, and Governance
text:
9.4 k-anonymity
k-anonymity is a privacy concept that addresses the risk of re-identifying individuals in a dataset, even after obvious identifiers (like names or SSNs) are removed. It recognizes that combinations of seemingly harmless features—such as age, sex, or ZIP code—can still uniquely identify people when combined. These features are known as quasi-identifiers.
A dataset is considered k-anonymous if every unique combination of quasi-identifiers appears in at least k different records. This means each individual is hidden in a crowd of at least k people sharing the same quasi-identifier values. The higher the value of k, the stronger the privacy guarantee: it’s harder to pick out an individual from the group.
Achieving k-anonymity often requires generalizing or coarsening the data (for example, grouping ages into ranges, or truncating ZIP codes) so that more records look alike, increasing the minimum group size. The following sections show how to measure and improve k-anonymity using real and generalized data.
Removing direct identifiers isn’t enough: quasi-identifiers (age, sex, ZIP) can re-identify people by combination. A dataset is k-anonymous if every combination of quasi-identifiers is shared by at least k records. We measure it, then generalize to raise the minimum k.

set.seed(1)
qi <- ehr$patients[, c("age", "sex")]
qi$zip3 <- sample(c("148", "149", "130"), size = nrow(qi), replace = TRUE)  # coarse ZIP (first 3)

min_k <- function(df, cols) {
  df %>% count(across(all_of(cols))) %>% pull(n) %>% min()
}

cat("Using exact age as a quasi-identifier:\n")

Using exact age as a quasi-identifier:

cat("  smallest group size (k):", min_k(qi, c("age", "sex", "zip3")), "\n")

  smallest group size (k): 1 

# generalize age into bands -> larger groups -> higher k
qi$age_band <- cut(qi$age, breaks = c(0, 40, 65, 120), labels = c("<40", "40-64", "65+"))
k2 <- min_k(qi, c("age_band", "sex", "zip3"))
cat("After generalizing age into bands:\n")

After generalizing age into bands:

cat("  smallest group size (k):", k2, "->", if (k2 >= 5) "meets k>=5" else "still too small", "\n")

  smallest group size (k): 6 -> meets k>=5

text:
9.5 Synthetic data and governance
The safest way to share is often not to share real records at all but a synthetic dataset that preserves statistical structure without mapping to real people — exactly what this series’ generator does.
Beyond technical methods, health data use sits inside a governance framework:

IRB approval for human-subjects research
Data Use Agreements (DUAs) governing what a recipient may do
Minimum necessary — access only the data required for the purpose
Limited Data Sets — a middle ground retaining dates/geography under a DUA

Production de-identification tools worth knowing: Microsoft Presidio, Philter, and NLM Scrubber. Formal privacy guarantees come from differential privacy.

# The generator IS the privacy strategy: no row maps to a real person.
synth <- make_synthetic_ehr(n_patients = 5, seed = 99)$patients
cat("Synthetic patients — statistically shaped, entirely fabricated:\n")

print(synth[, c("patient_id", "given_name", "family_name", "sex", "age")], row.names = FALSE)

Health Informatics in R · Part III: Privacy, Text & Applied Informatics · Module 11 of 16
Clinical Decision Support (CDS) delivers the right knowledge to the right person at the right point in the workflow — a screening reminder, a drug-interaction warning, a risk score. text:
Dataset
The synthetic EHR. We build a per-patient feature view (age, latest systolic BP, active conditions, current medications, most recent A1c), the exact input a CDS rule engine consumes.

# --- Self-contained synthetic EHR generator (identical to Parts I-II) ---
library(dplyr)
library(tibble)

# This function creates a synthetic (fake) Electronic Health Record (EHR) dataset for demonstration and learning purposes.
make_synthetic_ehr <- function(n_patients = 200, seed = 42) {
  set.seed(seed)  # Random seed for reproducibility

  # 1. Generate basic patient demographic info (IDs, names, sex, age, birth year)
  first <- c("Ava","Liam","Noah","Mia","Zoe","Omar","Ivan","Sara","Leo","Nina",
             "Ruth","Kai","Yara","Theo","Ida","Sam","Ana","Eli","Rex","Uma")
  last  <- c("Khan","Ortiz","Chen","Diaz","Patel","Ali","Brown","Nash","Reed","Vega",
             "Cole","Frost","Grant","Hale","Iqbal","Jain","Kerr","Lund","Mora","Park")
  ages <- sample(18:89, size = n_patients, replace = TRUE)
  patients <- tibble(
    patient_id = sprintf("P%d", 1000 + 0:(n_patients - 1)),
    given_name = sample(first, size = n_patients, replace = TRUE),
    family_name = sample(last, size = n_patients, replace = TRUE),
    sex = sample(c("male", "female"), size = n_patients, replace = TRUE, prob = c(0.49, 0.51)),
    age = ages,
    birth_year = 2026 - ages
  )

  # 2. Simulate multiple encounters (visits, admissions) for each patient
  enc_types <- c("ambulatory", "emergency", "inpatient", "wellness")
  enc_rows <- list()
  for (pid in patients$patient_id) {
    n_enc <- sample(1:4, 1)  # Each patient has 1 to 4 encounters
    for (i in seq_len(n_enc)) {
      day <- sample(0:(365 * 3 - 1), 1)  # Random date over 3 years
      enc_rows[[length(enc_rows) + 1]] <- tibble(
        encounter_id = sprintf("E%05d", length(enc_rows) + 1),
        patient_id = pid,
        encounter_type = sample(enc_types, 1, prob = c(0.55, 0.15, 0.10, 0.20)),
        date = as.Date("2023-01-01") + day
      )
    }
  }
  encounters <- bind_rows(enc_rows)

  # 3. Create sets of clinical observations (height, weight, etc.) for each encounter
  obs_defs <- list(
    list(name = "Body height", unit = "cm", lo = 150, hi = 195),
    list(name = "Body weight", unit = "kg", lo = 50, hi = 110),
    list(name = "Systolic blood pressure", unit = "mmHg", lo = 100, hi = 165),
    list(name = "Heart rate", unit = "/min", lo = 55, hi = 100),
    list(name = "Hemoglobin A1c", unit = "%", lo = 4.8, hi = 9.5)
  )
  obs_rows <- list()
  for (i in seq_len(nrow(encounters))) {
    e <- encounters[i, ]
    for (od in obs_defs) {
      if (runif(1) < 0.7) {  # About 70% of encounters have each observation
        obs_rows[[length(obs_rows) + 1]] <- tibble(
          observation_id = sprintf("O%06d", length(obs_rows) + 1),
          encounter_id = e$encounter_id,
          patient_id = e$patient_id,
          observation = od$name,
          value = round(runif(1, od$lo, od$hi), 1),
          unit = od$unit,
          date = e$date
        )
      }
    }
  }
  observations <- bind_rows(obs_rows)

  # 4. Assign random conditions (diagnoses) to each patient
  cond_pool <- c("Essential hypertension", "Type 2 diabetes mellitus", "Asthma",
                 "Acute bronchitis", "Major depressive disorder", "Osteoarthritis",
                 "Chronic kidney disease", "Anemia")
  cond_rows <- list()
  for (pid in patients$patient_id) {
    # Each patient can have 0-3 conditions
    n_cond <- sample(0:3, 1)
    if (n_cond > 0) {
      cs <- sample(cond_pool, size = n_cond, replace = FALSE)
      for (c in cs) {
        cond_rows[[length(cond_rows) + 1]] <- tibble(
          condition_id = sprintf("C%05d", length(cond_rows) + 1),
          patient_id = pid, condition = c
        )
      }
    }
  }
  conditions <- bind_rows(cond_rows)

  # 5. Assign random medications to each patient
  med_pool <- c("Lisinopril", "Metformin", "Albuterol", "Atorvastatin", "Sertraline",
                "Amoxicillin", "Ibuprofen", "Hydrochlorothiazide")
  med_rows <- list()
  for (pid in patients$patient_id) {
    # Each patient can have 0-3 medications
    n_med <- sample(0:3, 1)
    if (n_med > 0) {
      ms <- sample(med_pool, size = n_med, replace = FALSE)
      for (m in ms) {
        med_rows[[length(med_rows) + 1]] <- tibble(
          medication_id = sprintf("M%05d", length(med_rows) + 1),
          patient_id = pid, medication = m
        )
      }
    }
  }
  medications <- bind_rows(med_rows)

  # 6. Return all pieces as a list of data frames
  list(
    patients = patients,
    encounters = encounters,
    observations = observations,
    conditions = conditions,
    medications = medications
  )
}

# Create an EHR dataset and print table sizes
ehr <- make_synthetic_ehr()
cat("Tables:", paste(sprintf("%s (%d)", names(ehr), sapply(ehr, nrow)), collapse = ", "), "\n")

Tables: patients (200), encounters (505), observations (1750), conditions (305), medications (314)

title: Module 11: Clinical Decision Support Systems
text:
11.1 The Five Rights of CDS
Effective Clinical Decision Support (CDS) delivers interventions by closely adhering to the “Five Rights” framework:

The right information: Relevant, evidence-based guidance or data, such as clinical recommendations or alerts about abnormal values.
To the right person: Presented to the appropriate member of the care team—this could be a physician, nurse, pharmacist, or even the patient.
In the right format: The CDS can be shown as an alert, order set, documentation template, reference information, or other context-sensitive format appropriate to the workflow.
Through the right channel: Delivered within the system or application where the recipient is working—most commonly within the EHR, but sometimes via mobile apps, pagers, or verbal alerts.
At the right point in workflow: Provided at a time when it can make a difference, such as when entering orders, reviewing results, or during a clinical encounter.

There are two major approaches to CDS:

Rule-based CDS: Hard-coded, explicit logic that implements clinical guidelines as “if-then” statements (e.g., “If the patient has diabetes and no recent A1c lab, remind the provider to order one”). These are easy to audit and understand, but can be brittle and require maintenance as evidence evolves.
Model-driven (AI-based) CDS: Uses statistical or machine learning models trained on data to make predictions or recommendations (e.g. risk scores for sepsis, readmission). These can capture complex relationships but are less transparent and harder to trace.

In practice, most real CDS systems use a combination of both approaches: models for prediction, and rules for enforceability, safety, and auditability. Rule-based CDS is still dominant in many settings due to its simplicity and transparency for both developers and clinicians.

text:
11.2 Build the per-patient feature view
In preparation for clinical decision support, we need a consolidated “feature view” for each patient. This per-patient feature view should summarize key data elements relevant to CDS rules: - Demographics (e.g., age, sex) - Most recent results for important labs or observations - A set of all active conditions - A set of all current medications This structure makes it easy to apply rules and generate alerts on a patient-by-patient basis.

library(dplyr)
library(tidyr)

# Pull out patient and observation tables
patients <- ehr$patients
obs <- ehr$observations

# Helper function to get each patient's most recent value for a specific observation
latest <- function(observation_name) {
  obs %>%
    filter(observation == observation_name) %>%
    arrange(date) %>%
    group_by(patient_id) %>%
    summarise(value = last(value), .groups = "drop")
}

latest_sbp <- latest("Systolic blood pressure") %>% rename(latest_sbp = value)
latest_a1c <- latest("Hemoglobin A1c") %>% rename(latest_a1c = value)

# Set of conditions per patient (empty set if none)
cond_sets <- ehr$conditions %>%
  group_by(patient_id) %>%
  summarise(conditions = list(unique(condition)), .groups = "drop")

# Set of current medications per patient (empty set if none)
med_sets <- ehr$medications %>%
  group_by(patient_id) %>%
  summarise(medications = list(unique(medication)), .groups = "drop")

# Start building the per-patient feature table using age and sex, joined to the rest
feat <- patients %>%
  select(patient_id, age, sex) %>%
  left_join(latest_sbp, by = "patient_id") %>%
  left_join(latest_a1c, by = "patient_id") %>%
  left_join(cond_sets, by = "patient_id") %>%
  left_join(med_sets, by = "patient_id") %>%
  mutate(
    conditions = lapply(conditions, function(x) if (is.null(x)) character(0) else x),
    medications = lapply(medications, function(x) if (is.null(x)) character(0) else x)
  )

cat("Per-patient CDS feature view (first 5):\n")

Per-patient CDS feature view (first 5):

print(feat %>% select(patient_id, age, sex, latest_sbp, latest_a1c) %>% head(5), n = 5)

2 P1001         82 male         154.        9.5
3 P1002         42 female       136.        7.3

title: Module 11: Clinical Decision Support Systems
text:
11.4 A risk score
In addition to providing alerts as simple yes/no (boolean) rules, Clinical Decision Support (CDS) systems also frequently offer a risk score for a given clinical problem. A risk score quantifies a patient’s likelihood of a future adverse outcome (here, for cardiovascular disease) in a point-based, interpretable way. The following example implements a straightforward cardiovascular risk point system for educational purposes. This system assigns points to a patient based on their age group, elevated systolic blood pressure, and/or specific chronic conditions (such as diabetes, hypertension, or chronic kidney disease). The higher the total points, the greater the cardiovascular risk. This simple score is not a validated medical tool, but illustrates the logic that real world CDS uses to stratify risk and personalize care recommendations.

# The following function and code implement a simple, interpretable cardiovascular risk scoring system:

#' Compute a cardiovascular risk score for a patient.
#'
#' @param f A single-row feature tibble (patient features/row).
#' @return integer. Total risk points for this patient.
cv_risk_points <- function(f) {
  pts <- 0
  # Age points: 2 points if 65 or older, 1 point if between 50 and 64, otherwise 0.
  pts <- pts + ifelse(f$age >= 65, 2, 0) + ifelse(f$age >= 50 & f$age < 65, 1, 0)
  # Systolic blood pressure: 2 points if latest_sbp is 140 or higher.
  if (!is.na(f$latest_sbp) && f$latest_sbp >= 140) {
    pts <- pts + 2
  }
  # Chronic conditions:
  # 2 points if patient has Type 2 diabetes mellitus.
  pts <- pts + as.integer("Type 2 diabetes mellitus" %in% f$conditions[[1]]) * 2
  # 1 point if patient has essential hypertension.
  pts <- pts + as.integer("Essential hypertension" %in% f$conditions[[1]]) * 1
  # 2 points if patient has chronic kidney disease.
  pts <- pts + as.integer("Chronic kidney disease" %in% f$conditions[[1]]) * 2
  # Return the total risk points
  pts
}

# Apply the risk point calculation for every patient in the feat table.
feat$cv_points <- vapply(seq_len(nrow(feat)), function(i) cv_risk_points(feat[i, ]), numeric(1))

# Stratify patients into risk bands based on their total points:
# -1 to 1 = "low", 2 to 3 = "moderate", 4+ = "high".
feat$cv_band <- cut(
  feat$cv_points,
  breaks = c(-1, 1, 3, 99),
  labels = c("low", "moderate", "high")
)

cat("Risk stratification:\n")

Risk stratification:

print(feat %>% count(cv_band, sort = TRUE))  # Show how many patients fall into each risk band

# A tibble: 3 × 2
  cv_band      n
  <fct>    <int>
1 moderate    95
2 high        67
3 low         38

cat("\nHighest-risk patients:\n")


Highest-risk patients:

# Show top 5 patients with the highest risk scores, including age, latest SBP, total points, and risk band.
print(
  feat %>%
    arrange(desc(cv_points)) %>%
    select(patient_id, age, latest_sbp, cv_points, cv_band) %>%
    head(5),
  n = 5
)

title: Module 11: Clinical Decision Support Systems
section: 11.5 Delivering alerts as CDS Hooks cards
text:
11.5 Delivering alerts as CDS Hooks cards
CDS Hooks is a widely adopted standard for delivering clinical decision support within an Electronic Health Record (EHR) system. When a specific workflow event occurs in the EHR—such as a clinician opening a patient’s chart (patient-view)—the EHR triggers a request to an external CDS (Clinical Decision Support) service. The CDS service evaluates the latest patient data and context, and responds with a set of cards containing decision support information to be displayed to the clinician.
Each card is a structured message that typically includes: - summary: a concise headline summarizing the alert or advice (max 140 characters, shown prominently) - indicator: the severity level of the card—either "info", "warning", or "critical"—which influences the EHR’s visual display - detail: a longer explanation providing more context and justification for the recommendation - source: attribution information for the rule or CDS application generating the card (e.g., “Source: Medication Safety CDS v1.0”) - suggestions (optional): actionable buttons or choices that the clinician may execute directly from the card, such as ordering a lab test, adjusting a medication, or simply documenting acknowledgment.
CDS Hooks ensures this exchange is standardized, so that EHRs and external CDS services can interoperate reliably across settings and vendors.

library(jsonlite)

# This named list maps human-readable severity labels to the CDS Hooks "indicator" levels
INDICATOR <- c(info = "info", warning = "warning", critical = "critical")

#' Converts a single alert (row of the alerts table) into a CDS Hooks card list.
#' - summary: Up to 140 characters summarizing the message.
#' - indicator: Severity ("info", "warning", "critical") for visual emphasis.
#' - detail: Full message to show more context.
#' - source: Label indicating which rule generated the card.
#' - suggestions: Button for the clinician to acknowledge/document the alert.
to_cds_card <- function(alert) {
  list(
    summary = substr(alert$msg, 1, 140),                 # Truncate to 140 chars for the headline
    indicator = unname(INDICATOR[alert$severity]),        # Standardized severity value
    detail = alert$msg,                                    # Longer explanation, full message
    source = list(label = sprintf("HealthInformatics CDS (rule: %s)", alert$rule)),  # Source for audit/attribution
    suggestions = list(list(label = "Acknowledge and document"))  # Optional action button
  )
}

#' For a given patient id (pid), return a CDS Hooks-compliant response.
#' This looks up all alerts for the patient and packages them as cards.
#' list(cards = list(...cards for that patient...))
cds_response_for <- function(pid) {
  # Select only alerts for the specified patient
  pid_alerts <- alerts %>% filter(patient_id == pid)
  # Convert each alert row into a CDS card list
  cards <- lapply(seq_len(nrow(pid_alerts)), function(i) to_cds_card(pid_alerts[i, ]))
  list(cards = cards)
}

# Create a sample CDS Hooks response for a sample patient and print as pretty-printed JSON
sample_response <- cds_response_for(example_pid)
cat(toJSON(sample_response, auto_unbox = TRUE, pretty = TRUE))

{
  "cards": [
    {
      "summary": "BP 145 mmHg with hypertension — consider intensifying therapy.",
      "indicator": "warning",
      "detail": "BP 145 mmHg with hypertension — consider intensifying therapy.",
      "source": {
        "label": "HealthInformatics CDS (rule: uncontrolled_htn)"
      },
      "suggestions": [
        {
          "label": "Acknowledge and document"
        }
      ]
    }
  ]
}



Milestone 2 - this is what the EHR renders at the point of care
The following represents exactly what the clinician sees in the EHR interface at the moment of care—how clinical alerts, recommendations, and supporting information are displayed to guide decision-making in real time.

# For each card (alert) in the sample CDS Hooks response, display a summary
icons <- c(info = "\u2139\ufe0f", warning = "\u26a0\ufe0f", critical = "\u26d4")
for (card in sample_response$cards) {
  # Assign an icon based on the card's indicator severity
  icon <- icons[[card$indicator]]
  # Print the icon, severity, and summary of the alert
  cat(sprintf("%s [%s] %s\n", icon, toupper(card$indicator), card$summary))
  # Print the source rule that generated the alert for reference
  cat(sprintf("    source: %s\n\n", card$source$label))
}

⚠️ [WARNING] BP 145 mmHg with hypertension — consider intensifying therapy.
    source: HealthInformatics CDS (rule: uncontrolled_htn)

title: Module 11: Clinical Decision Support Systems
section: 11.6 Alert fatigue - the central usability risk
text:
11.6 Alert fatigue - the central usability risk
The most common failure of Clinical Decision Support (CDS) systems is known as alert fatigue. This occurs when clinicians are repeatedly exposed to a high volume of low-importance alerts—such as minor warnings or informational messages—which leads them to become desensitized. As a result, they may begin to ignore not just the low-value alerts, but also truly critical warnings that require immediate attention, potentially compromising patient safety. In practice, this is reflected by override rates (alerts ignored or dismissed by clinicians) sometimes exceeding 90% in CDS systems that are not carefully optimized. Effective CDS design uses two main strategies to address alert fatigue: 1. Prioritizing by severity: Ensuring that only the most clinically important and relevant alerts are highlighted prominently, while less urgent alerts are shown with lower priority. 2. Suppressing low-value alerts: Filtering out alerts that are unlikely to inform or change clinical decision-making, so as to minimize unnecessary interruptions for clinicians.

library(ggplot2)

# Calculate number of alerts per patient in original alerts table
burden <- alerts %>% count(patient_id, name = "n")
cat(sprintf("Alert burden — mean %.2f, max %d alerts/patient\n", mean(burden$n), max(burden$n)))

Alert burden — mean 1.14, max 2 alerts/patient

# Define a suppression/prioritization policy:
# For each patient, if there is at least one critical alert,
# suppress (i.e., remove) their informational ("info") alerts to prevent overload.
prioritize <- function(alerts) {
  keep <- list()  # This will collect the alerts to keep
  for (pid in unique(alerts$patient_id)) {
    grp <- alerts %>% filter(patient_id == pid)
    # Check if the group for this patient has any critical alerts
    has_critical <- any(grp$severity == "critical")
    for (i in seq_len(nrow(grp))) {
      a <- grp[i, ]
      # If any alert for this patient is critical, skip their "info" alerts
      if (has_critical && a$severity == "info") {
        next  # Skip "info" alerts due to higher-severity present
      }
      keep[[length(keep) + 1]] <- a  # Otherwise, keep the alert
    }
  }
  # Return all retained alerts as a new data frame
  bind_rows(keep)
}

# Apply prioritization strategy to alerts
filtered <- prioritize(alerts)
cat(sprintf("Alerts before: %d  ->  after prioritization: %d (%.0f%% reduction)\n",
            nrow(alerts), nrow(filtered), 100 * (1 - nrow(filtered) / nrow(alerts))))

Alerts before: 58  ->  after prioritization: 56 (3% reduction)

# Plot the total count of each severity level before and after prioritization
order_levels <- c("info", "warning", "critical")
before <- alerts %>% count(severity) %>%
  right_join(tibble(severity = order_levels), by = "severity") %>%
  mutate(n = ifelse(is.na(n), 0, n), stage = "before")
after <- filtered %>% count(severity) %>%
  right_join(tibble(severity = order_levels), by = "severity") %>%
  mutate(n = ifelse(is.na(n), 0, n), stage = "after")
plot_df <- bind_rows(before, after) %>%
  mutate(severity = factor(severity, levels = order_levels),
         stage = factor(stage, levels = c("before", "after")))

ggplot(plot_df, aes(x = severity, y = n, fill = stage)) +
  geom_col(position = position_dodge(width = 0.7), width = 0.6) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c(before = "#4C72B0", after = "#55A868")) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "alerts", fill = NULL, title = "Alert volume before vs after prioritization") +
  theme_minimal()

title: Module 11: Clinical Decision Support Systems
text:
Key takeaways

CDS is governed by the Five Rights; rule-based and model-driven support complement each other.
A clean design makes each rule a function, so the engine scales without churn.
CDS Hooks cards (summary/indicator/detail/source/suggestions) are the standard delivery format inside FHIR-based EHRs.
Alert fatigue is the defining usability failure; prioritization and suppression are essential, not optional.
