title: Module 13: Claims Data Analysis
text:
Health Informatics in R · Part IV: Advanced Topics · Module 13 of 16
Clinical informatics records care. Claims data records payment — the structured bills providers send payers after a visit, stay, or fill. This module treats claims as an informatics data type: what they contain, how they are coded and classified, how to clean them, and how to roll them up into member-level cost, risk, and quality measures.

title: Module 13: Claims Data Analysis
text:
Learning objectives
By the end of this module you will be able to:

Describe a claim (who, what, why, where, how much) and how it differs from an EHR.
Map claim codes to classification systems (ICD-10, CPT, HCC, DRG).
Clean raw claims: duplicates, adjudication status, financial integrity.
Build member-level features: PMPM, HCC risk score, Charlson index, utilization.
Risk-stratify a population and compute a simple care-gap (HEDIS-like) measure.

title: Module 13: Claims Data Analysis
text:
Dataset
A synthetic Medicare Advantage–style book: an eligibility file (members) and a claims file (service-level rows with ICD-10, CPT, place of service, and billed / allowed / paid amounts). We inject duplicate claims and a few dirty values so the cleaning step has something to do. No real patients or payers.

library(dplyr)
library(tibble)
library(ggplot2)

# --- Self-contained synthetic claims generator ---

# Eligibility file + service-level claims for a fake MA-style plan.
make_synthetic_claims <- function(n_members = 400, n_claims = 2400, seed = 42) {
  set.seed(seed)

  # 1. Member eligibility (who is covered, and for how many months)
  members <- tibble(
    member_id = sprintf("M%d", 1000 + 0:(n_members - 1)),
    age = sample(45:89, n_members, replace = TRUE),
    sex = sample(c("male", "female"), n_members, replace = TRUE, prob = c(0.47, 0.53)),
    region = sample(c("Northeast", "Southeast", "Midwest", "West"), n_members, replace = TRUE),
    plan_type = sample(c("HMO", "PPO", "PFFS"), n_members, replace = TRUE, prob = c(0.50, 0.35, 0.15)),
    enroll_months = sample(6:12, n_members, replace = TRUE)
  )
  # Chronic flags with roughly realistic prevalence (used to bias claim codes)
  members$has_diabetes     <- rbinom(n_members, 1, 0.22)
  members$has_chf          <- rbinom(n_members, 1, 0.10)
  members$has_copd         <- rbinom(n_members, 1, 0.12)
  members$has_ckd          <- rbinom(n_members, 1, 0.14)
  members$has_depression   <- rbinom(n_members, 1, 0.16)
  members$has_hypertension <- rbinom(n_members, 1, 0.45)
  members$has_cancer       <- rbinom(n_members, 1, 0.06)

  # Inject a few dirty eligibility values (~4%)
  n_bad <- max(8, n_members %/% 25)
  bad <- sample(seq_len(n_members), n_bad, replace = FALSE)
  half <- length(bad) %/% 2
  members$age[bad[seq_len(half)]] <- NA
  members$sex[bad[(half + 1):length(bad)]] <- "U"

  # 2. Code dictionaries: diagnosis (why) and procedure (what)
  icd <- c(
    "E11.9" = "Type 2 diabetes without complications",
    "I50.32" = "Chronic systolic heart failure",
    "J44.9" = "COPD, unspecified",
    "N18.3" = "CKD stage 3",
    "F32.9" = "Major depressive disorder, unspecified",
    "I10" = "Essential hypertension",
    "Z12.11" = "Encounter for screening for malignant neoplasm of colon",
    "M54.5" = "Low back pain",
    "J06.9" = "Acute upper respiratory infection",
    "Z00.00" = "Encounter for general adult medical examination"
  )
  cpt_desc <- c(
    "99213" = "Office visit, established", "99214" = "Office visit, moderate complexity",
    "99283" = "ED visit, moderate", "99285" = "ED visit, high severity",
    "99232" = "Subsequent hospital care", "93306" = "Echocardiogram",
    "71046" = "Chest X-ray, 2 views", "82947" = "Glucose, quantitative",
    "36415" = "Venipuncture", "27447" = "Total knee arthroplasty"
  )
  cpt_price <- c(
    "99213" = 150, "99214" = 250, "99283" = 1200, "99285" = 2500, "99232" = 180,
    "93306" = 800, "71046" = 300, "82947" = 50, "36415" = 25, "27447" = 15000
  )
  pos <- c("11" = "Office", "21" = "Inpatient hospital",
           "23" = "Emergency room", "22" = "Outpatient hospital", "81" = "Laboratory")

  # Condition -> likely primary ICD (so coded claims track the member flags)
  cond_icd <- c(has_diabetes = "E11.9", has_chf = "I50.32", has_copd = "J44.9",
                has_ckd = "N18.3", has_depression = "F32.9",
                has_hypertension = "I10", has_cancer = "Z12.11")
  icd_keys <- names(icd)
  cpt_keys <- names(cpt_desc)
  pos_keys <- names(pos)

  pick_icd <- function(mid) {
    idx <- match(mid, members$member_id)
    flags <- names(cond_icd)
    active <- flags[vapply(flags, function(f) members[[f]][idx] == 1, logical(1))]
    coded <- unname(cond_icd[active])
    if (length(coded) > 0 && runif(1) < 0.65) {
      return(sample(coded, 1))
    }
    sample(icd_keys, 1)
  }

  # 3. Service-level claims
  member_ids <- sample(members$member_id, n_claims, replace = TRUE)
  cpt_drawn <- sample(cpt_keys, n_claims, replace = TRUE)
  billed <- cpt_price[cpt_drawn] * runif(n_claims, 0.85, 1.40)
  allowed <- billed * runif(n_claims, 0.55, 0.80)
  paid <- allowed * runif(n_claims, 0.70, 0.95)
  start <- as.Date("2023-01-01")
  svc <- start + sample(0:363, n_claims, replace = TRUE)

  claims <- tibble(
    claim_id = sprintf("CLM%06d", seq_len(n_claims)),
    member_id = member_ids,
    service_date = svc,
    icd10_primary = vapply(member_ids, pick_icd, character(1)),
    cpt_code = cpt_drawn,
    place_of_service = sample(pos_keys, n_claims, replace = TRUE, prob = c(0.45, 0.12, 0.12, 0.18, 0.13)),
    billed_amount = round(billed, 2),
    allowed_amount = round(allowed, 2),
    paid_amount = round(paid, 2),
    provider_npi = floor(runif(n_claims, 1000000000, 2000000000)),
    claim_status = sample(c("Paid", "Denied", "Pending"), n_claims, replace = TRUE, prob = c(0.88, 0.08, 0.04))
  )

  # ~72% of diabetic members get at least one glucose test so the HEDIS-like gap is realistic
  dm_ids <- members$member_id[members$has_diabetes == 1]
  for (mid in dm_ids) {
    if (runif(1) < 0.72) {
      hit <- which(claims$member_id == mid)
      if (length(hit)) {
        pickrow <- if (length(hit) == 1) hit else sample(hit, 1)
        claims$cpt_code[pickrow] <- "82947"
      }
    }
  }

  # Inject ~3% duplicate submissions (same member / date / CPT / billed)
  n_dup <- floor(0.03 * n_claims)
  dup_idx <- sample(seq_len(n_claims), n_dup, replace = FALSE)
  claims <- bind_rows(claims, claims[dup_idx, ])

  list(members = members, claims = claims, icd = icd, cpt_desc = cpt_desc, cpt_price = cpt_price, pos = pos)
}

book <- make_synthetic_claims()
members <- book$members
claims <- book$claims
cat(sprintf("Tables: members (%d), claims (%d including duplicates)\n", nrow(members), nrow(claims)))

Tables: members (400), claims (2472 including duplicates)

cat("Date range:", format(min(claims$service_date)), "→", format(max(claims$service_date)), "\n")

Date range: 2023-01-01 → 2023-12-30 

status_counts <- table(claims$claim_status)
cat("Claim statuses:", paste(sprintf("'%s': %d", names(status_counts), as.integer(status_counts)), collapse = ", "), "\n")

Claim statuses: 'Denied': 217, 'Paid': 2154, 'Pending': 101

title: Module 13: Claims Data Analysis
section: 13.1 What claim data is (and is not)
text:
13.1 What claim data is (and is not)
A claim is the structured record a provider submits to a payer (commercial insurer, Medicare, Medicaid) to request reimbursement for services already delivered.
Patient receives care → provider submits a claim → payer adjudicates → claim is recorded







Layer
What it captures




Patient / member
ID, age, sex, geography, eligibility months


Provider
NPI, specialty, facility


Clinical (coded)
ICD-10 why, CPT/HCPCS what, revenue codes


Financial
Billed, allowed, paid, member cost-share


Context
Dates, place of service, claim status (paid / denied / pending)



Claim types. Professional (CMS-1500, office visits), institutional (UB-04, hospital stays), pharmacy (NCPDP), dental.
Why informatics cares. Claims are how ICD and CPT travel through the payment system (Module 3). They are also the main administrative feed into warehouses (Module 14), population programs (Module 12), and risk adjustment.
Limits. Claims are not the medical record. They lack vitals, labs, notes, and often secondary diagnoses. They are billing-driven, lagged (days to months), and sensitive to how providers code. Use them for what was billed and paid, not as a substitute for clinical truth.

title: Module 13: Claims Data Analysis
text:
13.2 Anatomy of a claim line
Each row below is one service line: a coded reason (ICD), a coded service (CPT), a setting (place of service), and three dollar amounts. Payers typically keep paid claims for analytics; denied and pending rows stay in operational queues.

# Peek at a few raw claim lines and decode CPT / POS for readability

title: Module 13: Claims Data Analysis
text:
13.3 Classification tools on claims
Claims do not store “this patient is high risk” as a field. Analysts group raw codes into payment and risk categories. Module 3 introduced the codes; here they become groupers.








Tool
Setting
Job on a claim




ICD-10-CM
All
Diagnosis / reason for visit


CPT / HCPCS
Outpatient / professional
Procedure / service billed


MS-DRG
Inpatient
Bundled hospital payment per stay


HCC
Medicare Advantage
Risk-adjust capitation from diagnoses


CCI / LACE
All
Comorbidity / readmission risk from codes



HCC (Hierarchical Condition Categories) collapse related ICD codes into categories that predict next-year cost. A higher HCC score means a sicker member and, under Medicare Advantage, a higher payment to the plan. The weights below are educational approximations, not the CMS model.

# Educational ICD-10 -> HCC crosswalk (NOT the official CMS-HCC model)
hcc_map <- tibble(
  icd10 = c("E11.9", "I10", "J44.9", "N18.3", "F32.9", "I50.32", "Z12.11", "J06.9"),
  description = c(
    "Type 2 diabetes without complications",
    "Essential hypertension",
    "COPD, unspecified",
    "CKD stage 3",
    "Major depression, unspecified",
    "Chronic systolic HF",
    "Colon cancer screening (no HCC)",
    "Acute URI (acute — usually no HCC)"
  ),
  hcc = c("HCC19", "HCC85", "HCC111", "HCC137", "HCC59", "HCC85", NA, NA),
  weight = c(0.318, 0.302, 0.335, 0.289, 0.309, 0.368, NA, NA)
)
cat("ICD-10 codes on this book's claims, with a toy HCC mapping\n")

title: Module 13: Claims Data Analysis
text:
13.4 Cleaning and validating claims
Production claims are messy: duplicates (resubmits), reversals, mixed adjudication status, missing demographics, and amounts that violate paid ≤ allowed ≤ billed. Analytics almost always start from paid claims after those checks — the same data-quality instinct as Module 8, applied to administrative data.

raw_n <- nrow(claims)

# 1. Drop duplicate submissions (same member, date, CPT, billed amount)
claims_clean <- claims %>%
  distinct(member_id, service_date, cpt_code, billed_amount, .keep_all = TRUE)
cat(sprintf("Duplicates removed: %s\n", format(raw_n - nrow(claims_clean), big.mark = ",")))

Duplicates removed: 72

# 2. Keep paid claims for cost / utilization analytics
claims_clean <- claims_clean %>% filter(claim_status == "Paid")
cat(sprintf("After status filter (Paid only): %s\n", format(nrow(claims_clean), big.mark = ",")))

After status filter (Paid only): 2,089

# 3. Repair eligibility: numeric age, recode unknown sex
members_clean <- members
members_clean$age <- suppressWarnings(as.numeric(members_clean$age))
members_clean$age[is.na(members_clean$age)] <- median(members_clean$age, na.rm = TRUE)
members_clean$age <- as.integer(pmin(pmax(members_clean$age, 0), 110))
members_clean$sex <- ifelse(members_clean$sex == "U", "female", members_clean$sex)

# 4. Financial integrity: paid cannot exceed allowed
over <- claims_clean$paid_amount > claims_clean$allowed_amount
claims_clean$paid_amount[over] <- claims_clean$allowed_amount[over]
cat(sprintf("Paid>allowed rows capped: %s\n", format(sum(over), big.mark = ",")))

Paid>allowed rows capped: 0

claims_clean <- claims_clean %>% filter(paid_amount >= 0)
cat(sprintf("Clean claims: %s | clean members: %s\n",
            format(nrow(claims_clean), big.mark = ","), format(nrow(members_clean), big.mark = ",")))

Clean claims: 2,089 | clean members: 400

title: Module 13: Claims Data Analysis
text:
13.5 Member-level features: PMPM, HCC, utilization
A claim is a transaction. Care management and risk models need a member. We aggregate paid claims to one row per member:







Feature
Meaning




PMPM
Paid amount ÷ enrollment months — the core actuarial unit


HCC score
Age/sex baseline + weights for coded chronic conditions


CCI
Weighted comorbidity count (Charlson-style)


Utilization
ER, inpatient, and office visits from place of service



Normalizing HCC so the book average is 1.0 is how plans talk about “sicker than average” (score > 1) versus “healthier” (score < 1).

# Join paid claims to eligibility, then roll up to the member
df <- claims_clean %>% left_join(members_clean, by = "member_id")

member_feat <- df %>%
  group_by(member_id) %>%
  summarize(
    total_paid = sum(paid_amount),
    n_claims = n(),
    n_icd = n_distinct(icd10_primary),
    n_providers = n_distinct(provider_npi),
    er_visits = sum(place_of_service == "23"),
    ip_visits = sum(place_of_service == "21"),
    office_visits = sum(place_of_service == "11"),
    .groups = "drop"
  )

member_feat <- member_feat %>% left_join(members_clean, by = "member_id")
member_feat$enroll_months <- pmax(member_feat$enroll_months, 1)
member_feat$pmpm <- round(member_feat$total_paid / member_feat$enroll_months, 2)

# Toy HCC: age/sex factor + condition weights (educational, not CMS)
hcc_w <- c(has_diabetes = 0.318, has_chf = 0.368, has_copd = 0.335,
           has_ckd = 0.289, has_depression = 0.309, has_hypertension = 0.118,
           has_cancer = 0.450)

age_sex_factor <- function(age, sex) {
  base <- 0.28 + age * 0.007
  if (sex == "female" && age >= 65) base <- base + 0.04
  round(base, 3)
}

member_feat$age_sex <- mapply(age_sex_factor, member_feat$age, member_feat$sex)
member_feat$hcc_raw <- round(
  member_feat$age_sex + Reduce(`+`, lapply(names(hcc_w), function(c) member_feat[[c]] * hcc_w[[c]])),
  3
)
member_feat$hcc <- round(member_feat$hcc_raw / mean(member_feat$hcc_raw), 3)

# Simplified Charlson weights on the same flags
cci_w <- c(has_diabetes = 1, has_chf = 1, has_copd = 1, has_ckd = 2, has_cancer = 2)
member_feat$cci <- Reduce(`+`, lapply(names(cci_w), function(c) member_feat[[c]] * cci_w[[c]]))
cond_cols <- names(hcc_w)
member_feat$n_chronic <- rowSums(member_feat[, cond_cols])

cat(sprintf("Members with claims: %s\n", format(nrow(member_feat), big.mark = ",")))

Members with claims: 397

cat(sprintf("Mean PMPM: $%s\n", formatC(mean(member_feat$pmpm), format = "f", digits = 2, big.mark = ",")))

Mean PMPM: $807.96

cat(sprintf("Mean HCC (normalized): %.3f  (1.0 = book average)\n", mean(member_feat$hcc)))

Mean HCC (normalized): 1.000  (1.0 = book average)

cat(sprintf("Mean CCI: %.2f\n", mean(member_feat$cci)))

Mean CCI: 0.95

cat(sprintf("Total ER visits: %s\n", format(sum(member_feat$er_visits), big.mark = ",")))

Total ER visits: 264

print(as.data.frame(head(member_feat[, c("member_id", "age", "pmpm", "hcc", "cci", "n_chronic")])), row.names = FALSE)

     M1001  45 2719.05 0.930   0         2

     M1003  54 1369.09 0.706   0         1
     M1004  80  380.86 0.801   0         0
     M1005  62  396.07 1.020   2         2



Milestone 1 — risk stratification
Care programs do not treat every member the same. A simple rule engine combines HCC, inpatient use, and ER use into four tiers — the same pattern as the CDS rule engine in Module 11, now at population scale.








Tier
Rule of thumb
Typical action




4 Critical
HCC ≥ 1.8 or IP ≥ 3 or ER ≥ 4
Intensive case management


3 High
HCC ≥ 1.2 or IP ≥ 1 or ER ≥ 2
Care-manager outreach


2 Rising
HCC ≥ 0.9 or 2+ chronic conditions
Prevention / coaching


1 Low
Everyone else
Wellness




assign_tier <- function(hcc, er, ip, n_chronic) {
  if (hcc >= 1.8 || ip >= 3 || er >= 4) return("4 - Critical")
  if (hcc >= 1.2 || ip >= 1 || er >= 2) return("3 - High")
  if (hcc >= 0.9 || n_chronic >= 2) return("2 - Rising")
  "1 - Low"
}
member_feat$risk_tier <- mapply(assign_tier, member_feat$hcc, member_feat$er_visits,
                                 member_feat$ip_visits, member_feat$n_chronic)

# Disease registries from the same flags (claims-derived cohorts)
member_feat$registry_diabetes <- member_feat$has_diabetes == 1
member_feat$registry_chf <- member_feat$has_chf == 1
member_feat$registry_copd <- member_feat$has_copd == 1

tier <- member_feat %>%
  group_by(risk_tier) %>%
  summarize(members = n(), total_paid = sum(total_paid), mean_pmpm = mean(pmpm), .groups = "drop")
tier$cost_share_pct <- round(tier$total_paid / sum(tier$total_paid) * 100, 1)
cat("Risk-tier distribution\n")

Risk-tier distribution

print(as.data.frame(tier), row.names = FALSE)

    risk_tier members total_paid mean_pmpm cost_share_pct

     3 - High     257  1911893.5  840.6679           68.4

cat(sprintf("\nRegistries: diabetes %d | CHF %d | COPD %d\n",
            sum(member_feat$registry_diabetes), sum(member_feat$registry_chf), sum(member_feat$registry_copd)))


Registries: diabetes 96 | CHF 34 | COPD 53



order_tiers <- c("1 - Low", "2 - Rising", "3 - High", "4 - Critical")
colors <- c("1 - Low" = "#55A868", "2 - Rising" = "#4C72B0",
            "3 - High" = "#DD8452", "4 - Critical" = "#C44E52")

counts_df <- tibble(risk_tier = factor(order_tiers, levels = rev(order_tiers)))
counts_df$members <- sapply(as.character(counts_df$risk_tier), function(t) sum(member_feat$risk_tier == t))

# Panel 1: members by risk tier
ggplot(counts_df, aes(x = members, y = risk_tier, fill = risk_tier)) +
  geom_col() +
  scale_fill_manual(values = colors, guide = "none") +
  labs(x = "members", y = NULL, title = "Members by risk tier") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 11)







Figure 1






# Panel 2: share of paid amount by risk tier
paid_df <- member_feat %>%
  group_by(risk_tier) %>%
  summarize(total_paid = sum(total_paid), .groups = "drop") %>%
  right_join(tibble(risk_tier = order_tiers), by = "risk_tier") %>%
  mutate(total_paid = ifelse(is.na(total_paid), 0, total_paid),
         risk_tier = factor(risk_tier, levels = order_tiers))
paid_df$pct <- paid_df$total_paid / sum(paid_df$total_paid) * 100
paid_df$label <- sprintf("%.0f%%", paid_df$pct)

ggplot(paid_df, aes(x = "", y = total_paid, fill = risk_tier)) +
  geom_col(width = 1, color = "white") +
  coord_polar(theta = "y") +
  scale_fill_manual(values = colors, name = NULL) +
  geom_text(aes(label = label), position = position_stack(vjust = 0.5), size = 3.2) +
  labs(title = "Share of paid amount", x = NULL, y = NULL) +
  theme_void(base_size = 11)







Figure 2

title: Module 13: Claims Data Analysis
text:
13.6 Quality measures and care gaps (HEDIS-like)
HEDIS-style measures ask: of the members who should have received a service, what share did? Numerators and denominators are built from claims (and sometimes pharmacy or labs). Members in the denominator but not the numerator are a care gap — an outreach list.
Here the denominator is members with diabetes on file; the numerator is those with at least one glucose test (CPT 82947) in the year — a simplified stand-in for HbA1c testing, not a certified HEDIS engine.

# Denominator: members flagged with diabetes
diabetics <- unique(member_feat$member_id[member_feat$has_diabetes == 1])

# Numerator: at least one glucose test billed in the year
tested <- unique(claims_clean$member_id[claims_clean$cpt_code == "82947"])
tested_diabetics <- intersect(diabetics, tested)

rate <- if (length(diabetics) > 0) length(tested_diabetics) / length(diabetics) else NA_real_
benchmark <- 0.80  # illustrative national-style target, not a real HEDIS rate
gap <- rate - benchmark

cat(sprintf("Diabetes denominator: %d\n", length(diabetics)))

Diabetes denominator: 96

cat(sprintf("With ≥1 glucose test (CPT 82947): %d\n", length(tested_diabetics)))

With ≥1 glucose test (CPT 82947): 76

cat(sprintf("Testing rate: %.1f%%  |  benchmark: %.0f%%  |  gap: %+.1f%%\n", rate * 100, benchmark * 100, gap * 100))

Testing rate: 79.2%  |  benchmark: 80%  |  gap: -0.8%

care_gap <- member_feat %>%
  filter(member_id %in% setdiff(diabetics, tested)) %>%
  select(member_id, age, pmpm, hcc, risk_tier) %>%
  arrange(desc(pmpm))

cat(sprintf("\nCare gap: %d diabetic members with no glucose test on file\n", nrow(care_gap)))


Care gap: 20 diabetic members with no glucose test on file

cat("Highest-PMPM gaps (outreach priority):\n")

Highest-PMPM gaps (outreach priority):

print(as.data.frame(head(care_gap, 8)), row.names = FALSE)

     M1287  55 3410.06 1.002 2 - Rising

     M1080  49 2383.68 0.856    1 - Low
     M1101  73 2012.65 1.153   3 - High
     M1298  88 1699.21 1.547   3 - High
     M1216  85 1609.08 1.086   3 - High
     M1348  88 1477.80 1.727   3 - High



# Visual: plan rate vs an illustrative benchmark
plotdf <- tibble(
  group = factor(c("Plan (claims)", "Benchmark"), levels = c("Plan (claims)", "Benchmark")),
  value = c(rate * 100, benchmark * 100)
)
ggplot(plotdf, aes(x = group, y = value, fill = group)) +
  geom_col(width = 0.45) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = benchmark * 100, color = "#C44E52", linetype = "dashed", linewidth = 0.8) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c("Plan (claims)" = "#4C72B0", "Benchmark" = "#8C8C8C"), guide = "none") +
  ylim(0, 100) +

       title = "HEDIS-like: glucose testing among members with diabetes") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 11)

title: Module 13: Claims Data Analysis
text:
13.7 Claims next to the EHR
Claims and EHR data answer different questions. Informatics pipelines often join them (eligibility + claims + clinical) inside a warehouse — the subject of the next module.









Claims
EHR




Unit
Billable service
Clinical encounter / observation


Strength
Complete for billed care; cost; population coverage
Vitals, labs, notes, orders


Weakness
Billing-driven, lagged, thin clinically
Incomplete across sites; not built for payment


Typical use
PMPM, HCC, HEDIS, fraud, network
CDS, quality of documented care, phenotyping



The data-scientist workflow on a claims book is: acquire → clean → feature (PMPM, HCC, CCI) → classify / risk-stratify → quality gaps → action. This module ran the middle of that pipeline on synthetic data. Production work adds 837/835 EDI, pharmacy claims, official groupers, and actuarial sign-off.

title: Module 13: Claims Data Analysis
text:
Exercises

Recompute PMPM using allowed amount instead of paid. How much does the book average move, and why would a plan care?
Build an age-banded table of mean HCC and mean PMPM (a standard actuarial cut). Does cost rise smoothly with age in this synthetic book?
Define a second care gap — e.g. members with hypertension (I10) and no office visit (POS 11) — and list the highest-PMPM members in the gap.

title: Module 13: Claims Data Analysis
text:
Key takeaways

Claims are the financial/administrative backbone of US healthcare, not a substitute for the EHR.
ICD, CPT, HCC, DRG are how a bill becomes a comparable, groupable record.
Analytics run on cleaned paid claims rolled up to the member-month.
PMPM + HCC + utilization feed risk tiers, registries, and HEDIS-like gaps.


Next: Module 14 - Clinical Data Warehousing and Analytics-Ready Data.

title: Module 15: Interoperability at Scale and Bulk Data
text:
Health Informatics in R · Part IV: Advanced Topics · Module 15 of 16
Module 5’s FHIR search retrieves one patient at a time — fine for an app, hopeless for population analytics across millions of records. This module covers FHIR Bulk Data (Flat FHIR), the asynchronous export pattern, the NDJSON format it produces, and the network layer: HIEs and TEFCA.

title: Module 15: Interoperability at Scale and Bulk Data
text:
Learning objectives
By the end of this module you will be able to:

Explain why bulk export exists and how it differs from per-resource search.
Describe the asynchronous kickoff → poll → download Bulk Data flow.
Produce and parse NDJSON (newline-delimited JSON), the bulk export format.
Reassemble bulk NDJSON back into analytics tables.
Place HIEs, QHINs, and TEFCA in the national interoperability picture.

title: Module 15: Interoperability at Scale and Bulk Data
text:
Dataset
We convert the synthetic EHR into FHIR NDJSON exactly as a $export would emit it, then parse it back — simulating both ends of a bulk data exchange locally.

library(dplyr)
library(tibble)
library(jsonlite)

# --- Self-contained synthetic EHR generator (identical to earlier parts) ---

# This function synthesizes a realistic EHR (Electronic Health Record) dataset.
make_synthetic_ehr <- function(n_patients = 200, seed = 42) {
  # Use a fixed seed for reproducibility.
  set.seed(seed)
  # Define pools of first and last names.
  first <- c("Ava","Liam","Noah","Mia","Zoe","Omar","Ivan","Sara","Leo","Nina",
             "Ruth","Kai","Yara","Theo","Ida","Sam","Ana","Eli","Rex","Uma")
  last  <- c("Khan","Ortiz","Chen","Diaz","Patel","Ali","Brown","Nash","Reed","Vega",
             "Cole","Frost","Grant","Hale","Iqbal","Jain","Kerr","Lund","Mora","Park")
  # Randomly assign demographic details to each patient.
  ages <- sample(18:89, n_patients, replace = TRUE)
  patients <- tibble(
    patient_id = sprintf("P%d", 1000 + 0:(n_patients - 1)),   # Unique patient IDs
    given_name = sample(first, n_patients, replace = TRUE),   # Given names
    family_name = sample(last, n_patients, replace = TRUE),   # Family (last) names
    sex = sample(c("male", "female"), n_patients, replace = TRUE, prob = c(0.49, 0.51)),  # Biological sex
    age = ages,                                                 # Age in years
    birth_year = 2026 - ages                                    # Calculated birth year (anchor to year 2026)
  )
  # Generate encounter ("visit") events for each patient.
  enc_types <- c("ambulatory", "emergency", "inpatient", "wellness")
  enc_rows <- vector("list", n_patients)
  eid <- 0
  for (i in seq_len(n_patients)) {
    pid <- patients$patient_id[i]
    n_enc <- sample(1:4, 1)  # Each patient has 1-4 encounters
    day <- sample(0:(365 * 3 - 1), n_enc, replace = TRUE)  # Encounter within a 3-year range
    ids <- sprintf("E%05d", eid + seq_len(n_enc))
    eid <- eid + n_enc
    enc_rows[[i]] <- tibble(
      encounter_id = ids, patient_id = pid,
      encounter_type = sample(enc_types, n_enc, replace = TRUE, prob = c(0.55, 0.15, 0.10, 0.20)),  # Most visits are ambulatory
      date = as.Date("2023-01-01") + day  # Random date
    )
  }
  encounters <- bind_rows(enc_rows)
  # Define common observations (vital signs, labs) and synthesize them for encounters.
  obs_defs <- tribble(
    ~observation,               ~unit,   ~lo,  ~hi,
    "Body height",               "cm",    150,  195,
    "Body weight",                "kg",    50,   110,
    "Systolic blood pressure",   "mmHg",  100,  165,
    "Heart rate",                 "/min",  55,   100,
    "Hemoglobin A1c",             "%",     4.8,  9.5
  )
  obs_rows <- vector("list", nrow(encounters))
  for (i in seq_len(nrow(encounters))) {
    e <- encounters[i, ]
    keep <- runif(nrow(obs_defs)) < 0.7  # 70% chance of having each observation per encounter
    if (any(keep)) {
      d <- obs_defs[keep, ]
      obs_rows[[i]] <- tibble(
        encounter_id = e$encounter_id, patient_id = e$patient_id,
        observation = d$observation, value = round(runif(nrow(d), d$lo, d$hi), 1),
        unit = d$unit, date = e$date
      )
    }
  }
  observations <- bind_rows(obs_rows) %>%
    mutate(observation_id = sprintf("O%06d", row_number())) %>%
    relocate(observation_id)
  # Assign up to 3 random conditions (problems/diagnoses) to each patient.
  cond_pool <- c("Essential hypertension", "Type 2 diabetes mellitus", "Asthma",
                 "Acute bronchitis", "Major depressive disorder", "Osteoarthritis",
                 "Chronic kidney disease", "Anemia")
  cond_rows <- vector("list", n_patients)
  for (i in seq_len(n_patients)) {
    pid <- patients$patient_id[i]
    n_c <- sample(0:3, 1)
    if (n_c > 0) cond_rows[[i]] <- tibble(patient_id = pid, condition = sample(cond_pool, n_c, replace = FALSE))
  }
  conditions <- bind_rows(cond_rows) %>%
    mutate(condition_id = sprintf("C%05d", row_number())) %>%
    relocate(condition_id)
  # Assign up to 3 random medications to each patient.
  med_pool <- c("Lisinopril", "Metformin", "Albuterol", "Atorvastatin", "Sertraline",
                "Amoxicillin", "Ibuprofen", "Hydrochlorothiazide")
  med_rows <- vector("list", n_patients)
  for (i in seq_len(n_patients)) {
    pid <- patients$patient_id[i]
    n_m <- sample(0:3, 1)
    if (n_m > 0) med_rows[[i]] <- tibble(patient_id = pid, medication = sample(med_pool, n_m, replace = FALSE))
  }
  medications <- bind_rows(med_rows) %>%
    mutate(medication_id = sprintf("M%05d", row_number())) %>%
    relocate(medication_id)
  # Return the synthetic tables as a list keyed by resource type.
  list(patients = patients, encounters = encounters, observations = observations,
       conditions = conditions, medications = medications)
}

# Generate the synthetic EHR dataset (all tables).
ehr <- make_synthetic_ehr()
# Print table names and their respective row counts.
cat("Tables:", paste(sprintf("%s (%d)", names(ehr), sapply(ehr, nrow)), collapse = ", "), "\n")

Tables: patients (200), encounters (507), observations (1746), conditions (302), medications (313)

title: Module 15: Interoperability at Scale and Bulk Data
text:
15.1 Why bulk data
Using per-resource REST (such as GET /Patient/123) is highly inefficient for retrieving data about many individuals: pulling a large patient population could require millions of repeated API calls, which is slow and places heavy load on the server.
To solve this, FHIR Bulk Data (also known as Flat FHIR) allows exporting entire resource types in a single operation. The server packages data—such as all Patient records, Observations, or Conditions—into compressed NDJSON (newline-delimited JSON) files. Each line in these files is a single resource, making them easy to process in parallel or with big data tools.
This capability is foundational for scenarios like population health analysis, clinical quality reporting, and large-scale payer–provider data exchanges, where working with an entire cohort is necessary rather than accessing records one at a time.

title: Module 15: Interoperability at Scale and Bulk Data
text:
15.2 The asynchronous export flow
Bulk export in FHIR is designed to be asynchronous because exporting large datasets can be resource-intensive and time-consuming, often taking several minutes or more. Rather than tying up server resources and leaving the client waiting for a response, an asynchronous workflow allows efficient handling for both client and server. Here’s how the asynchronous export flow works in detail:

Kickoff — The client initiates the export by making a request such as GET [base]/$export, and includes the Prefer: respond-async HTTP header. This header signals to the server that the client is willing to receive an asynchronous response.
Poll for Status — Instead of immediately returning the full response, the server replies with a 202 Accepted status and provides a content-location header containing the URL where the client can check on the progress of the export job.
Completion and Manifest — The client periodically polls the content-location endpoint. Once the job has finished, the server responds with a manifest JSON document describing the output. This manifest lists URLs to one or more NDJSON files, typically one file per resource type (e.g., one for all Patient records, one for Observations, etc.).
Download NDJSON Files — The client then downloads the bulk data by retrieving the NDJSON files from the provided URLs. These files contain the exported data, with each line representing a single resource instance as a JSON object.

In this notebook, we simulate the manifest that a server would return at the completion of a bulk data export job.

# This code simulates a FHIR Bulk Data (Flat FHIR) export manifest,
# which is the response a client receives from the server when a bulk
# data export job completes. The manifest describes the exported data files.

# The manifest is a list containing:
#  - "transactionTime": When the export was completed.
#  - "request": The URL used to initiate the export job.
#  - "requiresAccessToken": Whether the result URLs require authentication.
#  - "output": A list of exported resource files, each specifying:
#       - the resource "type" (e.g., Patient, Observation, Condition)
#       - and the downloadable "url" for each NDJSON file.
#  - "error": Any errors (empty in this simulated manifest).

manifest <- list(
  transactionTime = "2026-08-20T00:00:00Z",
  request = "https://ehr.example/fhir/$export",
  requiresAccessToken = TRUE,
  output = list(
    list(type = "Patient", url = "https://ehr.example/bulk/Patient.ndjson"),
    list(type = "Observation", url = "https://ehr.example/bulk/Observation.ndjson"),
    list(type = "Condition", url = "https://ehr.example/bulk/Condition.ndjson")
  ),
  error = list()
)

# Display the manifest in a readable JSON format
cat("Bulk export manifest (returned when the async job completes):\n")

Bulk export manifest (returned when the async job completes):

cat(toJSON(manifest, auto_unbox = TRUE, pretty = TRUE))

{
  "transactionTime": "2026-08-20T00:00:00Z",
  "request": "https://ehr.example/fhir/$export",
  "requiresAccessToken": true,
  "output": [
    {
      "type": "Patient",
      "url": "https://ehr.example/bulk/Patient.ndjson"
    },
    {
      "type": "Observation",
      "url": "https://ehr.example/bulk/Observation.ndjson"
    },
    {
      "type": "Condition",
      "url": "https://ehr.example/bulk/Condition.ndjson"
    }
  ],
  "error": []
}

title: Module 15: Interoperability at Scale and Bulk Data
text:
15.3 Producing NDJSON
NDJSON stands for Newline Delimited JSON, a format where each line in a text file is a separate JSON object, with no enclosing array or commas between records. This approach has several advantages for large-scale data handling: - Efficient Streaming: Clients and servers can read and write data one object at a time without needing to load the entire file into memory. - Easy Sharding and Parallelism: Files can be split and processed in chunks by simply dividing on newline characters. - Append-friendly: New records can easily be appended as new lines. For these reasons, FHIR bulk export utilizes NDJSON files to export large collections of resources efficiently. In the next cell, we demonstrate how to output FHIR Patient resources using the NDJSON format, with each patient represented as a separate line.

# Select the "patients" table from the synthetic EHR dataset.
patients <- ehr$patients

# Define a function to convert each row of the tibble
# into a FHIR-compliant Patient resource (nested list).
to_fhir_patient <- function(row) {
  list(
    resourceType = "Patient",
    id = row$patient_id,
    name = list(list(
      family = row$family_name,   # Last name
      given = list(row$given_name)  # First name as a list
    )),
    gender = row$sex,             # HL7/FHIR uses 'gender' field
    birthDate = sprintf("%d-01-01", row$birth_year)  # Use only the year for privacy
  )
}

# Take the first 200 patients. For each, serialize the FHIR resource
# as a JSON string (one per line), following NDJSON format.
n_take <- min(200, nrow(patients))
ndjson_lines <- vapply(seq_len(n_take), function(i) {
  toJSON(to_fhir_patient(patients[i, ]), auto_unbox = TRUE)
}, character(1))

# Join lines together with newline characters to form the NDJSON document.
patient_ndjson <- paste(ndjson_lines, collapse = "\n")

# Display the first 3 NDJSON lines to show the format, and summary stats.
cat("Patient.ndjson — first 3 lines:\n")

Patient.ndjson — first 3 lines:

for (line in head(ndjson_lines, 3)) cat(line, "\n")

{"resourceType":"Patient","id":"P1000","name":[{"family":"Grant","given":["Rex"]}],"gender":"male","birthDate":"1960-01-01"} 
{"resourceType":"Patient","id":"P1001","name":[{"family":"Grant","given":["Mia"]}],"gender":"male","birthDate":"1944-01-01"} 
{"resourceType":"Patient","id":"P1002","name":[{"family":"Nash","given":["Nina"]}],"gender":"female","birthDate":"1984-01-01"} 

cat(sprintf("...\n%d total resources, %d bytes\n", length(ndjson_lines), nchar(patient_ndjson)))

...
200 total resources, 25166 bytes



Milestone 1 - parse NDJSON back into a table
In this milestone, we’ll demonstrate how to read a bulk FHIR NDJSON file, where each line is a JSON-encoded resource—and convert it back into a tabular data frame. This allows us to round-trip structured FHIR data: exporting it using the NDJSON standard, and then parsing it back for analysis or visualization in R.

# Define a function that takes NDJSON text (each line a JSON-encoded Patient resource)
# and parses it back into a tibble for further analysis or visualization.
parse_patient_ndjson <- function(text) {
  # Split the text into lines, strip whitespace, and process each line
  lines <- strsplit(trimws(text), "\n")[[1]]
  rows <- lapply(lines, function(line) {
    # Each line is a JSON string representing a FHIR Patient resource
    r <- fromJSON(line, simplifyVector = FALSE)
    # Extract fields of interest from the FHIR structure and save as a tibble row
    tibble(
      id = r$id,
      family = r$name[[1]]$family,      # Family name (last name)
      given = r$name[[1]]$given[[1]],   # First given name
      gender = r$gender,                # Gender field
      birthDate = r$birthDate           # Birth date
    )
  })
  # Return as a tibble for easy manipulation
  bind_rows(rows)
}

# Parse the NDJSON (bulk exported) patient data back into a tibble
parsed <- parse_patient_ndjson(patient_ndjson)

# Display a preview of the round-tripped table and report how many patients were parsed
cat("Round-tripped NDJSON -> DataFrame:\n")

Round-tripped NDJSON -> DataFrame:

print(as.data.frame(head(parsed)), row.names = FALSE)

    id family given gender  birthDate
 P1000  Grant   Rex   male 1960-01-01
 P1001  Grant   Mia   male 1944-01-01
 P1002   Nash  Nina female 1984-01-01
 P1003  Grant   Ana   male 1991-01-01
 P1004    Ali   Kai   male 1960-01-01
 P1005    Ali  Omar female 1962-01-01

cat(sprintf("\nParsed %d patients back from bulk NDJSON.\n", nrow(parsed)))


Parsed 200 patients back from bulk NDJSON.




Milestone 2 - a mini end-to-end bulk client
This section demonstrates a miniature, end-to-end “bulk client” for FHIR data, showing how to handle downloading, parsing, and performing population-level queries across large sets of simulated bulk export files.

# --- Explanation of Code for Bulk FHIR Observation Export and Bulk Query ---

# 1. Emit Observations as NDJSON.
# We take the 'observations' table from our simulated EHR data.
obs <- ehr$observations

# 2. Define key LOINC codes for common observation types.
# LOINC codes standardize lab/measurement concepts in FHIR.
LOINC <- c(
  "Hemoglobin A1c" = "4548-4",
  "Systolic blood pressure" = "8480-6",
  "Heart rate" = "8867-4",
  "Body weight" = "29463-7",
  "Body height" = "8302-2"
)

# 3. Serialize each Observation into a line of NDJSON.
# Each line is a FHIR Observation resource in JSON, representing a different clinical measurement.
to_fhir_observation <- function(o) {
  list(
    resourceType = "Observation",
    status = "final",
    code = list(coding = list(list(
      system = "http://loinc.org",
      code = unname(LOINC[o$observation]),
      display = o$observation
    ))),
    subject = list(reference = sprintf("Patient/%s", o$patient_id)),
    valueQuantity = list(value = o$value, unit = o$unit)
  )
}

obs_ndjson <- paste(
  vapply(seq_len(nrow(obs)), function(i) toJSON(to_fhir_observation(obs[i, ]), auto_unbox = TRUE), character(1)),
  collapse = "\n"
)

# 4. Simulate Bulk Download
bulk_download <- function(manifest_output, local_files) {
  # Given a manifest describing bulk export files, look up each corresponding
  # NDJSON string in 'local_files', parse each line as JSON, and
  # collect them under their FHIR resource type.
  tables <- list()
  for (entry in manifest_output) {
    text <- local_files[[entry$type]]
    if (!is.null(text)) {
      # Split NDJSON into a list of JSON objects:
      lines <- strsplit(trimws(text), "\n")[[1]]
      tables[[entry$type]] <- lapply(lines, function(l) fromJSON(l, simplifyVector = FALSE))
    }
  }
  tables
}

# 5. Prepare the 'local' exports (Patient and Observation), representing files you might download in bulk.
local_files <- list(Patient = patient_ndjson, Observation = obs_ndjson)

# 6. Run the simulated bulk download process,
# which will fetch and parse the NDJSON back into R objects by type.
downloaded <- bulk_download(manifest$output, local_files)

# Show counts for each resource type downloaded.
cat("Downloaded resource counts:",
    paste(sprintf("%s: %d", names(downloaded), sapply(downloaded, length)), collapse = ", "), "\n")

Downloaded resource counts: Patient: 200, Observation: 1746 

# 7. Perform a population-level query: compute the mean Hemoglobin A1c value.
# This emulates an analytic use-case enabled by bulk export.
a1c_vals <- vapply(downloaded$Observation, function(o) {
  if (o$code$coding[[1]]$code == "4548-4") o$valueQuantity$value else NA_real_  # LOINC for HbA1c
}, numeric(1))
a1c_vals <- a1c_vals[!is.na(a1c_vals)]
cat(sprintf("Population mean A1c from bulk export: %.2f %% (n=%d)\n", mean(a1c_vals), length(a1c_vals)))

Population mean A1c from bulk export: 7.08 % (n=345)

title: Module 15: Interoperability at Scale and Bulk Data
section: 15.4 The network layer: HIEs, QHINs, and TEFCA
text:
15.4 The network layer: HIEs, QHINs, and TEFCA
While bulk data export helps move large volumes of health data within a single organization, exchanging data across organizations requires a more advanced network infrastructure. Here are the main components enabling such nationwide interoperability in the U.S.:

HIE (Health Information Exchange): These are typically regional networks that facilitate the sharing of clinical data (such as lab results, encounters, and medications) among multiple healthcare providers, hospitals, and health systems. HIEs help reduce duplication, improve care coordination, and enable providers to access patient information regardless of where care was delivered.
TEFCA (Trusted Exchange Framework and Common Agreement): TEFCA is a federal initiative designed to standardize the rules and technical requirements for health information exchange across the entire country. It provides a “network of networks” by creating a shared trust framework, data sharing policies, and technical standards, ensuring that all participants can rely on common ground rules and interoperability.
QHIN (Qualified Health Information Network): QHINs are large, certified networks that connect directly to TEFCA. They serve as hubs that link together different HIEs, health systems, payers, and other qualified entities. Once connected, a data request made in one region or network can securely reach and retrieve data from other regions through the mesh created by these QHINs.

Direction of travel: With the adoption of modern standards like FHIR and the national trust framework of TEFCA, exchanging health information across the U.S. is moving from custom-built solutions to standardized, routine interoperability at scale.

title: Module 15: Interoperability at Scale and Bulk Data
text:
Key takeaways

Bulk Data / Flat FHIR exports whole populations as NDJSON, unlike chatty per-resource search.
The flow is async: kickoff → poll → manifest → download.
NDJSON streams and shards; parsing it back yields analytics tables.
HIEs, QHINs, and TEFCA carry exchange across organizations nationwide.
